News.title: Treasure hunters strike gold after finding three Bronze Age bracelets worth over £300k during metal detecting rally
News.content:
FILTHY RICH Treasure hunters strike gold after finding three Bronze Age bracelets worth over £300k during metal detecting rally

TWO treasure hunters struck gold after finding three Bronze Age bracelets worth over £300,000 during a metal detecting rally.

Alan Daniels, 48, and Andy Crammond, 34, from Kilwinning, Ayrshire, found the impressive 3,000-year-old goods in an empty farmer’s field.



During an organised detecting rally in May, the pair unearthed a bracelet a few inches under recently-ploughed soil, which Andy joked almost gave him a heart attack.

It was in pristine condition, despite having been buried under mud for thousands of years.



Alan continued searching the area in Blackford, near Carlisle, and discovered the second torc a few minutes later.

At that point they alerted an event marshal and the field was roped off to allow the detecting duo to carry on searching when they found the third bracelet about 20ft away from the other two.

Alan said: “I think they have been struck by the blade of a plough which has brought them towards the surface,

“Gold doesn’t tarnish at all and they came out of the ground just the same as when they went in over 3,000 years ago.”



The torcs have been dated to around 1100BC and are at least 22 carat gold with a combined weight of 518 grammes.

They would have belonged to a high status, wealthy landowner who either buried them as an offering to the gods for a good harvest or hid them as he thought his settlement was about to be raided.

Andy, a gas engineer, said: “Detectorists dream of these things and that is how it still feels, like a dream.



“I’m waiting for someone to come out of the woodwork and say they aren’t real. It is the find of multiple lifetimes.”

The three torcs are now with the British Museum which is assessing them, with a coroner to rule if they are treasure or finders keepers.

If they are treasure then a museum or institution will be given the opportunity to buy them for the nation at their market value, with Alan and Andy getting a share of the proceeds.

If nobody wants them they will be returned to the finders to sell at auction and the duo will have to split the proceeds with the landowner.

Alan said: “We have been detecting together now for a few years. We don’t do it for the money, we go for the social side of it.



“We have never found anything valuable before and always come home disappointed – until now!

“It was a last minute decision for us to go, I thought it would be a waste of time.

“After about two hours all we had found were some bits of aluminium cans.

“We changed fields and there were a few people scattered around in the new field but they hadn’t found anything.

“I went off in one direction and Andy in the other. After a short while I saw the figure of Andy out of the corner of my eye walking towards me.



“He had his hands clasped together in front of him and said ‘I think I’m going to have a heart attack’.

“He opened his hands and I recognised what it was straight away.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The British Museum is expected to produce a report on the torcs in the next few months before a valuation committee will determine their worth.

In 2024 thieves stole a similar Bronze Age gold torc from the Ely Museum in Cambridgeshire. It was valued at £220,000.

News.title: Makeshift ‘shank’, bloodthirsty stab ‘threats’ & boiling water ‘attack’ – Southport killer’s terrifying reign in prison
News.content:
LOCKED in his cell at one of Britain’s highest security prisons, Southport monster Axel Rudakubana had not lost his thirst for violence.

For staff working in Belmarsh, every interaction with the killer was fraught with danger – not least because of his vows to allegedly “stab them up” whenever they entered his cell.



Most terrifying of all is that his threats may have been far from empty.

The child murderer was allegedly found with a makeshift “shank” and put a guard in hospital after allegedly hurling boiling water at them during his terrifying spell behind bars at the Category A jail in South East London.

Rudakubana has now been charged with a string of assaults and is due to appear in court next month. He is currently serving a 52-year sentence for the murder of Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, Bebe King, six, and Elsie-Dot Stancombe, seven, at the Taylor Swift-themed class in Southport in July 2024.



But evil child killer Rudakubana will not be phased by the latest charges, according to a source.

They said: “It is right that he has been charged over incidents at Belmarsh – but in reality this means nothing to him.

“He was accused of threatening to attack staff numerous times and saying things like, ‘I’m going to stab you up when you open my door’.

“And he was a known ‘spitter’ which is classed as an assault in jail – that was one of the things he did.

“But Rudakubana is serving a 52-year sentence and is never coming out so a short sentence for attacking a guard won’t have a huge impact on him.



“All the offences took place inside the prison so would be on CCTV and if he is convicted a concurrent sentence would be quite likely.”

Rudakubana has been specifically charged with two counts of assault, one of attempted GBH and one of possession of an offensive weapon.

The attempted GBH charge is linked to the attack where he allegedly poured scalding water over an officer after boiling a kettle in his cell last May.

We revealed that incident – on May 8, 2025 – the day after it happened.

Rudakubana, 19, is also accused of assaulting an emergency worker two days earlier – May 6 – and possession of an offensive weapon found last June.



He has been charged with a further assault on an emergency worker last October.

The Sun understands that charge relates to him spitting at prison officers – something he was known for in Belmarsh.

The fiend was charged with the four offences days after being moved to Broadmoor Hospital, Berkshire, where he will be treated as a patient.

The source added: “But the timing of this is pretty questionable.

“He has been moved to Broadmoor so that gives him his defence.”



London’s Met Police charged Rudakubana with the offences on Tuesday – a day before the second anniversary of his horrific attack at a Southport dance class on July 29, 2024.

He is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates Court via videolink on Friday, September 11.

Rudakubana’s move from prison to psychiatric hospital Broadmoor last week sparked anger, with a lawyer for the victims’ families accusing him of “playing the system”.



The switch could cost the taxpayer £13 million and Rudakubana will face a much softer regime at Broadmoor, which had a £250 million revamp in 2019 and looks like a posh health club.

Rudakubana – who also injured eight other children and two adults in the horror attack in Southport – was moved after assessments by medics and psychologists over more than a year.

Victims’ families were informed about the charges before they were made public by London’s Met Police yesterday.

News.title: UK model village forced to remove TOPLESS female streaker from football pitch after backlash slamming it ‘inappropriate’
News.content:
TOP FLOP UK model village forced to remove TOPLESS female streaker from football pitch after backlash slamming it ‘inappropriate’

A MODEL village has been forced to remove a topless female streaker from a football pitch after visitors slammed it as “inappropriate”.

The tiny pitch invader was shown a red card at Godshill Model Village on the Isle of Wight after years of entertaining visitors.



The cheeky figure, inspired by the wave of high-profile sporting streakers in the 1970s and 1980s, had become one of the attraction’s hidden jokes.

It brought “innocent delight” to children who saw it and laughed but bosses at the model village said visitors complained it was “inappropriate”.



Its disappearance was spotted by local and regular visitor Rupert Willoughby who was left “dismayed” to discover the miniature nudist had disappeared.

Praising the attraction’s “whimsical sense of humour”, he questioned whether the model could really cause offence.



Directors who removed the streaker said they were also worried that streaking was “very much a feature of a different era” and that children nowadays will “no longer recognise” it.

The attraction confirmed the tiny troublemaker had been removed following comments from a small number of visitors.



Penny Dyer, director of Godshill Model Village, said: “The streaker on the football pitch has been part of the model village for many years, and for most visitors has been seen as a light-hearted joke.

“However, we’ve received a small number of comments from visitors who felt it was inappropriate for a family attraction.”

She said the reference had also become less recognisable over time.

“Streaking was very much a feature of a different era,” she continued.

“It is far less common and is no longer something that younger visitors recognise, so the model has lost much of its original relevance.



“As a business, we listen to customer feedback and after considering the comments, we decided to remove her.

“We appreciate that not everyone will agree with the decision, but our priority is ensuring all visitors feel comfortable and enjoy their visit.”

Despite the tiny player’s retirement from the field, Godshill Model Village remains famous for its intricate scenes, hidden jokes and miniature characters tucked away throughout the attraction.

News.title: Residents evacuated as ‘explosion’ at block of flats shatters windows with man, 18, arrested
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

BLAST PROBE Residents evacuated as ‘explosion’ at block of flats shatters windows with man, 18, arrested

A MAN has been arrested after a suspected explosion forced emergency services to evacuate a block of flats.

Police responded to Princes Street, Ipswich yesterday evening after receiving reports that an apparent blast had damaged several windows.

The block of flats was evacuated and the street was closed as police conducted enquiries.

A short while later an 18-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of arson/criminal damage with intent to endanger life, police said.





He was taken to Martlesham Police Investigation Centre for questioning and remains in custody.

Fire and rescue services and ambulance crews were also scrambled to the scene.

Anyone with any information that may assist investigators is asked to contact Suffolk Police.

The force said: “Enquiries continue to establish the circumstances of the incident, however no injuries have been reported.

“Motorists are advised that a diversion is currently in place, as Princes Street is expected to remain closed overnight.

“Anyone with information relating to the incident is asked to contact police quoting CAD 416 of 31 July.”

News.title: Devastating earthquake hits near Naples as cars crushed under falling rocks & power wiped out with 8 injured in tremors
News.content:
AT LEAST eight people have been injured after a major earthquake struck southern Italy.

Emergency crews scrambled to the scene after what authorities say was one of the strongest quakes to ever hit the Campi Flegrei region, near Naples.



The magnitude 4.7 shock wave struck at around 7.46pm on Friday night.

People rushed out into the streets as tremors rippled through the area, filling the air with thick clouds of dust.



Boulders broke off cliffs and cascaded down into the streets of residential neighbourhoods, crushing parked cars on impact.

Shocking footage shows people looking on in horror at the destruction as debris and broken rocks scatter the ground.



According to Italian media reports, the injured were taken to the city’s emergency room for treatment.

The quake caused power outages across the region with transport brought to a standstill.



Aftershocks continued to strike the area throughout the night.

The Italian fire service said there were reports of minor damage to buildings in and around Naples.

But their crews did not received immediate requests to help or rescue residents.



According to Italy‘s National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology the quake occurred at a depth of 3km.

Campi Flegrei is a densely populated volcanic caldera covering a large part of western Naples.

The region has experienced increasingly frequent seismic activity in recent years, prompting the government to step up monitoring.

It has experienced increasingly frequent seismic activity in recent years, prompting the government to step up monitoring.

Small earthquakes are common in the area.



But stronger tremors have raised fears of a repeat of the crisis that struck Campi Flegrei in the 1980s, when thousands were forced to flee their homes.

Earthquakes are relatively frequent in Italy.

A series of powerful quakes struck central Italy in 2016, devastating parts of Lazio, Umbria and the Marche regions, killing around 300 people.

The deadliest in recent decades was a magnitude 6.9 quake that struck the Irpinia area of southern Italy in November 1980.

About 2,700 people were killed while hundreds of towns were devastated.

News.title: Man, 30, charged after two teenage girls ‘raped in alleyway’ in town centre
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

HORROR 'ATTACK' Man, 30, charged after two teenage girls ‘raped in alleyway’ in town centre

A 30-YEAR-OLD man has been charged after two teenage girls were allegedly raped in a town centre alleyway.

Police were called to reports of the horror on July, 26, in Deansgate, Blackpool at around 2:30am.

An investigation into the alleged rapes was launched and a man was arrested on Tuesday, July 28.

James Peters, of no fixed address, was subsequently charged with two counts of rape.





He was remanded into custody before appearing before Lancaster Magistrates Court on Thursday.

Blackpool police said at the time: “A man has been charged with raping two teenagers in Blackpool.

“Our officers were called at 2:36am on Saturday 26th July to an alleyway off Deansgate, to a report that two girls – both aged in their late teens – had been raped.

“An investigation was launched and following enquiries, a 30-year-old man was arrested in Blackpool on Tuesday evening.

“Following consultation with the Crown Prosecution Service, James Peters, 30, of no fixed address, has been charged with two offences of rape.”

News.title: Love rival jailed for nearly 30 years after killing ex’s new partner with samurai sword in ‘cold-blooded execution’
News.content:
BLADE MURDER Love rival jailed for nearly 30 years after killing ex’s new partner with samurai sword in ‘cold-blooded execution’

A JEALOUS ex who brutally murdered his love rival using a samurai sword has been jailed for 30 years.

Michael Bretton, 41, killed Craig Hurcombe using the deadly blade after visiting his workplace in Somerset on January 1, Bristol Crown Court heard.



He had become “obsessed” with Kate Saunders, who was dating Craig at the time but had also casually dated Bretton previously.

Bretton insisted his ex’s new partner had fallen and impaled himself on a metal shaft, but the jury returned a unanimous verdict on July 31.



Kate and Bretton met on an internet dating site but had cut contact after she decided she was not looking for a proper relationship with him.

She then went on to rekindle her relationship with old flame Craig, 39, leaving Bretton “clearly jealous”, the court heard.



After the break-up, Bretton stalked the pair, attaching GPS trackers to their cars and loitering outside Craig’s workplace.

On one occasion he even followed them to a pub, leading to a brawl between him and Craig and prompting police intervention.

The situation escalated after Craig returned to the yard where he worked on New Year’s Eve to discover Bretton had slashed his Audi’s tyres.

Bretton had returned the following day to “confront” Craig before inflicting the fatal wound.

A post-mortem revealed Craig had died from a single stab injury in what prosecutor Mark Cotter KC described as a “premeditated and cold-blooded execution”.



After murdering Craig, Bretton then removed his SIM card and inserted it in his own device, sending messages from his victim.

Kate received the fake texts from Craig, urging her “not to be so hard” on Bretton and telling her to get back together with him.

Craig’s mother later contacted Kate asking about her son’s whereabouts, after his boss reported him missing.

His Honour Judge Hart spoke after the verdict, describing Bretton as a “cowardly and secret assassin“.

“If you read about this case, you would think it is something from a crime novel,” he said.



Addressing Bretton, he said: “You were motivated by jealousy about a refusal to accept that you have been supplanted in her affections.

“It wasn’t love…you took him by surprise. You didn’t give him the slightest chance to live.”

Nicola Hurcombe, Craig’s mother, said: “His loss to us all is beyond measure.

“The fact that someone can murder Craig in such a brutal, horrific manner in the circumstances that have been disclosed to us and send messages to family and friends that have subsequently caused so much pain and distress is so very terrible and upsetting.”

She added that over 210 people attended his funeral, a reflection of how much he was adored.



“It is a testament to the impact that Craig had on so many lives and that his memory will always live on with us all,” she said.

Speaking in his own defence, Bretton told the court Craig had died in a “tragic accident” after falling onto a sharp piece of metal.

He said he panicked after seeing his eyes was “glazed over” and his body was cold.

“With everything that has happened, it doesn’t look the best,” he said.

Bretton was also charged with one count of stalking Kate.



Det Insp Neil Meade from Avon and Somerset Police’s Major Crime Investigations team described the fatal attack as “horrendous”.

He said: “I don’t think you can imagine the fear he must’ve gone through, firstly, being threatened and stabbed with a samurai sword.

“To meet his end in such tragic, scary circumstances – you cannot imagine the fear going through Craig’s mind that night.

“He may not have even seen it was Michael Bretton, but he would’ve no doubt seen the sword.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“A horrendous set of circumstances and a scary, lonely place to lose your life.”

News.title: Chilling texts show ‘Temu Barbie’ plot with her mum as she reveals ex’s location before killer drug dealer’s acid attack
News.content:
CHILLING texts show how a woman dubbed “Temu Barbie” and her mum discussed revealing her ex’s location to a drug dealer before he was subject to a fatal acid attack.

The texts lay bare Paris Wilson, 35, agonising over the plot before deciding “at least nobody but Dan gets hurt” as she discussed the plan with her mother Karen.



Winchester Crown Court heard Wilson tipped off drug boss Ryan Kennedy, known as Frost or Frosty, about ex-hubby Danny Cahalane’s movements.

Her ex had been “middle management” in a drug-dealing operation and owed Frost around £120,000 after gambling away drug profits.



On February 21 last year Danny was ambushed by two men who doused him in sulphuric acid at his Plymouth home – Wilson and Danny’s child was in the property at the time.

The dad-of-two suffered catastrophic burns over his entire body and died from his injuries ten weeks later.

Just weeks before the attack, Wilson revealed Frost had offered to reward her if she helped track Danny down.

In one message sent to her mum on January 8, she said: “He said he [Frosty] will pay me a few grand and double what Dan owes you and give you a oz…



“That’s Turkey paid for all of us.”

Moments later she admitted: “But I am worried about my karma.”

She then added: “But at least nobody but Dan gets hurt.”

Wilson went on: “I can’t get her address [a woman Danny was seeing] and tbh that’s the only way I know only Dan would get hurt. Nobody else. And he deserves it. He lies everyday.”

Karen replied: “Then do it your way, but don’t arrange for us to get her from school because that would look like you’d set it up then.”



Wilson answered: “I’ll just be home to get her. He’s always here like 20 past anyways.”

The following day she texted her mum: “I’m going to decorate my bedroom this month. And then I need to plan getting to Turkey in Feb before Dan has his limbs cut off.”

Then the next day on January 10 she told her mum Danny had supposedly injured himself putting his arm through glass.



But she added: “I don’t believe he slipped.”

She then texted: “I think someone cut him up.”

Karen replied that she also did not believe the story.

Wilson answered: “Oh yeah no I don’t either lol. I just think he sure does slip over etc a lot. Breaks and loses phones. Like are you okay hun.”

Her mum joked: “That’s because he’s ginger.”



Prosecutors said Wilson had tipped off Frost to Danny’s location on January 19, when members of the gang attempted to kidnap him.

After the failed plot, she texted her mum: “There was black guys here who tried to grab Dan. It genuinely wasn’t me. And he thinks it was.”

Karen replied: “No, don’t be paranoid. They didn’t come near you. It’s not you they want.”



Wilson insisted: “Mum I’d tell you. Because I’d want money. I haven’t told anyone anything.”

The court heard Wilson also expressed concern because Danny and their daughter were together at the property before the fatal acid attack.

Hours after the attack, she texted Karen: “I’ve just calmed down… Mum it was horrific I can’t stop being sick.”

Karen replied: “I’ve just woken up and seen this for f***’s sake.”

The pair then spoke on the phone for around two and a half minutes.



Wilson later texted: “I don’t even know what has happened to Dan, or how bad. But there was still three ambulances when I got there and he was at hospital.”

Wilson was jailed for nine years after being convicted of manslaughter, with a judge saying she was a “key participant” in the plot.

The court heard the relationship between Wilson and Danny had descended into a bitter feud over drugs, money and the daughter they shared.



Following their split, Wilson became a “go-to” contact for the gangster and agreed to reveal Danny’s whereabouts believing Frost would “make her wealthy”.

The prosecution said she acted out of greed, revenge, or both.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Two men who carried out the acid attack were convicted of murder, while Wilson was convicted of manslaughter and attempted kidnap before being jailed for nine years.

News.title: Inside Palestinian's horror Gaza genocide watching brother and dad die as Gary Lineker fundraises for UK dream
News.content:
A Palestinian woman that's living in a tent in Gaza said Gary Lineker's support has given her strength to keep fighting.

Heba Abaid, 26, is one of hundreds of young students in Palestine dreaming of a life in the UK after being offered a university place, away from the terrors of genocide. The UK government confirmed last month it would continue helping exceptional young people to leave Gaza if they were offered an unconditional place at a British university, as long as they have a full scholarship or can pay the tuition fees.

But, Heba - like so many other young Palestinians - has very little money to her name. She now lives in a tent with her entire family in the exact spot her house used to stand.

Heba's story, which is echoed hundreds of times across the country, sparked a host of British celebrities to launch a fundraiser. Their hope was to raise enough money in an online auction to help some exceptional students live their dream at a university in the UK.

‌



12 View 12 Images Heba is hoping to study in the UK (Image: SUPPLIED) 12 View 12 Images She currently lives with her family in a tent in Khan Yunis (Image: SUPPLIED)

Gary Lineker and Nicola Coughlan lead celeb Gaza fundraiser for Palestinian students to study in UK READ MORE :

Furious Donald Trump issues Iran a chilling threat with foul-mouthed outburst READ MORE :

Former Match of the Day host Gary Lineker donated a signed Nagoya Grampus Eight football shirt from Japan, where he spent the final two years of his playing career. Scottish actor Brian Cox offered a signed copy of his memoir and original flyers from his productions. Nicola Coughlan, Charlotte Church, and Paloma Faith were among 18 other celebrities from sport, music and film, who agreed to join the Scholarships for Gaza online auction.

Heba would receive a portion of any total funds raised in the scheme, which was organised by charity Phoenix Space and lasts until Thursday August 6. She paid tribute to the celebrities for their generosity, as well as all members of the public donating to the cause.

‌



You can take part in the auction here

View 12 Images Gaza has been decimated by Israeli airstrikes (Image: SUPPLIED)

She told the Mirror: "Seeing people I have admired for years, including Gary Lineker and others, stand behind my story means far more to me than I can put into words. It doesn't just make me happy… it gives me strength."

Throughout years of war and family tragedies, as well as hundreds of displacements, Heba believed her dream of continuing education was over. But, knowing people she hadn't even met were supporting her had changed her outlook on the future.

‌



View 12 Images The view from Heba's home (Image: SUPPLIED)

"It makes me hold on to my dream even more tightly. It has given me hope that my dream is not out of reach and it motivates me to keep fighting for it, no matter how difficult the journey is."

Heba needs to raise a total of £32,129 to move to the UK and study for her Master's degree in Design Management. She's so far raised a little more than £3,000 in a GoFundMe.

Genocide

Heba's harrowing past few years in Gaza has culminated in her family sleeping on the ashes of their former home. In the aftermath of Israeli bombs, the family's stunning home in Khan Yunis, Gaza, was completely destroyed, and her brother, Ahmed, was killed in the demolition.

‌



"It was a terrifying night," she said. "People were running through the streets with nowhere safe to go because the shelling surrounded us from every direction. Hundreds of people were injured in the streets and many were killed. That day, no one could move safely."

View 12 Images Two-thirds of the population was forcibly moved into Rafah from their Gaza homes (Image: SUPPLIED)

The five remaining members of the family managed to escape south to Rafah in January 2024. Within a few days, two-thirds of the entire Gazan population had been forcibly funnelled into the city by the Israeli Defence Forces (IDF).

Benjamin Netanyahu's government claimed the southern half of Gaza was a safe haven for civilians. But on February 9, he ordered the IDF to plan an offensive on Rafah. Just two days after Netanyahu's order, at least 44 Palestinians were killed by Israeli bombs inside the city in a single day.

‌



Heba and her mum, dad, and two younger brothers, continued to move among refugee camps for the next four months. They lived in cramped conditions, and struggled to sleep at night due to the ongoing destruction of Gaza around them, as well as the constant fear.

View 12 Images By December 2025, more than 70,000 people had died in Gaza during the war (Image: SUPPLIED)

The family were allowed to move into the central area of Gaza by May 2024. They might've been closer to their home in Khan Yunis, but they were still displaced hundreds of times over the following 18 months. It made finding anywhere to live impossible, and just when they were getting settled, they were forced to move again.

"We moved from one place to another so many times that I've lost count," said Heba. "Each time, we had to start over from nothing, fleeing under bombardment with almost nothing. It was incredibly difficult and expensive to rebuild our lives every time… to put up a new tent, buy clothes, and find food. It truly felt like starting from zero again and again."

‌



But, Heba's most difficult period was yet to come, with the heartbreaking death of her father.

View 12 Images Heba was a graphic designer before the war, but life is very different now (Image: SUPPLIED)

Her dad was living with dementia during the genocide. The constant displacements made his condition incredibly difficult to manage, on top of a brain tumour that was diagnosed a few months earlier.

During one particularly chaotic displacement under bombardment, Heba's dad was lost in the fray. It would've been difficult to find anyone in the frantic Gazan turmoil during that time - never mind an elderly man with Alzheimer's disease.

‌



"We searched for him everywhere," Heba said. "When we finally found him three weeks later, he was walking alone at night on one of the streets.

"At that moment, the area beside him was bombed."

View 12 Images She's desperate to continue her education in the UK at Lancaster University (Image: SUPPLIED)

Heba watched as her dad was caught in wreckage of unrestrained Israeli bombings. He was left bleeding for more than two hours before anyone could reach him.

‌



"The situation was so dangerous that night," she said. "No-one could even drive their car, including the ambulances, so he had to wait more than two hours before he was finally taken for treatment."

View 12 Images The family were displaced "hundreds" of times before moving back home (Image: SUPPLIED)

The family weren't able to go with the dad to the hospital, and had no idea where he'd been taken. They later discovered he was forced to wait in an overcrowded operating room that was filled with injured locals.

He died in that room after losing too much blood.

‌



"We didn't know that he had passed away," she said. "When he didn't return, we went from one hospital to another searching for him."

They eventually found him in a morgue, Heba recalled. He was registered as an unidentified person. Doctors told the family he'd died just moments before they arrived at the hospital.

Famine

Shortly before Heba's dad died, the IDF launched a total blockade on Gaza. Essential supplies, including aid and food, were banned from entering the Gaza Strip. By August 22 2025, Gaza was officially in a famine.

‌



The blockade sparked extreme shortages of food, water, and humanitarian aid across the country. Meanwhile, stockpiles of relief were stored in warehouses outside of the Gaza Strip.

Heba's mum became particularly ill during the famine, she said. She was severely malnourished, and they were all forced to drink contaminated water just to survive. Her mum's weight eventually dropped to a little more than six stone.

"The famine was an incredibly difficult period," said Heba. "After my father passed away, the famine became even worse. There was almost no food available and whatever food could be found was extremely expensive.

View 12 Images Heba's family cooks on a makeshift stove, after months of famine (Image: SUPPLIED)

‌



My family became ill, especially my mother. She was in a very poor condition, and there was no safe drinking water available."

Nearly 450 people died inside Gaza from starvation by mid-August 2025, including 147 children, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. It's still not entirely clear how many people have died since.

In November, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gallant. Judges said they "intentionally and knowingly deprived the civilian population in Gaza of objects indespensible to their survival, including food, water, and medicine". There were reasonable grounds that they held responsiblity for the war crime of stavation, the judges added.

Heading home

Heba's family has only recently been allowed back into their neighbourhood in Khan Yunis. When they returned, they found their home - a sanctuary from the chaos of the daily life before the war - was now rubble.

‌



A tattered old cupcake tin, the drawer from a bedside table, and a lone, solitary dinner plate were strewn across the floor - small reminders of a previous life that still contained Heba's brother and father.

View 12 Images They now live in a tent where their former home once stood (Image: SUPPLIED)

They're now living in a tent on top of its ashes, in a bid to keep a little part of home close to them. Heba, her mother, and two younger brothers were all living cramped inside, cooking whatever they can find on a small, makeshift stove.

"I refuse to give up," Heba said. "When I got my offer from Lancaster University, it felt like a dream come true. It showed me that dreams can survive, even in the middle of the war, even in the middle of genocide, even, through all things we've lived through here in Gaza."

‌



View 12 Images She lives inside the tent with her mother and two brothers (Image: SUPPLIED)

Heba managed to raise about £3,000 on a GoFundMe before she received her Master's offer from Lancaster. Now, she's hoping she can combine that with anything the celebrities raise to secure her education in the UK, and a chance to live a better future. She said the celebs' auction was a lifeline she never thought she'd get.

She said: "It reminds me that kindness can cross every border, and that even in the darkest moments, there are people willing to help someone they have never met, simply because they believe everyone deserves a chance."

You can take part in the auction here

‌



You can also donate directly to Heba's Master's degree fund using her GoFundMe

News.title: Mum sheds more than one third of her bodyweight after daughter's desperate plea
News.content:
Mum sheds more than one third of her bodyweight after daughter's desperate plea

Ally Wainman says she used to eat 'huge amounts of sugary or greasy foods' before being consumed with guilt afterwards

View 5 Images Ally Wainman before her incredible weight loss (Image: Slimming World)

A healthcare worker who gained weight after being diagnosed with a lung tumour has lost an amazing 7st following a desperate plea from her daughter. Ally Wainman, 55, lost weight after daughter Chloe, now 29, begged her to look after her health because she wanted her mum to be ‘around for as long as possible’.

“I’ll never forget the way Chloe looked at me when she gently suggested that I should try to lose some weight,” says Ally, from Warwickshire. “I know it can be hard to hear sometimes, but it was genuinely coming from a place of love. I’d had a tough few years fighting cancer – followed by the death of my beloved Dad – so prioritising myself had really taken a back seat.

“I knew I had an unhealthy relationship with food. I used it as a comfort – eating huge amounts of sugary or greasy foods and then feeling awful and guilty afterwards. I’m quite petite at 5ft 4ins, so weighing 18st 8lbs took a huge toll on my body, especially my knees and hips.

“Our family had been through so much – I knew I couldn’t have Chloe worrying about how long I’d be around, especially when I’d already lost one of my lungs. I decided to visit my doctor to see what weight loss options were available to me.”

View 5 Images Ally weighed 18st 8lbs at one stage (Image: Slimming World)

Ally was offered a 12-week referral to her local Slimming World group – which she believes changed her relationship with food forever. She says: “I knew a friend who’d got on well with Slimming World, so I figured I had nothing to lose – especially as I’d been referred by my GP so I trusted that it would be a healthy and sustainable way to lose weight. I was so nervous on my first night, but it happened to be my consultant Jacquie’s first night in group too, so we got each other through those first-day jitters.”

Ally, who also has a 33-year-old son called Joshua and works at a private hospital in Birmingham, soon got to grips with Slimming World's healthy eating plan . She says: “I’d tried lots of diets in the past and once lost three stone in three months on a shake diet.

"Four months later, I’d put it all back on. What I loved about Slimming World was that the food was just normal everyday things – spaghetti Bolognese, curries, stews, baked potatoes… it was so easy to stick with it. And because there were no big extremes, I lost weight steadily and easily without obsessing over food every minute of the day.

“The group support was also something totally new for me. I was used to losing weight alone – so to be surrounded by people who were all on the same journey made the whole experience much more enjoyable. I’ve since moved away from the area, but I love Jacquie and my group so much that I commute the 40 minutes each way for my weekly dose of support and inspiration.

"Everyone there is just amazing and has helped me through so much. I learned I’d easily go off track if I didn’t have a meal planned for when I got home from work – so I started keeping a stash of meals from the Slimming World range at Iceland in the freezer, which helped no end.”

View 5 Images Ally shed 7st (Image: Slimming World)

Part-way through her journey, Ally was told she needed a hip replacement. She says: “I’d lost a fair bit of weight, around six stone, yet my hip still caused me a lot of pain and needed replacing. I told the surgeon that I wanted to be dancing in my high heels afterwards. Well, just three months later, I was! I have no doubt that being lighter aided my recovery. I was prepared for it to take a while but honestly, I breezed through it.

“As well as all the dancing, I’m more active now than I ever have been. Slimming World’s active lifestyle programme helped me think about how I could weave exercise into my everyday life. I used to avoid stairs because of the pain it would cause for my joints – but now I can run up a set of stairs – sometimes even two at a time.”

View 5 Images Ally after her weight loss (Image: Slimming World)

Ally continues: “I feel like a different person. I’ve gone from someone who hid away at home to the first one on the dance floor, especially if I hear a bit of Beyonce. I couldn’t have done it without the support of my amazing Slimming World group – their tips, support and love have helped me enormously. Staying to my group each week has been the key thing for me – that’s my top tip for sure.

“These days I’m looking forward to the future – I don’t know what lies ahead but I know I’ll be dancing along whatever happens – in really fabulous shoes.”

And Chloe couldn’t be prouder of her mum’s new zest for life. She says: “I’m so glad I had that conversation with Mum about her weight. It wasn't an easy one but seeing how much her life has changed makes it all worth it.

"She's happier, healthier and so much more confident. Joshua and I call it her ‘life glow-up’ because she genuinely shines now. We're incredibly proud of everything she's achieved.”

View 5 Images Ally now loves dancing (Image: Slimming World)

Before menu:

Breakfast: Big bowl of sugary cereal with milk

Lunch: A canteen lunch of a panini or burger with chips

Dinner: Shepherd’s pie with a few slices of bread and butter

Snacks: Sweets, chocolate, biscuits, cakes

After menu:

Breakfast: Fat-free Greek yogurt with fruit

Lunch: A large homemade salad with cold meats, pickles and a low-fat dressing

Article continues below

Dinner: A frozen meal from Slimming World’s range at Iceland, such as Marry Me Chicken Pasta

Snacks: Slimming World Hi-Fi bars, meringue with yogurt and fruit, rice cakes, grapes

News.title: 'Doctors fobbed off my son's chest pain with Gaviscon - but 'bad diet' agony was cancer'
News.content:
'Doctors fobbed off my son's chest pain with Gaviscon - but 'bad diet' agony was cancer'

Mum Ffion Smith said she was 'fobbed off' by doctors who allegedly claimed that her son Ruben should take Gaviscon for his back pain - before tests revealed he had leukaemia

View 5 Images Ruben Troy, eight, has been diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (Image: Kennedy News and Media)

A 'heartbroken' mum has claimed doctors told her to give her eight-year-old son Gaviscon for his back pain - only for it to turn out to be cancer.

‌



Ffion Smith said that when her son, Ruben Troy, first started complaining of shooting pains in April 2026, she assumed it was down to his love of rough-and-tumble play. But a week later, Ruben suddenly collapsed at his pal's house while playing, and began writhing on floor, screaming in pain.

‌



After calling 111 and taking her son to an urgent care centre, the 28-year-old claims doctors "fobbed her off", telling her it was just a sickness bug that would clear up naturally.

‌



View 5 Images Mum Ffion Smith, 28, said she was 'fobbed off' by doctors who said her son's back pain was triggered by a 'bad diet' (Image: Kennedy News and Media)

When Ruben collapsed again, Ffion said they told her to give him Gaviscon, as they believed his chest and back pain was gastritis triggered by a 'bad diet'. The baffled mum-of-four says doctors also told her not to give Ruben coffee - a beverage he doesn't drink.

On top of the pain, Ruben also appeared pale, had small bruises on his legs, arms and chest, struggled to walk, and lost one-and-a-half stone After multiple trips to the GP, Ffion pushed for blood tests on June 29 that revealed he had acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, a cancer that affects the blood and bone marrow.

‌



Ruben is now recovering at home after undergoing two rounds of chemotherapy and lumbar puncture surgery. But mum Ffion is still "angry" at how her son's ailments were dismissed - and is urging other parents to speak up if they suspect something is wrong with their child.

View 5 Images The brave boy has undergone two rounds of chemotherapy and lumbar puncture surgery (Image: Kennedy News and Media)

Ffion, from Northallerton, North Yorkshire, said: "I can't get my head around it, it's so traumatic that it makes me feel sick when I think about it.

‌



"It makes me feel so angry that the doctors just wouldn't listen. Some days it'd be really bad and some days it'd be bearable where he'd walk a bit. He would be screaming.

"He missed school and couldn't walk. He was in so much pain and we were giving him Calpol and Nurofen but nothing would take away the pain and he'd just lie in bed all day. We took him to the doctors and we were a bit relieved at first because they said he'd got gastritis and they told us to give him Gaviscon.

"He was still having the Gaviscon and we noticed it was making no difference and they said 'there's no need for anything else, it's his stomach, it's hurting'. They just said he must have a lot of acid in his stomach and that's what's hurting him. They were saying that it was his diet that was the issue and all that was triggering the gastritis.

‌



View 5 Images Ruben's mum is still 'angry' at how her son's complaints were dismissed (Image: Kennedy News and Media)

"He doesn't eat 'well' but we are working on that ourselves. He doesn't eat fatty foods, he eats a lot of potato and bread, that's basically his diet. We didn't really think he had that [gastritis] but we thought 'the doctor said it so they think it is'.

"They'd asked what he drinks and we said water. They said 'don't let him drink coffee' and I said 'he's an eight-year-old boy, why would I give him coffee?'. They asked if he eats chocolate, which he doesn't because he prefers crisps.

‌



"[At the urgent care centre] I was getting a bit frustrated and I said 'nobody's listening to me, I need someone to take bloods'. I said to the doctor 'why are his legs hurting? It's not just his stomach, it's his chest, his legs and he can't walk'. He turned to me and Ruben's dad and said 'you don't know how painful gastritis is'."

View 5 Images Ffion has set up a fundraiser to help pay towards essential equipment and care (Image: Kennedy News and Media)

Ffion has set up a GoFundMe page to help pay towards essential equipment and care that Ruben needs during his recovery.

‌



The mum said she is sharing her son's story to make other parents aware, and added: "We have so much anger inside of us because of how much pain he was in, they completely fobbed us off. It's like life got sucked out of him. He didn't want to do anything, we didn't realise how much pain he was in."

"Keep going and don't take no for an answer. You need to speak up and tell them there's something wrong. It was so heartbreaking seeing him going through all that knowing it wasn't what they were saying it was. He used to be so uplifting and be the one to come in and try to make you laugh. I'm hoping when all of this is over he'll ring the bell and be like 'yes I got over it, I've done it'."

A spokesperson for NHS Humber and North Yorkshire Integrated Care Board said: "We are very sorry to hear about Ruben's diagnosis, and our thoughts are with him and his family at this difficult time. However, it is not appropriate for us to comment on the details of an individual patient's care.

Article continues below

"The ICB take any concerns raised by patients and their families seriously. We work closely with providers to ensure high standards of care are maintained for residents in Humber and North Yorkshire."

News.title: Chilling truth about 'humane rat traps' as heatwave creates UK rodent plague
News.content:
Chilling truth about 'humane rat traps' as heatwave creates UK rodent plague

People don't realise, scientist says 'there are no really good ways of doing this'

View Image 'Humane' rat traps are anything but, according to one scientist (Image: Getty)

People who are trying to tackle a huge rise in rats have been told that there is a serious issue for anyone who is using ‘humane’ traps to catch them. Many people don’t want to use lethal traps or poison - but a scientist has given a chilling update.

‌



Radio 4’s You and Yours reported that callouts have gone up massively from June this year by pest control experts. And an expert said that callouts have gone up 80 per cent in 5 years.

‌



Steven Belmain, Professor of Ecology at the University of Greenwich, said: “In terms of welfare, I think a lot of people will be thinking ‘I’m going to trap the rats alive and then let them go somewhere else. That way, they don’t think they’re actually harming the animal; there’s some sort of welfare effect. What I would say is that when you take a rat from one habitat and you release it somewhere else, you’re actually causing that rat quite a lot of stress. You’ve put it into a new place where it’s not familiar with the surroundings, it’s still going to have to find food and shelter. Unfortunately, even though there are good intentions, you’re probably killing that rat anyway.

‌



“There are no really good ways of doing this - we have to kill them, and unfortunately, we can’t just move them somewhere else. We want to stop them in the first place and that means stopping the food resources that they’re feeding on. That’s really the most welfare-friendly approach is to improve our sanitation.“

If they are poisoned: “It does take a few days.” He said research was going into rodent contraception but poisons was the key way. He said: “We have different kinds of poisons. They do cause suffering, and that’s unfortunate. Trapping might be more sustainable if they’re killed quickly by a trap - so a kill trap that could be a very welfare-friendly method. But again not all traps are the same and being able to buy a trap in a shop doesn’t necessarily mean that’s a good trap in terms of both efficacy in catching the rat, but also in terms of welfare where it may not kill them quickly for example and that could also be quite distressing - if you trap a rat and it’s not dead yet. It might take a while for it to actually die.”

‌



The heatwaves are contributing to the problem - and a pest control expert said a key point was winters are less cold - meaning they breed all year long. The National Pests Technicians Association has said call-outs for rats are rising up 11 per cent in June, compared with the month before.

Nick Robertson from HF Pest Control based in Tunbridge Wells in Kent: “Basically we don’t have cold winters any more, so they’re breeding all year round. I don’t know when the last time we had a really cold winter. Last year I think it dropped under zero for about a week or two weeks, if that, so it’s genuinely warm all year round now and climate change has caused a big problem with the increase of rats.”

In terms of getting rid of rats, he said that a lot of methods they used to use have been ‘taken away from us’: “We have to go down the non-poison route to start off with. So we’d start off with snap traps, if it’s social housing we go for proofing which is to block the holes up to stop them entering the property, and just to try to improve the housekeeping of the general area.

Article continues below

“Poisoning is still in the methods we use, but we’ve got to go down the other methods first before we use poison. It’s a last resort because when the rat dies that can cause a problem with the smell, the decomposing, but the main issue is to try to improve the housekeeping of area to stop the rats going into the area because they’re only foraging for food basically.”

Prof Belmain was asked if they are a health hazard and he said: “Oh yes definitely. So we’ve all just been through a pandemic caused by diseases transmitted by animals, so Coronaviruses we know came from bats, but rodents also transmit many many diseases. It’s a very long list. In the UK we have issues with a disease called leptospirosis or Weil’s disease and that is found in this country.” He said lots of food-borne illnesses like salmonella and ecoli can be transmitted by rats. “So if you had a rat in your house and it was in your kitchen cupboards you would really want to be worried about contamination of food that way. If people are going around picking up dead rats in their house, again, be careful wear gloves, wash your hands.”

To listen to the full Radio 4 program click here.

News.title: The Odyssey's Tom Holland shares favourite classic 60s dish - 1 ingredient could slash heart disease risk
News.content:
The Odyssey's Tom Holland shares favourite classic 60s dish - 1 ingredient could slash heart disease risk

The Odyssey actor said he loved the 'creamy shredded chicken dish' for its taste and 'sentimental reasons'

View 3 Images Tom Holland plays Telemachus in Christopher Nolan's film, The Odyssey (Image: Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images)

Tom Holland’s been doing the rounds promoting Spider-Man and The Odyssey this month, and during an appearance on the podcast Dish, he shared a classic 60s dinner that holds a special place in his heart - and it could boast a number of health benefits.

‌



Holland, who plays Telemachus in Christopher Nolan's film, recorded the episode with hosts Nick Grimshaw and Angela Hartnett the day after England played against Mexico in the World Cup. Starring alongside his wife in the film, Zendaya, who plays Athena, he raved about a dish called C hicken Véronique.

‌



And according to WebMD, one of its ingredients, chicken, could help with weight management and, as a result, reduce the risk of heart disease and high blood pressure. The health experts explain: " Research suggests that 25-30 grams of protein per meal can help us feel more full.

‌



"Protein-rich meals can make us feel fuller despite us eating less, which helps to promote better weight management. Healthier weight leads to improvements in risk factors for heart problems, such as high triglyceride levels and high blood pressure.

"A food rich in protein, chicken can help with weight management and reduce the risk of heart disease."

View 3 Images (L-R) Charlize Theron, Samantha Morton, John Leguizamo, Tom Holland, Matt Damon, Anne Hathaway, Lupita Nyong'o, and Zendaya attend the premiere of "The Odyssey" presented by Universal Pictures on July 14, 2026 in New York City (Image: Mike Coppola/Getty Images for Universal Pictures)

‌



The health experts also note that chicken is a lean protein that provides the amino acids our bodies need to build and maintain muscle, which becomes more important as we age. A higher-protein diet can also help support bone density.

Because of this, eating chicken can help keep muscles strong and bones healthier. This can lower the risk of injuries and conditions like osteoporosis.

So the chicken in Tom Holland's dish could actually provide some benefits to our health. But as with everything, always make sure you are having a healthy and balanced diet, as while a dish may include a healthy ingredient or two, it doesn't always make the dish itself healthy.

‌



'

During the podcast, Holland’s younger brother, Sam, who is a chef, shared a pre-recorded video, explaining that their mum and Granny Tess "cooked Chicken Véronique and an apple crumble on a beach in Thailand for the cast and crew of Impossible".

Now, 15 years later, and it's "our favourite family meal" especially after Tom has a "long stint away" filming, Sam said, calling it a dish he loves for many "sentimental reasons."

Tom shared the same memories, re-calling: "We were making a movie in Thailand. It was my first ever film. It was a real family.

‌



"The crew were such lovely people, and we would always go down to this beach called Memories Beach. Cast and crew would be down there every weekend - all weekend.

"We started cooking down there, we became friends with the people that ran the beach bar, and they would let us cook. The English guys would cook one week, and then the Italians would cook the next week.

"Naomi Watts was the star of that movie. So, my granny roasted two chickens in her oven at her house in Thailand. She then drove it through the jungle to this beach, because you had to kind of go down this dirt road for about 25 minutes.

‌



"She made Chicken Véronique. It's like a kind of creamy shredded chicken dish, but then you peel and roast the grapes. And then you shred the potatoes. It's absolutely delicious.

"So now if I've ever been away and I come home to the family house for dinner, that's always what we always have."

Host and chef Angela Hartness replied: "Now you've mentioned it's a really old, classic French dish. And one that you'd have had in the '60s."

‌



While they did not cook the classic dish during the podcast, they did cook a dish Tom called a "treat" - spicy pork and pineapple skewers with Greek salad.

Spicy pork & pineapple skewers - full recipe

View 3 Images Tom Holland also stars as the hero himself in Spider-Man: Brand New Day (Image: Amy Sussman/Getty Images)

Ingredients

‌



500g pack British diced pork shoulder

½ supersweet medium pineapple

Vegetable oil, for griddling

1 satsuma, halved

2 salad onions, thinly sliced

For the marinade

1 satsuma, juice

2 clove/s garlic, crushed

1 tbsp Cooks' Ingredients Turkish Pepper Flakes

1 tsp cayenne pepper

1 tsp smoked paprika

2 tsp ground coriander

½ tsp ground cumin

1 tbsp light soy sauce

1 tbsp olive oil

Article continues below

Method

Soak 8 wooden skewers in cold water for at least 30 minutes to prevent them burning. In a mixing bowl, combine the marinade ingredients and add a few cracks of black pepper. Add the pork (halve any large pieces) and stir to coat. Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 30 minutes, or preferably overnight. Peel, core, then cut the pineapple half into 24 chunks. Thread 3-4 pieces of pork and 3 pieces of pineapple alternately onto each skewer and discard any remaining marinade. Heat a griddle pan over a medium-high heat, brush the pan lightly with oil, then cook half the skewers for 12-15 minutes, turning twice, until the pork is cooked through with no pink meat, juices that run clear, and is charred in places. Keep hot, while you cook the second batch. Char the satsuma, cut-side down, on the hot pan. Serve the skewers scattered with the salad onions and the warm satsuma juice, squeezed over at the table. Perfect with a leafy salad on the side, if liked

Angela Hartnett serves this recipe with a village Greek salad. You can find check out the recipe for that and handy cooking tips and tricks on the Waitrose website here.

News.title: Naples earthquake live: Italy struck by 4.7 magnitude quake as rocks crush cars
News.content:
Residents in Naples have been left terrified after a powerful earthquake caused damage to the Italian city - it registered at 4.7 magnitude

A powerful earthquake has struck southern Italy, causing damage in the city of Naples.

The 4.7 magnitude quake has left neighbourhoods without power, and residents are taking to the streets in fear. It occurred just before 8pm (local time).

According to data released by the INGV (National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology), the magnitude was 4.7. Power outages have been reported from Pizzofalcone to Fuorigrotta, and there has been a massive landslide in Pozzuoli.

Images show buildings have crumbled, with debris crushing cars.

News.title: Mum received text saying 'I'm 30 seconds from your home' – she was never seen alive again
News.content:
Mum received text saying 'I'm 30 seconds from your home' – she was never seen alive again

Mobile phone data uncovered a chilling exchange that became a key piece of evidence after a much-loved mum was found murdered in her Hampshire flat

View 3 Images Samantha Holden's daughter told the court it was "difficult to put into words the full impact" of her mother's death

A killer sent a chilling seven-word text message to a much-loved mum just minutes before he arrived at her flat and brutally strangled her.

‌



Channel 4's The Digital Detectives revisits the killing of Samantha Holden, 56, who was found dead at her flat in Farnborough, Hampshire, in September 2022 after being suffocated and strangled by Adam Watson.

‌



The programme reveals how mobile phone data helped investigators establish Watson's movements and his contact with Ms Holden in the hours before her death.

‌



Just before the fatal attack, Watson sent Ms Holden a message at 12.44pm saying: "Joanna I am 30 seconds from your door x." She replied moments later: "come up x".

Explaining the significance of the messages, higher analyst Elaine Lucas says in The Digital Detectives: "When we download the data from Watson's phone, we found texts between Sam and Watson on the day of her death.

View 3 Images Adam Watson (Image: PA)

‌



"Watson doesn't refer to Sam by her name, he calls her Joanna. Digital media confirmed that, despite his 'no comment', he was the client. Sam had seen Adam Watson before, on at least three occasions.

"So the text messages suggest that he was arranging to go to Sam's that day."

The episode, which aired on Thursday, July 30, examines how investigators used digital evidence to build the case against Watson after he fled the UK following the killing.

‌



Ms Holden, a sex worker, died at her home on September 9, 2022. After murdering her, Watson travelled to Belgium, where he was arrested at a hotel two days later before being extradited to the UK.

The court heard Ms Holden's body was discovered by her 18-year-old son shortly after 4pm. She was lying on the floor, covered with a blue dressing gown, and was pronounced dead at the scene. Watson's DNA was later found on her neck and beneath her fingernails.

View 3 Images New episodes are released every week (Image: Channel 4)

‌



During his trial, jurors heard Watson had first contacted Ms Holden through an adult website in May 2022, where she advertised under the name "English blonde lady". The pair had met several times before, leading the judge to conclude Ms Holden trusted him.

After the killing, Watson disposed of Ms Holden's phone at St Pancras station before boarding a Eurostar train bound for Belgium.

At Winchester Crown Court in 2024, Watson, then 37, was handed a life sentence with a minimum term of 21 years.

Article continues below

In a heartbreaking victim impact statement, Ms Holden's daughter, Rebecca Elliott, described her mother as her "best friend, my soul mate and most importantly my mum".

The court also heard during sentencing that Watson had a violent criminal history. He was on extended licence after serving a sentence for sexually assaulting another woman in 2013, having admitted the offence. The court was also told he had previously been charged with wounding members of his own family in 2008.

Episode three of Murder Case: The Digital Detectives is available to watch on Channel 4 now

News.title: 'Bath with a friend' and no beer - why the 1976 drought was never forgotten
News.content:
'Bath with a friend' and no beer - why the 1976 drought was never forgotten

As Brits face potential water restrictions, with half the country plunged into drought, the Mirror speaks with those who sweltered through the infamous summer of 1976, including how they dealt with unflushed toilets and pubs without beer

View 13 Images The aftermath of the fire at Dunwich Heath in eastern England, which is still burning (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

It was a summer Malcolm Donovan would never forget: working at an enormous canning factory on the banks of the River Medway.

‌



Now 73, he recalls: "The job I did throughout that summer was inspector of the oven, which was about 20° hotter than anywhere else. No further explanation is needed as to how uncomfortable that was!"

‌



The summer was, of course, the legendary heatwave of 1976 - a historic scorcher that brought 15 consecutive days of sweltering heat between June 23 and July 7.

‌



As temperatures soared to 32.2°C across England, tarmac melted on the roads and grass turned stark white under the blistering sun.

View 13 Images Madeleine Donovan recalls seeing the lawn at Buckingham Palace scorched in the heat (Image: Popperfoto via Getty Images)

For millions of Brits, memories of that scorching season are flooding back as the summer of 2026 cements itself as another one for the history books. With a fourth heatwave on the horizon, the Environment Agency has officially declared a drought across seven regions of England.

‌



Record-low rainfall and relentless temperatures mean that half of England is now facing drought conditions - the third in just five years - leaving millions urged to restrict their water use.

It is a warning that feels eerily familiar. Madeleine Donovan, then 23 and working in Sheffield, recalls attending a 1976 Royal Garden Party where even the famous Buckingham Palace lawn was burned crisp and brown. Just like ordinary lawns across the nation, it hadn't been watered.

View 13 Images The dry spell has revealed a long-forgotten 18th-century garden at Blenheim Palace (Image: Pete Seaward / SWNS)

‌



The freakish heatwave followed a year-long 'drought of the century', sparking water shortages, raging wildfires and ruined crops that cost farmers an estimated £500 million. It was the driest year since World War II, causing river and reservoir levels to drop to record lows nationwide.

Paul Hutchinson, 60, from Sunderland, remembers how water levels at Ladybower Reservoir plummeted so low that the submerged village of Derwent made a ghostly reappearance. Locals walking along the parched reservoir bed swore they could hear the ghostly ring of the old church bell.

View 13 Images Denis Howell was appointed Minister for Drought, on August 24, 1976 (Image: PA)

‌



A similar historical echo has emerged in recent days at Blenheim Palace, where scorched lawns revealed 'parch marks' outlining a long-forgotten 18th-century garden, dismantled in the 1760s. This summer, the past seems strangely close.

Yet for those who were children at the time, the heat brought pure joy. Natalie Connolly, 57, from Bacup, Lancashire, has halcyon memories of that summer. "I was only seven, but I remember me and my sister were always down at the reservoir on our lilo," she said. "I remember the water got really low, and then it dried up altogether. That whole summer was heaven."

View 13 Images It's feared that, in the worst-case scenario, water would be restricted, 'with serious impacts on industry, agriculture and businesses' (Image: Getty Images)

‌



To combat the crisis, the government introduced the emergency Drought Act on August 6, 1976, granting authorities wide-ranging powers to restrict and ration water. Public campaigns urged households to conserve every drop - encouraging people to put bricks in their toilet cisterns, and rallying behind the famous slogan "Save water, bath with a friend."

Janice 'Jan' Clarke, 67, from Manchester, was a 16-year-old school leaver that summer. She remembers pavements being so hot "you could cook an egg on them", and watching her mother queuing to get enough water to wash her dad's taxi.

View 13 Images For many children, it was the summer of a lifetime (Image: Getty Images)

‌



For many, sharing bathwater remains one of the defining memories. Households were urged to limit bath depth to five inches, and used 'greywater' was recycled to water thirsty plants, scrub floors, or manually flush toilets.

David Murray, also from Manchester, recalls carrying enamel buckets back and forth in the baking heat. The 83-year-old Tai Chi instructor told the Mirror: "You'd go out in the street to a standpipe and fill them, and bring them home. And if you had a bath, fill the bath."

With flushing heavily restricted, unflushed toilets quickly became a familiar sight. Malcolm's parents, who were living in a static caravan while building a house in Gloucester, faced even tougher conditions.

‌



View 13 Images People were encouraged to do their bit and conserve water for the good of the nation

"The foundations had been dug previously, but I remember the builders complaining about how hard all of the surrounding ground was, making every building job much more difficult," Malcolm recalled. "We had to get water from next door, because there was no direct waterline to the plot, and routine stuff like number twos became a major problem. They were having to dig holes in the ground and deposit their waste of all types into the ground, and then re-cover with dusty soil!"

Every corner of British life felt the impact. "Cricket for the whole of that summer was a bit of a joke, because none of the pitches had any grass on them, and therefore could not be prepared with mowers in the usual way," laughed Malcolm.

‌



View 13 Images The drought even made it tricky to have a decent beer (Image: Getty Images)

"Some pubs ran out of beer, which is why a lot of our beer drinking generation switched to lager, nicknamed 'Euro fizz', because the brewing process was a bit different. Most of that was imported from abroad, so they did not need as much water as our own brews."

Madeleine agrees: "I do remember the pubs running out of beer, which is when I had to start drinking lager, so that summer had a lifelong effect on me!"

‌



As the crisis deepened, Prime Minister James Callaghan appointed Denis Howell as Minister for Drought on August 24.

View 13 Images September and October proved to be the wettest since records began in 1727 (Image: Hull Daily Mail / Hull Live)

Tabloids joked that Howell was instructed to do a rain dance for the nation. Taking his duties seriously, Mr Howell invited journalists to his Birmingham home to reveal that he and his wife, Brenda, were sharing baths to save water.

‌



The spell finally broke over the August Bank Holiday weekend when torrential thunderstorms ended the drought - and Mr Howell's brief role. Malcolm remembers "kissing the ground, and making dust angels" in the downpour.

Madeleine recorded the moment in her diary on September 1: "Just wanted to stay in and watch the rain."

This novelty, unfortunately, wore thin as rock-hard earth couldn't absorb the sudden deluge, causing widespread flash flooding and earning Howell a new title: 'Minister for Floods.'

‌



View 13 Images The biblical rainfall that followed the heatwave caused chaos (Image: Mirrorpix)

The autumn of 1976 went on to be the wettest on record, reshaping how the government responds to climate emergencies.

Long-term water management plans were introduced, and following the 2010 Flood and Water Management Act, the Environment Agency (EA) was designated a category one civil contingency responder, leading to improved monitoring, environmental controls, and water restrictions.

‌



Yet experts warn that half a century later, the UK remains unprepared for the reality of climate change.

Helen Wakeham, Director of Water at the Environment Agency and Chair of the National Drought Group, warned this week that Brits are "currently using water faster than nature can replenish it".

View 13 Images Brits were forced to queue for buckets of water, which they would then carefully ration (Image: Mirrorpix)

‌



Ali Morse, Water Policy Manager at The Wildlife Trusts, says urgent infrastructure changes are needed: "Our climate is really changing, and what we're not doing very well at the moment is capturing that water when we have it.

"During those wet winters, we need to make sure we have the reservoirs, and those are coming down the track. We also need our landscape to be a lot better at holding water to replenish underground aquifers and top up river flows."

View 13 Images The EA has this week declared a drought across central, eastern and southern England (Image: PAUL GILLIS / Reach Plc)

‌



The UK’s National Risk Register warns that a worst-case scenario, based on three consecutive years of very dry conditions, would result in mandatory public water supply restrictions.

The emergency document reads: “Severe environmental damage due to drought conditions will occur, along with an increased fire risk due to the prolonged dry conditions. This would be combined with a reduced ability to fight fires due to water scarcity."

As wildfires blaze across the country again this summer, many fear whether Brits would comply with strict rationing. Public trust in water companies has hit an all-time low of 6.07 out of 10, according to the Consumer Council for Water, largely due to ongoing leaks and sewage pollution.

‌



"I don’t think people will follow water saving measures because water companies are wasting so much," Natalie noted.

David believes younger generations would struggle with the realities of a 1976-style drought: "Everything is online. They'd expect somebody to turn up with a van, and a bucket of water."

View 13 Images Half a century on from the 'drought of the century', society is very different, with a notable drop in trust in water companies (Image: PA)

Article continues below

Ali Morse hopes the current crisis serves as a wake-up call: "I think water is very much something that we take for granted - we turn on the tap and expect it to be there. A drought prompts people to think about the fair use of water and where it's coming from, and whether we are managing it properly."
