News.title: Labour's Bev Craig elected Greater Manchester mayor, succeeding Andy Burnham
News.content:
In the first round, Craig secured 47% of the vote, compared with Astley's 21%.

This meant the ballot papers from voters who did not select either of them as their first choice were brought back into play.

They were checked to see if the second-preference votes were for either the Labour or Reform candidate.

They were then added to the first-preference votes.

Craig expanded her already significant lead.

More than two million people across Greater Manchester's 10 boroughs were eligible to vote in the contest but turnout was just under 25%.

Analysis of the votes showed that Craig came top of the poll in the first round of voting in all the 10 local authority areas that make up Greater Manchester.

Astley came second in eight of the 10 areas, while the Green candidate Geraldine Coggins came second in Manchester and the Conservative candidate Phil Eckersley was second in Trafford.

In her speech, Craig said: "For too many people across our region, life is simply too hard. The generational belief that we had, that if you work hard and do the right thing, your life will be better and the life of the community will be better, is something that many people just don't feel at the minute."

She continued: "Everyone deserves a quality home in a good neighbourhood," said Craig, adding that people should be able to plan for their future and for that of their children.

She added: "We have to move away from divisive politics, and we'll do it together."

Congratulations came from Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell, the MP for Manchester Central, who posted on X, external: "Huge congratulations to @bevcraig our fantastic new Mayor of Greater Manchester.

"Thank you to our tireless activists who have worked so hard to help deliver this win."

News.title: Police release Nancy Guthrie ransom notes in latest bid to find kidnappers
News.content:
Police in Arizona have released two ransom notes in the hope the public can help identify whoever abducted the mother of US news presenter Savannah Guthrie.

The first note, which is treated as apparently credible, demanded millions of dollars in Bitcoin. The other claimed Nancy Guthrie died shortly after she was abducted from her home near Tucson six months ago.

The Pima County Sheriff's Office say they cannot verify her death, and the investigation remains active.

Officials released the two notes on Friday, asking the public for help identifying the writer, whose "distinct linguistic characteristics may be recognisable".

Investigators believe that Nancy Guthrie, who was aged 84 when she was last seen on 31 January, was taken against her will from her home, but they have not shared a possible motive or arrested a suspect.

The notes were addressed to Savannah Guthrie and the Guthrie family, and sent to a local TV station in Tucson, Arizona, in the days after Nancy Guthrie disappeared, according to the sheriff.

"A friend, family member, coworker, classmate, or acquaintance may recognise these patterns of expression and possess information that could help identify the individual responsible," the sheriff's office said in a statement.

The first note, which was received on 2 February, began: "Hello Savannah, we have your mother Nancy. She is safe but scared. She will be held for ransom and once payment is received she will be released unharmed. We will be holding her for a maximum of 7 days. You will need to send bitcoin in the amount of $4 million USD before 5PM on Thursday the 5th.

"If payment is not received, the ransom will be increased to 6 million USD which will need to be paid by 5PM on Monday the 9th. Once payment is received to the bitcoin address below she will be released within 12 hours of deposit to a safe drop off location back in Tucson. If payment is not recieved [sic] by the last deadline on Monday the 9th at 5PM, she will be killed.

"Your mother is aware of this and her life is in your hands. It is in the best interest of everyone to have this completed as soon as possible.

"You will not be able to contact me from here on out, there will be no negotiation. Do not play games, law enforcement will not be able to help you," the note continued.

After what appears to be a redacted sentence, it ends: "She had a white smart watch on the floor of the foot of her bed and the white flood light in backyard was destroyed."

News.title: Trump administration drops Reflecting Pool vandalism charge and admits 'botched' repairs
News.content:
US prosecutors have dropped charges against a former Olympian who had been accused of vandalising the Reflecting Pool in Washington DC, writing in court documents that the damage is now believed to be "the result of flawed installation by the contractor".

President Donald Trump had previously blamed the damage on "sick, deranged" vandals.

But a document filed by prosecutors in Washington DC on Friday says new information "strongly suggests that a rushed and botched installation" job overseen by the US Department of Interior led to the damage.

David Hearn, a champion canoeist, had been facing a 10-year prison sentence if found guilty after his arrest last month.

News.title: He thought a fitness supplement was safe but it sent him into psychosis
News.content:
Daniel Murphy thought he was taking a safe and tested dietary supplement that would help him put on muscle in the gym.

But over the following two years, his mental health spiralled to such a degree he ended up in a state of psychosis in which he believed his wife was trying to steal his business and his mother-in-law was going to kill him.

Unknown to Daniel, the daily pills he had been taking had been mixed with testosterone.

The 32-year-old is one of 54,000 consumers listed in a case against a multimillion-pound peptide company based in the US, which sold its products around the world.

The owner of Paradigm Peptides, Matthew Kawa, was jailed for five years and 10 months on Thursday after he admitted deliberately selling unapproved medicines, trying to deceive people about what they were and illegally bringing the products into the country.

His sister, Jennifer Stechkober, who also pleaded guilty to selling unapproved medicines, was sent to prison for a year and four months.

Both admitted they had lied about where the pills were sourced, their purity and their company's testing procedures. Despite claiming the supplements were manufactured in the US, they were actually imported from China, India and several other countries. The pair also faked certificates of analysis, the documents that prove the safety and quality of a product.

Paradigm Peptides' website had stated it "stringently" tested all their products to ensure "efficacy, purity and potency", but the pair admitted not testing or analysing any of the products they sold, so they had not been aware they had been mixed with testosterone.

News.title: Scientist's lifelong obsession with mystery of elusive 'pink zebra' seaweed
News.content:
The Great Barrier Reef might be the world's most famous underwater ecosystem, but hidden in UK waters lies an ancient marine world you may not have heard of.

Known as maerl beds, these carpets of coral-like seaweed create some of the richest habitats in the sea.

And 40 years ago, while studying one such bed for her PhD, Prof Christine Maggs found a fragment of pink-striped seaweed living on maerl she had never seen before.

The discovery would become a lifelong obsession and a decades-long scientific puzzle.

News.title: What is Iran's Pickaxe Mountain and why does Trump say he wants to bomb it?
News.content:
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to bomb a suspected underground nuclear site in Iran known as Pickaxe Mountain, where recent satellite images appear to show construction work taking place.

Pickaxe Mountain is one of the few Iranian sites linked to the country's nuclear programme that has not been the target of US and Israeli strikes. There have been unproven claims that some of Iran's stock of highly enriched uranium may be kept there, which could be further enriched for use in nuclear weapons.

"We'll be hitting that area pretty soon, and very heavily," Trump told reporters on 21 July. And on 28 July he said: "I know exactly what's going on at Pickaxe. It's not a big problem - we took out their nuclear sites, and we'll have to take out Pickaxe if we don't make a deal."

Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said on 22 July that "no nuclear activity is taking place" at Pickaxe Mountain, and described US threats as "a fabricated pretext for aggression, destruction, and sabotage".

BBC Verify and BBC Persian have spoken to experts and analysed satellite imagery to piece together what we know about the site, and the potential impact of any strike.

News.title: I was working to survive and I wasn't paid
News.content:
What happens when your boss is also the HR department, the grievance handler and the person deciding whether you get paid?

"I just want my wages. It's my hard work. I just want what I'm owed."

Sonia Garcia Monuz is one of several workers trying to recover money she believes she is owed by a catering firm based in Berkshire.

Latest figures show early conciliation cases involving unpaid wages rose by about 17% between 2024 and 2025, according to Acas â the independent body that helps resolve workplace disputes.

Acas says nearly half of hospitality workers, 49%, experience problems at work.

News.title: The Papers: 'Spanish border crisis' and 'iron chancellor'
News.content:
The Daily Telegraph reports, external that Prime Minister Andy Burnham is considering plans to exempt rapists, from the government's early release scheme from prisons in England and Wales. The paper understands that no final decision has been made, and the option is part of a list under review, ahead of an announcement early next week.

In his interview with the Times, external, Chancellor John Healey hinted at benefit cuts when he said that the UK's "inexorably rising welfare bill must be controlled". Healey also echoed the prime minister in declining to commit to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, saying a "target date" will instead be set at the next spending review in 2027.

The Guardian says, external Andy Burnham has been warned he faces the first revolt of his premiership, after indicating he would support fresh drilling in the North Sea. Many Labour MPs are, according to the paper, worried about how that will sit with an electorate alarmed by this summer's soaring temperatures, drought and wildfires. The Guardian quotes the UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, who warned on Friday that every new fossil fuel project makes "tomorrow's heatwaves more dangerous".

The Financial Times leads, external on the influx of migrants into the Spanish territory of Ceuta, saying right-wing leaders including US President Donald Trump have seized on the incident. The paper notes that the 60,000 people who crossed into the exclave is five times the daily peak set in 2015 when hundreds of thousands of refugees entered Europe via Turkey. Ministers in the UK are under pressure from the Conservatives and Reform UK to strengthen Britain's borders, according to the Daily Mail, external. Nigel Farage is quoted saying: "This is a battle for our civilisation." The Daily Express, external, also leading on the story, cites a Conservative MP, Katie Lam, as describing the crisis as a "wake-up call".

The Daily Mirror reports, external that grieving families are calling for a public inquiry into the actions of a funeral director in Hull, who mistreated the remains of dozens of people. Robert Bush was jailed for 20 years. The paper's headline is, "Never Again".

News.title: Victims of disgraced funeral boss demand industry regulation
News.content:
Tristan Essex is standing on the steps of Hull Crown Court, shoulder to shoulder with several others whose lives have been devastated by disgraced funeral director Robert Bush.

The 27-year-old is fighting alongside his sister Claire for regulation of the funeral industry, a journey that has seen them take their campaign to Downing Street and resulted in a new pledge from the government "to take urgent action to crack down on rogue funeral operators".

Their grandmother Jessie Stockdale was one of Bush's victims â her body one of the 35 found at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, five months after her funeral was held.

The news knocked the family off its feet, Tristan said. Even worse, they learned the ashes they had been given were not Jessie's remains.

This story contains details some might find distressing.

News.title: CPS to target assets of jailed funeral director
News.content:
A disgraced funeral director's bank accounts and assets have been frozen, as prosecutors seek to recover cash fleeced from his victims.

Robert Bush was jailed for 20 years at Hull Crown Court on Friday for 67 offences, including denying 30 people a decent and proper burial and giving families the ashes of strangers.

Bush, 48, who ran Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull, stole up to Â£12,000 from charities and sold fake funeral plans.

Laura Tams KC, deputy chief crown prosecutor at the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), said: "We will be looking at him, at the financial aspects of this case, to see if we can confiscate any of the proceeds of his crimes and try to compensate the families."

Sentencing Bush following a five-day hearing, Mr Justice Hilliard said it was clear that he "benefited very substantially" and "obviously lived very well".

Speaking exclusively to the BBC, Tams said it "was not a case of somebody that had recently fallen on hard times".

She added: "I think the scale of the offending, the length of time it had gone on for, showed that really this had become something of his business model."

News.title: Budget in October, Healey announces, as ministers urged to stick to spending limits
News.content:
Healey said the budget would "meet our fiscal rules" and "give businesses and families some of the stability they need to plan for the future".

A report in the Times says the joint letter told ministers they must "within the budgets they have already got" even while "pay[ing] for new things they want to do this year and next".

While the ongoing war in Iran is pushing up inflation and borrowing costs, senior Treasury sources confirmed the government is determined to stay "well within the fiscal rules" inherited from Sir Keir Starmer and his chancellor Rachel Reeves.

But Burnham has said his government will stick to Labour's fiscal rules on spending and borrowing as well as the party's 2024 manifesto pledges not to increase income tax, VAT or national insurance contributions.

He also said he will honour the fiscal rules imposed by Reeves, which include a pledge to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues by the end of the decade.

An influential think tank said earlier this week that the prime minister only has a small margin of error to do this, and that Healey may have to cut spending or raise taxes to meet Burnham's policy priorities such as such as extra defence spending and better social care.

Healey was Defence Secretary under Keir Starmer, but resigned after a row over defence spending commitments - saying he was "certain" that Britain should lift its spending to 3% by 2030.

Questioned about funding on Thursday, Burnham's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting repeatedly refused to commit to that target.

"Before we set out specific spending commitments, we will also set out how we pay for them at the same time," he said.

Reeves left a Â£22bn buffer in her last budget, but persistent inflation due to the Iran war could have eroded it.

On Friday, the PM said he would give all mayors of city regions in England a share of income tax revenue for the first time, as part of his efforts to move power out of London.

Reeves had previously said that regional mayors could be given control of some tax revenue to spend on their local priorities.

Labour pledged to devolve more powers to local councils and mayors as part of its 2024 election manifesto, in areas such as housing and transport.

More details of Burnham's plan are expected to be announced in the Budget, but the government said the rate of income tax will not change as a direct result of the reforms.

AJ Bell public policy director Tom Selby said Healey "doesn't have the luxury of pointing the finger of blame at the last administration".

"Healey will likely spend a chunk of his time leafing through the thesaurus looking for new ways to rephrase the 'tough choices' message of his predecessor," he said.

Shadow chancellor Sir Mel Stride said the announcement of the budget date meant "89 more days of unfunded spending commitments and damaging tax speculation until we get some details".

"89 more days for Brits to wait before they know how much their taxes are going to go up to fund Burnham's spending addiction", he said.

News.title: Southport killer charged with prison attacks and possessing weapon
News.content:
Southport killer Axel Rudakubana has been charged with three attacks while in prison and possessing a weapon.

Police say the offences took place at HMP Belmarsh over six months from May to October 2025.

The 19-year-old murdered Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, Bebe King, six, and Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, and injured eight other children and two adults in an attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in July 2024.

He was given a 52-year sentence in January 2025. Earlier this month he was moved to a secure psychiatric hospital.

Rudakubana is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court remotely on 11 September.

He has been charged with the following four offences:

Assault on an emergency worker on 6 May 2025

Attempted grievous bodily harm on 8 May 2025

Unauthorised possession of an offensive weapon in prison on 26 June 2025

Assault on an emergency worker on 28 October 2025

In May 2025, it was reported boiling water had been thrown on a prison officer at Belmarsh. They were taken to hospital and discharged on the same day.

When Rudakubana was jailed, the judge was unable to impose a whole life order due to him being under-18 when he carried out the attack. He will likely never be released.

On 23 July, the MoJ confirmed Rudakubana was transferred from HMP Belmarsh to Broadmoor, a high-security psychiatric hospital in Berkshire.

Under the Mental Health Act, the MoJ is likely to have had no choice but to accept doctors' recommendations about whether Rudakubana could be held safely in prison.

The decision to transfer him was criticised by a lawyer representing the families of victims.

News.title: Two more small boat pilots jailed for Channel crossings
News.content:
Two men who piloted overcrowded small boats have been jailed for endangering others while crossing the Channel.

Omar Heidari, a 34-year-old Afghan national who steered a dinghy carrying 95 people to the UK in June, has been jailed for two years.

Manas Yuk, an 18-year-old Sudanese national, was sentenced to 18 months in youth detention after piloting a boat carrying 81 people - including a number of children - just days prior.

The men were sentenced at Canterbury Crown Court on Friday having earlier pleaded guilty to endangerment.

It means 10 people have now been sentenced under a law targeting those who risk the safety of others by piloting small boats since it came into force in January.

The Home Office said Heidari had endangered the largest number of lives of anyone so far sentenced for the offence.

The boat was overcrowded during the crossing on 23 June, with some passengers hanging their legs over the sides of the vessel, it said. A number of the passengers were not wearing life jackets.

He was jailed for endangering others as well as arriving in the UK without valid entry clearance.

News.title: Puberty blockers trial can start recruiting children after judge rejects legal challenge
News.content:
A high-profile clinical trial of drugs that can delay puberty in children questioning their gender can go ahead after the High Court rejected a legal challenge by campaigners.

The Pathways trial, run by researchers at King's College London (KCL), will start recruiting more than 220 children aged between 11 and 16 years old from 1 August.

The study was commissioned to assess the benefits or risks of puberty blockers, after a landmark review into gender services found the evidence for treating young people with the drugs was "remarkably weak".

Campaigners who brought the legal action had argued the safeguards in place were inadequate and raised concerns about the long-term physical and psychological effects on young people.

The judge, Mr Justice Chamberlain, refused the application for a judicial review saying that none of the claims made by the campaigners had a realistic chance of success.

He said that each patient involved in the trial will have been assessed over "many months" by specialist doctors who will have "formed the opinion that a child has a reasonable prospect of receiving a clinical benefit from the treatment".

A spokeswoman for KCL welcomed the court's decision, saying the "safety and welfare of young people will remain our highest priority in carrying out this research".

Campaigners, including parents of gender-questioning children, said they were disappointed by the decision saying the "world is watching" a case which has "global implications and high stakes".

News.title: I was in a coma for 42 days after a tick bite on a holiday to Greece
News.content:
A woman has been left with memory loss and seizures and has to take 18 tablets a day after a tick bite on a Greek holiday left her in a coma for nearly six weeks.

Victoria Stellas, from Anglesey, had flu-like symptoms while on the island of Syros in 2019, then - once back home - started having night seizures.

She went to hospital but "no-one knew what was wrong" so had an MRI scan and was flown by helicopter to Liverpool's Walton Centre, external, where she was put in an induced coma for 42 days.

From there Victoria was diagnosed with tick-borne encephalitis, external (TBE), a potentially fatal brain inflammation.

"It's changed my life completely. Apart from the work I don't go out as much," the 51-year-old said.

Mum-of-one Victoria believes she was bitten when she was at her brother-in-law's home as he has goats that can attract ticks.

She said: "I just kept on having seizures and no-one knew what was wrong. It was an unusual infection, and they didn't have the experts I think to diagnose this.

"Altogether it was about six months from when I was in hospital, the treatment afterwards.

"Sometimes I just keep quiet. I was outgoing before."

Victoria said she lost her jobs in a pub and as a teaching assistant at a school for children with special educational needs and disabilities, due to her symptoms.

News.title: Meet the people keeping endangered skills alive
News.content:
Some skills have survived for centuries, passed carefully from one pair of hands to the next using historic techniques that have changed little over time.

But many traditional crafts are now on the brink of extinction, as advances in technology render them obsolete and valuable knowledge fades into the past.

Heritage Crafts' red list reveals those with limited training opportunities and low financial viability are at "serious risk" of disappearing within a generation or two.

While artificial intelligence (AI) and mass production take over, artisans across the west of England are determined to prevent these skills from disappearing forever.

News.title: Used car tycoon sacked for lewd remarks wins High Court fight over takeover plot
News.content:
Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

A used car tycoon who went from living on the street to building a £500 million fortune has lost a legal bid to prove that he was wrongfully dismissed from his own business.

However, he has secured an overall ruling that his company was the victim of a “pre-conceived and orchestrated plan” designed to sideline him and assume control of the £200m company.

Peter Waddell went from being a homeless teenager in Glasgow to owning a London mansion recently listed for £23.5m and a fleet of luxury cars.

The driving force behind the Kent-based used car empire Big Motoring World, Mr Waddell sold a third share of his companies to the private equity firm Freshstream for £72m in 2022, in hopes of spending less time working and more with his family.

The agreement included a "call option" clause, which would have enabled Freshstream to acquire another third of the business, along with overall control, for an additional £72m.

However, in April 2024, the investors initiated a process to oust Mr Waddell as chief executive and seize control of Big Group without paying the further £72m.

They accused him of numerous incidents of gross misconduct, including making sexist, racist, and abusive comments toward colleagues.

It was alleged that he told a female cleaner “I bet you'd like to suck my d***” and referred to Hindi people as Hyundais.

open image in gallery The case was heard at the High Court in London ( PA Archive )

The sacked tycoon, personally and through the company through which he holds his two thirds Big Group stake, Peter Waddell Holdco Ltd (PWHL), went on to sue.

He claimed that he was wrongfully dismissed and that the actions of those aligned with Freshstream, in orchestrating a deliberate plot to sideline him and “strip value” from the formerly thriving business, were “unfairly prejudicial” and not in the best interests of the business.

After a 28-day High Court trial followed by three months of deliberation, Mr Justice Marcus Smith on Friday ruled that Mr Waddell’s dismissal was not unfair.

The judge said that he was guilty of a string of incidents of gross misconduct, the first of which was the comment to the cleaner.

But he went on to find that the unfair prejudice petition on behalf of Mr Waddell's company must succeed, saying that there had been a deliberate plan to oust him and take control of the company by those aligned with Freshstream.

Part of that unfair prejudice had involved not giving Mr Waddell warnings over his language and a chance to moderate his behaviour before he committed gross misconduct, the judge said.

“An otherwise valuable employee can be taught to avoid inappropriate conduct and disciplined through warning, rather than the nuclear option of immediate termination,” he said.

“Mr Waddell’s early inappropriate behaviour was not gross misconduct – although it was misconduct – and I consider that if spoken to firmly and clearly enough... Mr Waddell would have ameliorated his behaviour and not been dismissed in April 2024, or at all. I consider that Mr Waddell was able to control his behaviour, if incentivised to do so.”

He continued: “I have found the formation and execution of a pre-conceived and orchestrated plan which worked backwards from Freshstream’s aim of achieving permanent control of, and Mr Waddell’s removal from, the business without having to exercise the call option.

“The prejudice to PWHL is obvious. Instead of receiving £72m for its shares, PWHL has seen BIG lost to strife, with money lost on massive and commercially unproductive litigation.

“This plan was, in substance, successful.

“The unfair prejudice to PWHL would appear to be obvious. As majority shareholder, PWHL had an interest in BIG being operated lawfully under the direction of its properly appointed CEO, Mr Waddell.

“The execution of the plan was enormously damaging to BIG, with more-or-less open warfare being conducted between the Waddell 'team' and the Freshstream 'team'.

“Whilst it is difficult to quantify the extent of this prejudice, I do not need to do so. It is sufficient that PWHL was deprived of its chosen CEO; and that over a period of two years, the business was run extremely badly and in a state of conflict, some overt, some covert.”

open image in gallery Mr Waddell spent time living on the street as a teen and went on to run a multimillion-pound business ( Champion News )

He went on to say that the consequences of his ruling for the company would be decided at a later hearing.

A spokesman for Mr Waddell said outside court after the ruling, “Mr Waddell now sits back on the board from today”, adding that he intends to “take back control of his company”.

In a statement, Mr Waddell said that the fight had personally cost him £20m, as well as costing the business a similar sum.

Mr Waddell has an astonishing rags-to-riches story, being taken into care at a children's home in Fairlie, North Ayrshire, aged four and living rough on the streets of Glasgow as a teenager before moving to London and becoming a taxi driver.

From a base in Teynham, Kent, he went on to build Big Motoring World, Britain's second biggest second-hand car empire, selling 60,000 vehicles a year and now worth around £500million after branching out into property and haulage.

His Grade-I listed 56-room mansion Holwood House, near Bromley, Kent, was put on the market at £23.5m in 2025.

Mr Waddell has reportedly built an identical pile on Spain's billionaire's row in Puerto Banus, where his neighbours include Novak Djokovic and Simon Cowell.

The house is steeped in history and boasts a swimming pool complex, two gyms, a cinema, music room and tennis court and is set in 50 acres of parkland.

But the tycoon's life was thrown into turmoil when he was removed as the boss of his business in April 2024, after an internal investigation found he had made sexist, racist and abusive comments towards colleagues.

The businessman, suing, said that private equity firm, Freshstream, drove the “unfair” investigation to kick him out of his company.

Alan Gourgey KC, for Mr Waddell, told the court in his written submissions that Freshstream as part of its investment had a contractual “call option” right to eventually buy out the rest of the company and also a right to “step-in” and remove Mr Waddell from the helm of the business under certain circumstances.

Bluebell Cars Holding Ltd said that after a series of complaints of misconduct by staff relating to Mr Waddell making racist, sexist or offensive statements, the “step-in” clause was triggered and it was entitled to remove him and bring in new management.

But his barrister said: “A plan was hatched to oust Mr Waddell from the business through these means. Needless to say, all this took place behind Mr Waddell’s back.

“Whilst the Big Group was hugely profitable under the management of Mr Waddell, its performance significantly deteriorated under the management of [the new chairman] and the FS-controlled board.”

He added that consumer complaints have soared since 2024 and that the business's Trustpilot and Google review scores have plummeted since Mr Waddell was ousted.

“Big Group’s performance has performed disastrously since Mr Waddell’s exclusion from management. It is clear that had he remained in control, he would have steered the business in a very different direction and the business would have been profitable.”

Accusing Freshstream of “unfairly prejudicial conduct”, the barrister said: “It is submitted that the investor is continuing to prioritise its own collateral interests in these proceedings over the objective interests of the business in the mistaken belief that it can simply take the cash from the assets of the business to ultimately achieve a return on its investment.”

Giving his ruling, the judge said that some of Mr Waddell's behaviour at work had been “deeply unattractive” and that he had not been unfairly dismissed.

But he went on to find that there had been a plan to get rid of him, which had caused unfair prejudice to the business overall.

“The unfair prejudice alleged is in essence that the business has been less well run than it would have been had Mr Waddell been CEO. Mr Waddell’s witness statements are full of examples where Mr Waddell asserted that the business had been 'run into the ground'.

“I have found the formation and execution of a pre-conceived and orchestrated plan which worked backwards from Freshstream’s aim of achieving permanent control of, and Mr Waddell’s removal from, the business without having to exercise the call option.

“The execution of the plan was enormously damaging to BIG, with more-or-less open warfare being conducted.

“The prejudice to PWHL is obvious. Instead of receiving £72m for its shares, PWHL has seen BIG lost to strife, with money lost on massive and commercially unproductive litigation.

“Mr Waddell’s early inappropriate behaviour was not gross misconduct – although it was misconduct – and I consider that if spoken to firmly and clearly enough, Mr Waddell would have ameliorated his behaviour and not been dismissed in April 2024, or at all. I consider that Mr Waddell was able to control his behaviour, if incentivised to do so.

“Again...the prejudice to PWHL is obvious.

“In conclusion, I find that the petition succeeds,” the judge concluded.

The remains of a US climber were among three bodies recovered by rescuers on Pakistan’s Broad Peak, where at least 10 mountaineers went missing in an avalanche.

Sarah Mallory Geis from Texas was part of a 10-person expedition being led by the renowned Nepal-born British mountaineer Nirmal Purja, who served in the British Army and Royal Marines.

Her body was identified on Friday, as were those of Nadhira Ahmed ​Abdullah ⁠Al Harthy from Oman and Nepalese citizen Pur Bahadur Gurung, said the regional government in Pakistan's Gilgit-Baltistan.

Purja’s team was attempting to summit Broad Peak, the world’s 12th tallest mountain located on the border with China, when the avalanche struck at midday on Thursday.

Drone footage on Friday showed signs of several more bodies in the search area, said Gilgit-Baltistan officials, although attempts to reach them on the ground have been hampered by bad weather.

The remains of the three mountaineers recovered so far have been taken to hospital by helicopter for "legal formalities regarding identification", according to the Information Department of Gilgit-Baltistan, the local region.

open image in gallery In this photo released by the Alpine Club of Pakistan on Friday, members of a mountaineers rescue team prepare to depart from an airbase on a search operation for climbers missing after an avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak ( AP )

Regional police said the rescue operation ⁠was suspended on Friday night because of weather conditions.

"We hope to continue our operations, both aerial search and the ​ground rescue, ⁠till the time we find the survivors ‌or the dead bodies," said Irfan Arshad, president of the Alpine Club of Pakistan.

The area ‌in which the search is taking place is "remote and difficult", said Sajid Hussain, deputy director of the tourism department in Gilgit-Baltistan.

The Alpine Club of Pakistan earlier reported that four bodies had been located on the mountain, but later clarified that two bodies had been recovered as well as a body part of a climber.

Geis, 39, a resident of San Antonio, was an avid traveller who loved being outdoors, according to her Instagram page.

She announced on social media earlier this year that she was closing her Pilates studio to take “a giant leap of faith into the unknown to see where life goes. I have a sneaking suspicion there will be lots of helmets, harnesses, and crampons involved.”

Rescuers backed by military helicopters resumed the search Saturday for at least six members of a 10-member expedition swept away by an avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak, officials said, a day after authorities recovered three of four bodies found so far.

A local police official, Tahir Khan, said the remains of Omani climber Nathira Ahmed were being flown to the capital, Islamabad, while the bodies of American climber Mallory Geis and Nepalese climber Bahadur Gurung remained at a hospital in Skardu, the main city in Pakistan’s northern Gilgit-Baltistan region.

He said the search and rescue efforts were ongoing despite fading hopes.

The team lost contact with their base camp Thursday after an avalanche struck Broad Peak as they attempted to scale the mountain, said Karrar Haidri, vice president of the Alpine Club of Pakistan on Friday.

He said there has been no contact since then and that experienced Pakistani climbers and army helicopters are taking part in the search-and-rescue operation.

According to the Alpine Club, the expedition included five Nepalese climbers, the Omani and American climbers, Pakistani climber Sohail Sakhi, a Chinese climber identified only as Wang and another foreign climber whose identity has not been released.

The expedition was led by renowned mountaineer Nirmal Purja, the Nepal-born former British Army soldier widely known as Nims Dai. He climbed the world’s 14 highest peaks in a record 189 days in 2019, an achievement featured in the Netflix documentary “14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible.” His record was broken in 2023.

Moving Mountains, a travel company based in Pakistan, announced late last month that the expedition team was on its way to the small town of Askole and wished them a safe journey climbing Broad Peak.

The expedition was Geis’ first try at an 8,000-meter peak in Pakistan, while it was expected to be the final one for Sakhi, who is a guide for the company, as well as a geographer and high-altitude photographer who has climbed some of the world’s major peaks, according to the Moving Mountains website.

Accidents are common on climbing expeditions in northern Pakistan because of avalanches, falling ice and rock, high altitude and rapidly changing weather.

___

Khan reported from Peshawar, Pakistan.

Donald Trump has criticised the “catastrophe” in the Spanish enclave of Cueta, which has been dealing with the mass influx of 60,000 migrants from Morocco.

The US president told a cabinet meeting: “I saw Spain yesterday, and I watched the catastrophe that took place. It looks like an invasion of a country.

“Hundreds of thousands of people. And that same thing’s going to happen to us if the Republicans don’t get elected, except worse, much bigger, much easier to get into.”

His comments echo others made by senior US officials, with the US department of state placing the blame on the socialist administration of Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez.

“This unacceptable incident is the direct result of the Spanish Government’s deliberate efforts to enable and facilitate mass illegal migration into Europe,” they said.

Meanwhile, Italy is suspending the EU's border-free Schengen arrangements with Spain, and has agreed to strengthen controls along the Franco-Italian land border to try to prevent any undocumented migrants ⁠from crossing.

Thousands of migrants have made the journey in the past few days, with Spanish troops deployed to battle the growing crisis on the border.

At least 57 people died while attempting to cross.

Ceuta, along with Melilla, another Spanish autonomous ‌city in northern Morocco, represents ​the European Union's ‌only land border ⁠with Africa.

Arsenal take their pre-season campaign in front of fans for the first time with a trip to Catalonia as they take on LaLiga outfit Girona.

The Gunners eased past MK Dons in a 3-0 behind-closed-doors win a few days ago, with Mikel Arteta hoping to go two for two as preparations continue for their Premier League title defence.

Fans have been whipped up into a frenzy by the Vinicius Jr transfer saga but all eyes will be on Christos Tzolis, the new arrival from Club Brugge who is set to get his first official run-out.

A number of World Cup stars have also rejoined the squad so could be in line to feature for the first time since the end of last term, with the last sight of Arsenal being their Champions League final shootout defeat to Paris Saint-Germain.

Here’s everything you need to know about the clash.

When is Girona vs Arsenal?

Arsenal’s pre-season friendly with Girona kicks off at 7pm BST on Saturday 1 August at Estadi Montilivi.

How can I watch it?

Fans can watch the clash on Arsenal.com by purchasing the pre-season pass, which costs £14.99 - or £9.99 if purchased before 9am on the day of the match. This will also allow you to stream the club’s remaining pre-season fixtures against Real Betis, Borussia Dortmund and Como.

Team news

Arsenal are already lumbered with defensive injury problems after Ben White and Jurrien Timber left the camp nursing fresh woes, joining William Saliba who is out for a number of months with a back issue picked up at the World Cup. Piero Hincapie, Kai Havertz and Viktor Gyokeres have all joined up with the squad after the World Cup so could be in contention.

Girona, meanwhile, welcomed back Morocco midfielder Azzedine Ounahi from World Cup duty who could feature in a midfield against one-time Manchester United flop Donny van de Beek.

Predicted line-ups

Girona XI: Krapyvytsov; A. Martinez, Lopez, Yaakobishvili, Moreno; Beltran, Ounahi; Camara, Misehouy, Gil; Vanat.

Arsenal XI: Kepa; Mosquera, Salmon, Calafiori, Hincapie; Lewis-Skelly, Norgaard; Dowman, Nwaneri, Tzolis; Jesus.

The Tour de France Femmes returns for 2026 on Saturday with possibly the toughest edition yet of what has rapidly become the flagship race for women’s cycling.

Now in its fifth year, the 2026 race features just shy of 19,000m of elevation gain across 1,175km of largely hilly and testing terrain, with an individual time trial on the menu alongside an historic first trip up the legendary Tour climb of Mont Ventoux on stage seven, the race’s queen stage.

The nine-stage race, which begins with three days in Switzerland before crossing into France, could go right down to the wire with an explosive final stage in Nice featuring four climbs of the tough Col d’Eze crammed into less than 100km of racing.

Dutchwoman and 2023 champion Demi Vollering is arguably the favourite to regain her crown but will face fierce competition from reigning champion Pauline Ferrand-Prevot, who has had a mixed season but with everything building towards her title defence.

2024 winner Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, who has finished on the podium in every edition, is another major contender, while the start list also features this year’s breakout star, Paula Blasi, former Giro d’Italia winner Elisa Longo Borghini, and world time-trial champion Marlen Reusser.

Route guide

open image in gallery Tour de France Femmes 2026 route ( ASO )

Stage 1: Lausanne > Lausanne (138km, flat)

The race begins in Lausanne, Switzerland, with a parcours officially classified as ‘flat’ but actually rolling, heading north out of Lausanne and following the shores of the Lac de Neuchatel and Lac Leman. There are four categorised climbs and an uphill finish on the category four Côte Saint-François, which is 2.5km long at an average of 4.6%. The undulating terrain and drag to the line means any number of different types of rider could feature in the finale, which should make for a frantic first day of racing, and a reduced group sprint the most likely outcome.

open image in gallery ( ASO )

Stage 2: Aigle > Geneva (147.9km, flat)

Stage two is much more sprinter-friendly despite another five categorised hills along the way to a flat finish in Geneva, on the second of three days in Switzerland. The stage hugs the shores of Lake Geneva as it heads west away from Lausanne, with all the climbing in the first 100km and a largely flat final 40km, including the last 8km returning to the shore of Lac Leman, for the sprinters’ trains to get organised. Lorena Wiebes, as on every flat finish, is the favourite here.

open image in gallery ( ASO )

Stage 3: Geneva > Poligny (156.5km, hilly)

The hills return on a surprisingly tough stage three, with climbing straight out of the gate as the race leaves Geneva and enters France via the Jura mountains. The Col de la Faucille is the first and most brutal ascent of the day, a category one at 11.4km, averaging 6.3% and kicking off from the gun.

The category three Cote de Lajoux follows straight after the descent off the Faucille and there’s another two categorised climbs on an undulating parcours towards Poligny, before the climbing drops off entirely with the final 24km all flat or downhill. This could be one for a breakaway if enough riders can get organised on the difficult early climbs, or another bunch sprint.

open image in gallery ( ASO )

Stage 4: Gevrey-Chambertin > Dijon (21km, ITT)

After an absence from last year’s edition the individual time trial returns to the Tour de France Femmes; this is the first major test for the general classification contenders and a chance for the TT specialists to have their day in the sun. The first 7km wind their way through flat vineyards before a short but steep climb, the 1.8km Lacets de Marsannay, which pitches uphill at 6.9%. It’s a climb that will suit reigning world TT champion Marlen Reusser to a T but isn’t too long and gruelling for the likes of under-23 rainbow jersey Zoe Backstedt.

The intermediate time check is towards the top but the climb continues at a more gentle incline afterwards, before 6km of fast descent on straight roads into Dijon and a flat finish.

open image in gallery ( ASO )

Stage 5: Macon > Belleville-en-Beaujolais (140km, hilly)

There’s no rest on this Tour as immediately after the time trial the peloton heads back into the hills on what should be a great day of action in the general classification. There are a whopping eight categorised climbs encompassing 2,900m of elevation gain on the jagged profile of stage five, all condensed into 140km.

The first five ascents are all in the first 75km, then there’s a brief break of just under 30km before yet more climbing, with the last categorised rise the cat-two Mont Brouilly. It’s 11.5km from the finish and tough enough without all that prior climbing in the legs: the second half features ramps up to 14% and rarely dips below 10%.

open image in gallery ( ASO )

Stage 6: Montbrison > Tournon-sur-Rhone (153.4km, hilly)

Stage six continues with the same medium-mountain formula as the race enters the Ardeche and Massif Central, with another six categorised climbs, almost all of them short and punchy barring the biggest test of the day, the category two Col de Lalouvesc. That clocks in at 8.6km averaging 5% and comes 105km into proceedings, straight off the descent of an uncategorised rise, before another long descent to a category three climb 16km from the line and a flat finish.

The Col de Lalouvesc will be key: either a breakaway will make a move stick there, or there will be fireworks in the GC; with Mont Ventoux on the horizon there may well be a pause in hostilities among the big names.

open image in gallery ( ASO )

Stage 7: La Voulte-sur-Rhone > Mont Ventoux (146.8km, mountains)

Each year the Tour de France Femmes has visited a legendary climb, from the Col du Tourmalet to the Col de la Madeleine last year, and this year it’s time for the infamous Mont Ventoux to make its debut. There are three other categorised climbs first - the Col de la Grande Limite (6.6km at 5%), Col du Colombier (3.2km at 6.4%), and the Col de Suzette (3.9km at 6.4%) - but today’s action is really entirely condensed into the final 20km.

The Giant of Provence (15.7km at 8.8%) is approached from its toughest side from Bédoin, with a summit finish atop its iconic lunar-like slopes, while if there’s a headwind, as there often is, the 11% final drag will be even more leg-sapping than usual. Expect fireworks.

open image in gallery ( ASO )

Stage 8: Sisteron > Nice (171.9km, flat)

After the explosive stage seven stage eight is somewhat calmer, a transitional run towards the coast, albeit not easy by any stretch: it’s the longest stage of the race at over 170km and with another four categorised climbs, encompassing 1,420m of elevation gain in total. After the Col de Routes Aures there’s a very long descent towards the Cote d’Azur - 75km, in fact - with another two short, sharp category four climbs inside the final 15km before a descent onto the Promenade des Anglais and flat finish in Nice.

open image in gallery ( ASO )

Stage 9: Nice > Nice (99.2km, mountains)

A processional, champagne-sipping run to the Champs-Elysees this is not: the final stage of the Tour de France Femmes is a punchy one, with a shark’s-tooth profile featuring four laps of the Col d’Eze climb (famous for its inclusion in Paris-Nice). The riders will be climbing and descending all day with no let-up, and there’s every chance the GC standings could be radically overhauled.

The first three ascents are category two, 7.7km at 5.9%, with the last time up shorter but harder, 6km at an average of 7.6% via the Chemin du Vinaigrier, with the descents all the same. The last 2km are flat with the finish line on the Promenade des Anglais.

This could be won by a general classification hopeful, the yellow jersey stamping their authority on the race one last time, or any climber let off the leash on the last day. It should make for a dramatic final day’s racing.

open image in gallery ( ASO )

Who are the contenders?

Chief among the contenders is the Netherlands’ Demi Vollering, who won this race in 2023 and won the Giro d’Italia in June to complete the full set of Grand Tour wins. The European champion is in stunning form, having won Liege-Bastogne-Liege and the Tour of Flanders among other races in a glittering Classics campaign before that recent Giro triumph. Her FDJ Suez-United team is assembled entirely around her, with the likes of French climber Evita Muzic and this year’s Paris-Roubaix champion Franziska Koch excellent lieutenants.

Defending champion Pauline Ferrand-Prevot has had a middling season so far; third place at Paris-Roubaix was the highlight but her results have otherwise been average, including a rather anonymous showing at the Vuelta Femenina. But she has been open about building her season entirely towards the Tour and having cemented her triumph on the Col de la Madeleine last year the inclusion of Mont Ventoux will suit her, although the individual time trial is much better suited to Vollering than the Frenchwoman.

2024 champion Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney has been on the podium of every edition and reliably brings her best to the Tour; her Canyon-SRAM squad is a strong one, too, including former Giro d’Italia podium finisher Antonia Niedermaier, who will provide support in the mountains. But although she has been putting in significant time on the TT bike the time trial does not play to her strengths, and she has not looked able to match Vollering on the climbs so far this year.

open image in gallery Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney has finished on the podium at every edition of the race, as has Demi Vollering ( AFP/Getty )

Young Spanish prodigy Paula Blasi blew away the field at this year’s Vuelta Femenina and will be co-leader for UAE Team L'IMAD alongside two-time Giro winner Elisa Longo Borghini, with the team able to play multiple cards. Longo Borghini has had a difficult year hampered by illness but is the more natural leader of the team; the squad will likely have to balance the pair’s competing interests, particularly if Blasi arrives in the same barnstorming form as she displayed in Spain, where she was particularly impressive on the toughest climbs - which bodes well for Mont Ventoux. UAE also have Maeva Squiban, who won two stages last year, and Dominika Wlodarczyk, who finished fourth last year.

Movistar leader Marlen Reusser has had a run of bad luck at the sport’s biggest races, including abandoning last year’s Tour with illness on stage one, and crashes and illness have held her back at points this season too. But she won her home race, the Tour de Suisse, earlier this summer and looks to be back at her best; the 34-year-old can climb with the best and as reigning time-trial world champion will expect to gain time on her rivals on stage four.

Finally, SD Worx-Protime will be led by Anna van der Breggen, a legend of the sport who may not be quite at her electric best but is certainly not far off it. Second at the Vuelta and third at the Giro, where she wore the maglia rosa for much of the race, indicate she remains a serious threat. High mountains like Mont Ventoux have always suited her and the ITT also plays in her favour.

News.title: Massage guns vs compression boots: Which is better for muscle recovery?
News.content:
Looking after your body is no longer just about getting a good workout in; it’s ensuring that you’re properly recuperating afterwards, too. Luckily, in 2026, there is a huge range of products designed to aid recovery.

In fact, the recovery tech boom is playing a big role in the growth of the sports technology market overall. Estimates show it’s projected to grow from $39.6 billion in 2026 to $192.3 billion by 2034.

Two of the most popular products in this category are massage guns and compression boots. Both claim to ease muscle soreness and help you bounce back to training sooner, but they sit at very different price points. You can pick up a basic gun from around £40, whereas the cheapest boots we tested were £300. But which method is actually better for improving workout recovery?

Massage guns can help to improve flexibility in older muscles

Massage guns work by delivering repeated percussion and vibration to one specific area, which helps improve the mobility and flexibility of a specific muscle. In turn, this can make your muscles feel less tense and stiff. These gadgets can be used before and after workout sessions.

While useful for all ages, massage guns can be helpful for anyone looking to improve range of movement, ease muscle stiffness and boost blood flow – whether exercising or not.

“It will help temporarily improve your mobility so that you feel like you’ve got a bit more flexibility in that muscle,” explains Jonathan Wreaves, clinical physiologist at preventative health clinic Viavi.

But how do they actually work?

Most massage guns offer a revolutions per minute (RPM) range, which refers to how many times the massage head moves back and forth every minute. This tends to be somewhere between 1200 and 3500. The lower range is ideal for gentle massage and warming up, while a higher RPM is better for targeting bigger muscle groups and more intense tightness.

News.title: Battle rages over access to new ‘miracle’ HIV drug
News.content:
For the first time in the four-decade fight against HIV there is a “miracle” drug that can all but eliminate the risk of infection, but in the Latin American countries where it was tested almost no one can get it.

Trials show that Lenacapavir, made by Gilead Sciences, is almost 100 per cent effective in preventing HIV infection. With just two shots a year, those taking it will avoid contracting the virus even when frequently exposed.

The drug, which many believe could bring an end to the global HIV pandemic, costs $14,000 a dose in the United States. Gilead has agreed to licence generic versions of the pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) medication at around $40 a dose in 120 low-and middle-income countries, but almost all of Latin America is excluded.

Brazil, Mexico, Argentina and Peru are among those with serious HIV epidemics that are shut out, despite having run some of the clinical trials that proved the drug works.

Their status as “upper-middle income countries” means they are too rich to qualify for the cut price generic version and yet they remain too poor to pay the US price.

News.title: Senior dating: a guide to finding love later in life
News.content:
Whether you’re a widow, widower or divorcee, the thought of online dating in later life can feel daunting. However, more and more people are turning to the internet to find romance. Roughly 16 per cent of UK adults are using online dating services to meet a partner, according to Statista. Among them, there are lots of singles over 50 using dating sites.

So here’s how to navigate your senior dating online, with expert advice from psychologist and dating coach Dr Pam Spurr, and sex and relationship coach Angela Vossen.

How do I know if I'm ready to date again as a senior?

Coming out of any relationship is hard. If you’re hoping to date after a divorce, bereavement or break up, it can take a long time to feel ready to date again. Dr Spurr advises taking your time.

“Many people feel bruised, even traumatised, after coming out of a long-term relationship or having been bereaved,” she explains. “Your feelings naturally vary from day to day about whether you're ready to get back out to look for love – or even for fun. A crucial factor is if you've come to the point where you have more good days compared to bad days”.

Dr Spurr explains that good days are the days on which you feel more optimistic about life generally, and you find your thoughts turning to meeting someone new. “That's an important sign that you are healing,” she says. “However, if you're still feeling deeply insecure or are riddled with self-doubt about your worthiness, take your time. When you feel worthy, you will find someone worthy of you”.

Feeling heartbroken? Learn how to get over a break up

How to start senior dating online

If you’re new to online dating, it can feel intimidating at first. The secret is taking things step by step so that you do things at your own pace. The first step, however, should be choosing a senior dating site that will help match you with like-minded people. This will narrow your search and ensure your dating experience is more successful.

Step 1: Create an online profile

Once you’ve decided on a dating site or app and signed up, you’ll be asked to write a dating profile. This should reflect who you are along with your passions, values and what you seek in a partner.

Try to be authentic rather than creating a fantasy version of yourself. If you exaggerate your accomplishments, your date will only feel deceived once they get to know you. Likewise, don’t be tempted to use a photo of yourself from 10 years ago.

What are you waiting for? |  Single and looking to find true love? Sign up today for Telegraph Dating and join more than 220,000 like-minded people. Join today

Step 2: Spark meaningful chats with potential dates

Once you have signed up to a senior dating site and created a profile, you will be free to start looking at other people’s profiles and sending messages to anyone that catches your attention. But how can you initiate a conversation after an introduction?

“When messaging people on dating sites, ask open-ended questions to spark meaningful chats,” says Angela. A good example would be, ‘I can see you enjoy travel. What place have you always wanted to visit but haven’t yet?’ or “tell me more about your love of tennis? Did you watch the US Open?” If things go really well and the chat seems to flow naturally, you may decide to organise a phone chat or ask them out on a date. An initial chat over the phone can help gauge how well you get on and how easily the conversation flows. If this goes well, meeting in person may feel less nerve wracking and a little less ‘blind’.

Step 3: Prioritise your safety

“While most people are well intentioned online, it’s important to protect your safety,” advises Ms Vossen. “Keep personal details private (like where you live or your social media profiles) until you’ve met in person and built trust”. You should also arrange first dates in public places, share your plans with a friend, and trust your instincts if something feels off.

If the first date or two doesn’t quite hit the mark, try not to be too disappointed and remember that you can say no to another date. Ms Vossen says: “Be patient – online dating takes time, but with practice, you’ll gain confidence and enjoy the journey”.

Traditional ways to meet senior singles

Of course, couples continue to meet in a manner that predates online dating sites. If you’re keen to join the older dating scene but find the online world overwhelming, there are plenty of ways to meet people in real life.

1. Holidays and group trips

We are often our best selves on holiday, so it’s the ideal place to find a single senior woman or to meet men if the opportunity presents itself. Why not organise a trip on which you meet new people while doing what you love, whether that’s cycling, walking, sightseeing or just travelling around a new part of the world. There are many escorted tours that cater to specific age groups and interests. They also take away the stress of organising a trip yourself.

“An organised holiday or trip can be a great place to meet someone new and there are many organisations offering these for the over 50s,” says Dr Spur. “A word of caution though, you can spend a lot of money and there's no guarantee that you will meet that special person. However, if it's a place you've wanted to travel to then go with the mindset that you're going to have a great trip. If you meet someone, that's an added bonus”.

2. Activities and social groups

Whether you enjoy walking, reading or volunteering, taking up a new hobby or joining a social group is a great way to enhance your social life and increase your chances of meeting a new romantic interest.

“Joining a club or taking up a hobby can be a fantastic way of meeting singles who enjoy the same pastimes,” says Dr Spur. “You're doing an activity you enjoy knowing that there might also be someone there that will catch your eye”.

If you do meet someone that you’re interested in at a social event, Dr Spur advises starting with a simple ‘hello’ and an easy question such as how long they've been doing that particular activity or hobby. “This can open-up a friendly conversation that might lead to flirting down the line,” she says.

Start online dating for seniors today

Whichever way you decide to start looking for love, approach it in a way that you feel comfortable with. Signing up to an online dating service is a great way to meet other seniors. Remember, it’s never too late to begin a new chapter.

News.title: UK economy to flatline, warns Bank of England
News.content:
Britain’s economy is set to almost grind to a halt for the rest of the year, the Bank of England has warned.

Growth will drop to just 0.1pc per quarter, the Bank predicted, slowing sharply after a strong start to 2026.

Higher petrol prices and energy bills, a weak jobs market and rising mortgage costs are all draining confidence and spending power from the economy.

Inflation, which slowed to a 15-month low of 2.6pc in June, is also expected to rise again to 3.2pc later this year, the Bank warned.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s Governor, said inflation had “fallen faster than we’d expected” but warned that war in the Middle East would lead to a fresh spike.

He added that growth would “weaken slightly further in the near term as the effects of the conflict weigh further on demand”.

The Bank also predicted that unemployment will rise back above 5pc in the coming months, limiting workers’ ability to ask for higher wages to cope with rising living costs.

It presents a challenging backdrop for Andy Burnham and his Chancellor, John Healey, who have pledged to help voters struggling with the cost of living.

The forecasts came as policymakers led by Mr Bailey held interest rates at 3.75pc.

Although three members of the nine-strong Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) voted for higher rates, up from two at the previous meeting, the Governor dismissed suggestions the Bank is moving towards higher interest rates.

The public should “not… [think] the Bank of England is edging towards a hike,” Mr Bailey said.

“Frankly there is nothing I have said, or any of us have said, along those lines. We took a decision today to leave the Bank Rate unchanged and that is the relevant conclusion.”

Clare Lombardelli, a Deputy Governor, said voting to keep rates at 3.75pc “was not a close judgement”, calling the decision “pretty clear” given slowing inflation in the domestic economy.

Officials are monitoring the economy for any signs that increases in oil, gas and petrol prices caused by the war in Iran are creeping into higher costs and wages in the wider economy.

Mr Bailey said: “The possibility of repeated resumptions of conflict, combined with lower than usual European gas stock levels and a fall in global refining output, mean that risks to energy prices lie to the upside.”

He added: “Reassuringly, there are few signs so far that second-round effects are generating more broad-based inflationary pressures.”

Companies are struggling to pass higher costs on to their customers because of the economy’s weakness, he added.

Workers are typically securing only modest pay rises as the weak jobs market leaves them in a poor position to push for bigger salaries.

Mr Bailey stressed there are still major risks to the outlook given the war and promised to “monitor the situation carefully” and was “ready to adjust our stance”.

“It is our job to ensure that inflation gets back to the 2pc target and stays there, and that is what we will do,” he said.

Borrowing costs dropped in financial markets after the decision.

The Government’s two-year borrowing cost fell from 4.44pc to 4.34pc, the sharpest fall in a month.

The FTSE 250 index of mid-sized UK companies rose 0.8pc to a record high of 24,184.10.

Traders still believe the Bank will raise interest rates twice within a year.

However, Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said rate rises “remain more a threat than a reality”.

He said there was evidence of disinflation in the economy and interest rates could be “cut to 3pc in 2027”, adding: “That’s very different to market pricing for rates to be close to 4.5pc in 2027.”

News.title: Arsonists torch more Ebola clinics as misinformation spirals in DRC
News.content:
Two more Ebola treatment facilities have reportedly been burned down in recent days as health officials struggle to overcome violent public mistrust of medical teams.

At least a dozen facilities have now been attacked since Congo declared its Ebola outbreak amid fear, misinformation and suspicion of outside authorities.

The outbreak is the fastest growing on record and officials said the virus had now killed more than 1,500 people.

The official death toll from the outbreak centred on the north eastern Ituri province of Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has risen by 500 in only a week.

Sources told the Telegraph the large jump in deaths was largely caused by a “data harmonisation exercise” between different regions, and the new deaths may not have all happened in the past week.

However, the daily confirmed toll has also continued to climb sharply with the latest government update reporting 50 people dying in the previous 24 hours.

Airfinity, a health analytics firm, said the outbreak “continues to outpace detection and the response” and there is a high chance of it spreading further inside DRC.

News.title: Race for vaccine against new Ebola strain gets $8.5m boost
News.content:
The “most promising” vaccine to tackle the Ebola strain behind an explosive outbreak in the Congo has been given an $8.5 million boost, as researchers race to develop an effective shot.

So far at least 3,360 people have been infected and 1,487 people have died in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), in an epidemic triggered by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola.

But unlike past outbreaks of the more common Zaire strain, there are currently no approved vaccines to tackle Bundibugyo.

On Thursday, the Coalition of Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (Cepi) revealed up to $8.5 million of funding for the only single-dose inoculation, which was described as the “most promising vaccine candidate” by the World Health Organization (WHO) in an analysis in May.

It is being developed by researchers at Hilleman Laboratories – a unique partnership between the pharmaceutical giant Merck and the British philanthropic powerhouse Wellcome, which is headquartered in Singapore.

The vaccine candidate is a Bundibugyo version of the Ervebo shot, which was created by Merck (MSD in Europe) and has already been approved for Ebola Zaire.

It uses a rVSV platform, where a modified version of VSV virus is used to train the immune system to react to target pathogens – in this instance, the Bundibugyo species replaces Zaire.

News.title: AMR chatbot could prevent drug-resistant infections in African hospitals
News.content:
A phone-based chatbot advising medics how to prescribe antibiotics has helped raise the quality of care in African hospitals and should stop bugs developing dangerous resistance, developers say.

Staff at four hospitals across Zambia and Kenya have been using two digital tools in a pilot project to try to address one of the world’s biggest health threats.

Anti-microbial resistance (AMR) is caused by germs evolving so that medicines such as antibiotics designed to kill them no longer work.

The menace is linked to nearly five million deaths each year and makes it increasingly difficult to treat infections. The annual death toll could nearly double in the next 25 years, according to some forecasts.

The rise in AMR is being significantly driven by the misuse and overuse of antimicrobials in human medicine and in agriculture.

Using antibiotics when they are not necessary, using the wrong ones, or getting the dosage wrong, all add to the chances that bugs will develop resistance.

With a shortage of new drugs in the development pipeline, one push to defeat AMR has been to get medics to stick to existing prescription, dosage and treatment advice.

The Antibiotic Stewardship Programme through Innovation, Research, and Education (ASPIRE) is trying to give them guidance using technology they already have in their pockets.

Sports.title: Who is FIFA president Gianni Infantino’s wife Leena Al Ashqar and how many children do they have together?
Sports.content:
FIFA'S FIRST LADY Who is FIFA president Gianni Infantino’s wife Leena Al Ashqar and how many children do they have together?

GIANNI INFANTINO has been in charge of FIFA since 2016, when he took over from Sepp Blatter.

The Italian, who was re-elected in 2019, has courted controversy for his off-script comments at times.

And his recent bid to sell off a chunk of a new sister company in charge of the World Cup collapsed following Uefa’s boycott promise and a “brand nightmare” for potential investors.



But one person who will stick by his side no matter what is wife Leena Al Ashqar, and here is what SunSport know about Fifa’s first lady.



Who is Leena Al Ashqar?

Infantino is married to Leena Al Ashqar, a woman of Lebanese heritage.

The pair are thought to have met in the early 2000s when Leena worked for the Lebanese Football Federation.

The couple share four daughters together and currently resides in Zug, Switzerland.



Their youngest daughter, Dhalia Nora, became ill at the 2018 Russia World Cup.

It was reported that she needed to have an emergency operation to treat her appendicitis.

Infantino, who was with his wife at the time, is said to have been very grateful to the hospital in St Petersburg.



What was Gianni Infantino’s World Cup sell-off plan?

FIFA president Gianni Infantino was plotting an outlandish move to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

The scheme, which would involve forming a company to control the World Cup and Club World Cup and potentially earn Infantino tens of millions of pounds, was quickly blasted by Uefa.

Potential investors were reportedly briefed on the plot that would also see each of Fifa’s 211 member associations handed a £15m share of the company that they could choose to sell themselves.

According to The Times, figures close to Donald Trump’s administration are amongst those consulted about the plans.

The blueprint would likely drive Fifa – currently a non-profit organisation – to focus more on commercial revenue due to outside pressure from investors.



That could see the World Cup expanded from 48 teams to 64 and prioritising host nations based on their commercial potential.

However, on Friday, July 31, Fifa announced that they have scrapped Infantino’s plans.
