Sports.title: Fifa scraps proposal to sell off stakes in World Cup after widespread backlash
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino’s proposal to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors has sensationally collapsed, with the Fifa president admitting the project “has created divisions of a nature that are no longer in the interest of the objective”, amid widespread anger globally.

The plan had caused ructions within football around the world, leading Uefa to threaten a boycott of future Fifa tournaments if it was not shelved. Other confederations had also come out in opposition while one of Infantino’s senior advisors, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned on Friday in protest at the scheme. The Fifa chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, had also aimed a scathing rebuke at Infantino’s “serious lack of respect” in seeking to force it through with minimal consultation.

It has led Infantino to back down amid speculation the venture capital firm Thrive Capital, which was leading the proposed investor group, had also expressed doubts after a week that threatened to tear the sport apart. Infantino’s previously secure presidency has come under severe pressure and it remains to be seen whether his climbdown will be enough to save his position.

“Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place,” Infantino said in a statement.

“Our purpose has always been – and will always be – to unite and improve. As a result, this proposal will not proceed. Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, particularly in those countries that mostly need our support.”

The proposed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), unveiled earlier this week, had been intended to raise hundreds of millions of dollars by selling a significant stake in the commercial rights of the men’s and women’s World Cups, and the Club World Cup, to investors. It promised an increase in distribution to “over $10bn” (£7.5bn) being spread back among Fifa’s 211 member associations. A deadline of 19 September had been set for member associations to sign up to the scheme, which offered an optional $20m (£14.8m) to those participating.

But the plan was roundly rejected by European countries’ FAs, who agreed upon a boycott at an emergency meeting on Thursday. Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation, the latter with a stinging statement on Friday morning, had also made their distaste clear. While Infantino retains a stronghold in Africa he was left with nowhere to go, the numbers to push through the plan in any credible form having eluded him.

Attention will now turn to Infantino’s future given the scale of the internal revolt within Fifa and the severe hit his standing has taken elsewhere. It is unlikely his withdrawal of the plan will sway member associations who had already become deeply disenchanted by his handling of the Folarin Balogun affair, which unfolded three weeks previously during the World Cup. But some observers have wondered whether recourse to Fifa’s reserves, which stand at around $4bn (£2.97bn), for the promised FFE cash would convince enough federations to save his skin.

Uefa and other confederations have stepped up their search for candidates to run against Infantino in next year’s Fifa election, in which he had been expected to comfortably win a fourth term. Their appetite is unlikely to change and time will tell whether Infantino can turn his fortunes around after an episode that has had a shattering impact on his credibility.

Sports.title: Marketing stunt or ‘extraordinary’ transfer? Ravenna fans ride wave of the Ronaldinho Effect
Sports.content:
On a scorching summer afternoon in Ravenna, a city far better known for its fifth-century Byzantine mosaics and Dante’s tomb than for footballing glory, eyes are peeled in the historic centre for one of world football’s most recognisable figures – a man who featured in the World Cup final half-time show alongside Madonna and Ronaldo: Ronaldo de Assis Moreira, better known as Ronaldinho.

“We haven’t seen him yet,” four Ravenna supporters sitting at a cafe say with dry irony as they flip through La Gazzetta dello Sport, Italy’s famous pink sports daily. They are undeniably sceptical, viewing the signing as a purely commercial operation, yet deep down they still harbour the dream of seeing the 2005 Ballon d’Or and 2002 World Cup winner wear their yellow and red shirt.

It is a small, surreal glimpse into the whirlwind that has engulfed this quiet corner of Emilia-Romagna, thanks to the business instinct of Ignazio Cipriani. Heir to the Venetian hospitality dynasty behind the renowned Harry’s Bar, Cipriani took over the club in 2024 when they were in Serie D, the fourth tier of Italian football. A native of Ravenna, he is the grandson of Raul Gardini, the Italian chemicals tycoon and sailor who steered Il Moro di Venezia to the 1992 America’s Cup final.

In his first year as president, Cipriani oversaw victory in the Serie D Cup and promotion to the professional ranks of Serie C. But that is merely the first step in a long ascent, he says: “It’s not a provocation. Serie A is the goal I declared from day one because I intend to reach it. And the Champions League remains the ultimate horizon we want to walk towards, step by step. I made this statement because I like working with my back against the wall: when you have no way out, you are forced to find solutions instead of excuses. I prefer to remove every alibi from the beginning.”

And this summer, Cipriani pulled off a surprise move – so surprising that anyone reading the headlines assumed it was a prank: bringing the 46-year-old Ronaldinho back as a player.

View image in fullscreen Ronaldinho holds up a Ravenna top with Ignazio Cipriani, the club president, after the surprise move was announced in Miami in June. Photograph: Rebecca Blackwell/AP

“We met through Lorenzo Tonetti and Ariedo Braida,” Cipriani says, “two people who worked for over 20 years at AC Milan and had Ronaldinho as a player. The idea of involving him was a dream I cultivated as soon as I bought the club. Thanks to Lorenzo and Ariedo, we met, started talking, and a genuine friendship grew. From that relationship came many ideas for the club’s growth. And to the question everyone is asking, I am happy to answer: Ronaldinho will wear the Ravenna shirt as a player, and he will try – maybe scoring the last goal of his career with us!”

Meanwhile, a dedicated website has already put a special-edition shirt on sale featuring the “R10” logo – the Brazilian’s personal brand – which sold out within a few hours. It represents a striking collision of high-end global branding, small-town football, and brilliantly executed marketing stunt.

“If someone had told me three years ago that Ronaldinho was coming to Ravenna, I would have sent them straight to the psychiatric ward,” says Fabio laughing, a lifelong supporter. “The night the news broke, international headlines everywhere read ‘Ronaldinho to Ravenna’. It was an extraordinary operation.”

Ravenna is no footballing giant. Plagued by bankruptcies in 2001 and 2012, the club has spent decades bouncing around the lower tiers, with seven seasons in Serie B the highest point. Historically a volleyball stronghold, the football scene was accustomed to modest budgets and regional rivalries.

View image in fullscreen Ronaldinho will be aiming to wow the crowds at Ravenna’s Stadio Bruno Benelli this season. Photograph: Roberto Salomone/The Guardian

“Ronaldinho is a unique icon,” Cipriani says. “His way of playing made my generation fall in love with the game. We want him today to make the next generation of fans, in Italy and around the world, fall in love with Ravenna . It’s not just a visibility stunt; it’s about building a bridge between different eras of football and growing a truly global fanbase around it.”

To support this ambitious sporting and industrial project, the club is working with the municipality to renovate the Stadio Bruno Benelli, increasing its capacity beyond 6,300. But the president’s ultimate dream is a new multi-purpose venue open seven days a week, featuring retail spaces, concert facilities, and an integrated Hotel Cipriani linked to the city’s international tourism expansion.

For Ravenna’s mayor, Alessandro Barattoni, the arrival of a world-famous figure fits neatly into a broader strategy to promote the city globally. In recent years, Ravenna has been expanding its international reach beyond traditional beach tourism and commercial ports. The city is enjoying renewed ties with the Anglo-Saxon world, highlighted by a recent visit from the British royal family and the opening of the Lord Byron Museum.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“Ronaldinho brings a whole new level of global fame,” Barattoni says. “When the news broke, my phone exploded with messages from former schoolmates. For younger kids today, he might be someone to discover on YouTube, but the fascination remains intact.” With a smile, the mayor adds that, schedule permitting, he would be delighted to personally guide Ronaldinho on a tour of the city’s cultural heritage.

However, Barattoni is quick to clarify the institution’s role: “Our common ground with the club is internationalisation: bringing Ravenna’s image to the world. Ronaldinho has been a global ambassador for countless brands. There is an overarching project that can bring great visibility to the team and allow the city to showcase its initiatives beyond standard routes.” He adds: “Even before Ronaldinho’s arrival, the club did a fantastic job engaging younger generations. The average age in the stands is lower, more vibrant, and more engaged than ever before. A genuine sense of community is forming.”

View image in fullscreen Alessandro Barattoni, the mayor of Ravenna, is confident the Ronaldinho transfer will be positive for the Italian city. Photograph: Roberto Salomone/The Guardian

Yet, fears of a hyper-commercialised image linger among traditional supporters. In the Curva Mero, such marketing moves are approached with caution. “There is a certain reluctance among some factions,” Fabio admits. “Modern football pushes values that many don’t share: rising ticket prices, losing accessibility for lower-income families. As a result, visibility and marketing stunts risk being viewed sideways.”

Cipriani demonstrates an acute awareness of these dynamics: “Without roots, no global project makes sense,” the president says. “Ravenna is not a brand we are building from scratch; it’s a history and an identity that existed before us. Tradition isn’t a brake on ambition: it’s the foundation. A club without its people is worth nothing.”

“I’m 50 years old and I’ve been coming to the stadium since my school days,” says Giovanni, another fan. “I’m rediscovering the enthusiasm of the past. If it takes an icon like Ronaldinho and a local entrepreneur to make us dream of Serie A, then so be it. The important thing is never to forget the people in the stands.”

Riding the wave of the “Ronaldinho Effect”, the season-ticket campaign has just launched with a target of selling 2,800. Ticket prices have risen by an average of about 12%, with variations across different stadium sections.

For now, Ravenna is soaking up a dizzying, galvanising atmosphere. On the pitch, the club is assembling a squad to win the league; off it, the city awaits 20 August, when Ronaldinho is expected to appear during a three-day summer festival in nearby Marina di Ravenna, organised in signature Cipriani style.

Sports.title: Have you ever switched allegiance as a football fan? You are not alone | Luke McLaughlin
Sports.content:
“I was fanatically pro-German when the Germans were here to protect us against the Americans, and now that Americans are here to protect us against the Germans, I am fanatically pro-American … you and your country will have no more loyal partisan in Italy than me – but only as long as you remain in Italy.”

This passage from Joseph Heller’s Catch-22 – as an old Italian man explains the logic behind his fickle wartime expedience to a naive American soldier – plays with the question of what constitutes true strength. Universally perceived as weak, Italy are in fact the strongest nation in the second world war, according to the old man. And that, sort of, explains my feelings on football fandom.

My dad was passionate about cricket and chess. But I was a football-mad kid, and he dutifully escorted my brother and I to watch West Ham v Nottingham Forest at Upton Park in November 1987. Dad naturally knew about Brian Clough and correctly predicted it would be an entertaining game: the hosts won 3-2.

After that ridiculously exciting day as a 10-year-old, and despite living in south London, I became a Forest supporter, despite photos existing of me in Everton and Tottenham kits earlier in childhood. My mid-1980s decision to support Everton, for clarity, had been pure, unadulterated glory-hunting. Why I then decided to switch to Tottenham, I don’t recall, but it may have had something to do with Paul Gascoigne’s unique ability.

Geographically I should have supported Crystal Palace or Millwall given I was brought up between their grounds: I vividly remember visiting the Den with a Swindon-supporting schoolmate during the era of Terry Hurlock.

As a cricket fan, I have stuck with Middlesex since childhood, but there was never any familial impetus to support a football club. My brother became an Arsenal fan and when I was old enough to regularly attend games alone I started following Forest around London, including a draw at the Den in 1993-94 marred by post-match violence after a Stan Collymore equaliser ended Millwall’s playoff hopes.

When Forest sank into the doldrums after the magical mid-90s, I started to pay less attention to them in classic fairweather-fan fashion. Recently, when living in Somerset, I dabbled with being a Yeovil supporter. Now back living in London I am a regular patron at the Den and have begun to follow Millwall’s results more than Forest’s.

It’s not unusual to support an overseas club either, and after a formative experience watching Napoli lose to Chelsea in 2012 a passion for the Italian club emerged. I’ve visited Naples several times, made good friends there and seen a few games. The most memorable trip was in May 2023 when the Serie A title was sealed under Luciano Spalletti. I didn’t have a ticket but ultimately didn’t need one: the entire city was electrified by their (our) third scudetto.

View image in fullscreen ‘As a teenage follower of Forest, I felt my personal fortunes were linked to the club’s.’ Bayern Munich’s Jürgen Klinsmann takes on Steve Chettle in 1996. Photograph: Lee Beskeen/Action

For some people switching, or even mixing, football allegiances remains taboo. Devoted supporters of a single club may regard my experience as a sign of weakness, or at least exceptional fickleness. But “fan” is short for “fanatic”, and I am no longer convinced so much emotional energy should be invested in supporting any club. Why, after all, would I associate my happiness and sense of fulfilment with something I can’t control? Was the obvious and sustained misery of Arsenal fans as they edged nervously to the Premier League title worth the payoff? Perhaps it was, but there is clearly something unhealthy in that level of obsession.

It is possible, after all, to be too emotionally invested in a certain outcome for your own wellbeing. As an avid teenage follower of Forest, I felt my personal fortunes were linked to the club’s. I regarded one particularly inept late-90s defeat by Wimbledon as a personal tragedy that raised serious questions about my future happiness. I still love football – I am just more ambivalent to its outcomes.

Not only is it acceptable to switch allegiance, it actually makes more sense to base your support on what’s going on in your life at the time. If professional athletes can represent more than one country, let alone several clubs, why shouldn’t fans switch teams?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The disparity between mercenary players and loyal fans grows ever bigger and more grotesque. The players earn obscene amounts of money, and wield a disproportionate amount of power, but often show zero loyalty to a club and its fans when a better offer appears. How can any of this make sense for the lifelong supporter?

And being a diehard fan can be a compromising position in so many ways, frequently leading to defending the indefensible, from unethical petro-state sportwashing and financial doping to obvious on-field foul play and even spying. If you are a glory-hunting Manchester City devotee with a hidden Manchester United-supporting past, or have ever done a football-supporting switcheroo of any kind, do not be ashamed. There is help available. There are people who understand.

Since becoming a regular attendee at Millwall, I’ve enjoyed watching matches with one of my oldest friends and his son. A tight, noisy, old-fashioned ground, no video assistant referee, close to home … have I finally become a real fan?

As long as I live in London I will enjoy following Millwall … with Forest and Napoli thrown in. Not forgetting Dulwich Hamlet. Should I ever return to Somerset, though, I’ll be Yeovil till I die.

Sports.title: Rangers held by Dundee United to kick off McInnes era and Scottish Premiership
Sports.content:
Thelo Aasgaard earned Derek McInnes his first point as Rangers manager as they fought back for a 1-1 draw against Dundee United.

Lachlan Rose struck the first goal of the Premiership season to give United a half-time lead at Tannadice.

Rangers lacked control in possession in the opening period but they looked more threatening after the break and Aasgaard finished brilliantly in the 56th minute. They could not build on the equaliser, though, as United soon stemmed the tide of pressure.

View image in fullscreen Dundee United’s Lachlan Rose celebrates after opening the scoring. Photograph: Russell Cheyne/Reuters

Jesse Randall should have won the game for the home side with eight minutes left when substitute Daniel Bennie’s swerving pass put the New Zealand international clean through on goal. However, the winger totally lacked conviction as he dinked a shot straight into goalkeeper Ivor Pandur’s hands.

McInnes named Youssef Chermiti on the bench in his first team selection with Ryan Naderi handed a role on the right of Rangers’ attack, and Pandur, Ben Godfrey, Cammy Devlin and Lawrence Shankland making their debuts.

There were only two Scots in the two starting lineups but both led their teams, former Falkirk midfielder Dylan Tait wearing the armband for United and Shankland the new Rangers captain.

The former Hearts striker was the first to threaten with a flick that drew a reaction stop from Jack Walton, but the home goalkeeper’s only other first-half save came from a Naderi header which looked like it was slightly off target. Rose and Zac Sapsford got in behind for the home side but could not get shots on target and the Rangers defence was busy on other occasions as United worked the ball into the box.

View image in fullscreen Derek McInnes began his time at Rangers with a hard-fought 1-1 draw at Dundee United on the opening day of the season. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

Dujon Sterling and Mohamed Diomande were off target from outside the box for Rangers, before the hosts made the breakthrough in the 38th minute. Rangers centre-back Emmanuel Fernandez was out of position as Sapsford dummied Randall’s low cross and Rose watched in delight as his left-foot effort spun off the post and over the line.

Chermiti and Dan Neil came on for Naderi and Djeidi Gassama as McInnes tried to affect the game at half-time and his side immediately looked more threatening.

Quick Guide Bellingham watches Birmingham beat Barça in friendly Show Jude Bellingham returned to St Andrew's as a spectator to see Birmingham City beat Barcelona on penalties in a pre-season friendly. The England and Real Madrid midfielder (pictured) emerged from Birmingham's academy, making his first-team debut at 16 years old before joining Borussia Dortmund in 2020. August Priske put Birmingham ahead in the 31st minute, but teenage Barça striker Hamza Abdelkarim levelled from the penalty spot before half-time. Abdelkarim struck again on the hour, reacting fastest after Roony Bardghji's shot was saved. Jhon Solis responded for the hosts, volleying home in the 68th minute. The game ended 2-2 after 90 minutes, with Birmingham keeper James Beadle saving twice and 17-year-old Barcelona defender Jordi hitting the crossbar. The shootout ended 3-2 to Birmingham as the hosts enjoyed a memorable victory over an admittedly inexperienced Barcelona line-up. Guardian sport Photograph: Nigel French/PA Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Aasgaard forced an excellent diving save from Walton before the Norway international levelled moments later. Shankland’s physical presence caused problems as United were made to defend another high ball and Aasgaard took an excellent touch to take out Joshua Rawlins before firing a left-foot strike into the top corner from 16 yards.

Rangers could not keep up the momentum, and Randall squandered a glorious chance to mark his league debut with a famous winner. Chermiti almost made the home side pay but Walton stopped the striker’s effort with his feet before home substitute Idjessi Metsoko delivered a weak effort straight at Pandur from a decent opportunity.

Sports.title: Arsenal’s title defence: keeping tired players fit and the Vinícius question
Sports.content:
After beating MK Dons 3-0 in a training-ground friendly last weekend, Arsenal truly begin their pre-season programme against Girona on Saturday evening. It marks a return to action for the Premier League champions, who will want to show their success last season was not a one-off.

Retaining the English title is incredibly difficult if you are not Manchester City. No other club has done it since Manchester United won three in succession from 2007 to 2009. Chelsea have done it once, Liverpool have not managed it for more than 40 years, and it is the best part of a century since Arsenal retained the crown. Mikel Arteta faces a sizeable challenge.

Reaching a second successive Champions League final will not be simple either. Manchester City in 2021-22 are the only one of England’s previous five finalists who made it as far as the semi-finals the next season. With the Premier League stronger than ever, competing on two fronts has never been tougher. Transfer business may improve Arsenal’s chances, though their spending has been modest to this point. More than half of the £79m spent was on making Piero Hincapié’s loan permanent.

Elsewhere Arsenal have replaced Leandro Trossard with Christos Tzolis, a Greek winger, from Club Brugge. Seven years younger than the Belgian, his arrival is a logical move in future-proofing the squad. However, the left side of Arsenal’s attack would be elevated to truly elite level if they could secure reported target Vinícius Júnior. The on-field argument speaks for itself. Vinícius made 92 carries of at least five metres that ended with him either taking a shot (49) or creating a chance (43) last season, the most of anyone in Europe’s top five leagues. Open-play threat, for a side that has often relied on set pieces, would be considerably increased.

Those holding the purse strings at Arsenal may have pause for thought. Capology’s wage data estimates that Vinícius is the joint-third highest paid player in Europe’s top five leagues, earning in excess of £100,000 a week more than anyone at his potential new club. Would Arsenal be willing to rewrite their wage structure? They should expect calls from the agents of their current players if they are. In this sense, Bradley Barcola, with whom they have also been linked, makes a more plausible target. The issue there would be competition from Liverpool, who are in far greater need of wingers.

This is the test facing Andrea Berta, Arsenal’s sporting director. Improving a squad that is already one of the best around is not easy. When Berta’s arrived last year, the club’s primary targets were said to be Alexander Isak and Benjamin Sesko, both of whom joined rivals instead. The pool of players who could add something significant to Arteta’s options is drying up.

Keeping existing players fit may be more beneficial than enhancing the squad. Arsenal did well to win the league given only a handful of clubs had players that missed more games. Kai Havertz was reportedly their top earner before Bukayo Saka signed a contract extension in February, but he only started seven league games. The captain, Martin Ødegaard, was also unavailable for spells, meaning he and Saka started only 10 Premier League matches together in 2025-26. One of them coincided with the only game for which Declan Rice was injured (the 4-1 home win over Aston Villa), another (another home win, 2-1 against Brighton) when he started at right-back.

View image in fullscreen Mikel Arteta indulges in a bit of training-ground banter with first-team coach Miguel Molina in Girona. Photograph: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC/Getty Images

This meant Arteta was rarely able to give key men a breather. Arsenal have five of the Premier League’s top 20 players for club minutes in all competitions since the start of last season. Granted, the goalkeeper David Raya is one of them. But their outfield players with more than 4,200 minutes were Rice (4,456 minutes, the 11th most for a Premier League club), Martín Zubimendi (4,298, 15th), William Saliba (4,254, 17th) and Gabriel Magalhães (4,210, 19th), all vital components of the side’s spine.

Saliba also played 795 minutes for France, pushing him past 5,000 minutes before his World Cup was prematurely ended by a back injury that looks likely to sideline him for some time. It is remarkable Rice was able to play 1,026 minutes for England on top of his Arsenal commitments, not least as he has managed nerve pain in a hamstring throughout 2026.

This workload clearly impacted his ability to contribute at his best for Thomas Tuchel this summer, and that will be a concern for Arteta. With Viktor Gyökeres also clocking up plenty of playing time for Sweden, Arsenal have six players with at least 4,400 minutes for club and country since the start of last August.

This may have been a factor in Arsenal opting for a relatively low-key pre-season. They visited Asia last summer, but the trip to Catalonia to play Girona is the furthest they will travel this year. Arsenal also have games in Dublin (against Real Betis) and Cardiff (the Community Shield against City) sandwiching home friendlies against Borussia Dortmund and Como.

With players still recovering from their World Cup exertions, it may be some time before we see the true Arsenal. A combination of fatigue, injuries and potential squad additions means the process could take far longer than would be ideal.

Sports.title: Inter make new approach to Liverpool for Curtis Jones with £30m offer likely
Sports.content:
Inter have made another approach for Curtis Jones and are willing to raise their offer for the Liverpool midfielder to €35m (£30m). The Italian champions had a €25m bid for the 25-year-old rejected in June by Liverpool, who value their homegrown player at closer to €40m.

Quick Guide Bellingham watches Birmingham beat Barça in friendly Show Jude Bellingham returned to St Andrew's as a spectator to see Birmingham City beat Barcelona on penalties in a pre-season friendly. The England and Real Madrid midfielder (pictured) emerged from Birmingham's academy, making his first-team debut at 16 years old before joining Borussia Dortmund in 2020. August Priske put Birmingham ahead in the 31st minute, but teenage Barça striker Hamza Abdelkarim levelled from the penalty spot before half-time. Abdelkarim struck again on the hour, reacting fastest after Roony Bardghji's shot was saved. Jhon Solis responded for the hosts, volleying home in the 68th minute. The game ended 2-2 after 90 minutes, with Birmingham keeper James Beadle saving twice and 17-year-old Barcelona defender Jordi hitting the crossbar. The shootout ended 3-2 to Birmingham as the hosts enjoyed a memorable victory over an admittedly inexperienced Barcelona line-up. Guardian sport Photograph: Nigel French/PA Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Intermediaries representing Inter have made fresh contact with Liverpool this week and outlined their willingness to go to €35m for a player who has only one year remaining on his contract at Anfield. Whether Liverpool accept that sum is doubtful, but a deal for Jones to leave his boyhood club does appear to be edging closer.

Jones has been unable to establish himself as a regular starter at Liverpool and cut a frustrated figure at times last season under Arne Slot. He was also involved in a row with Dominik Szoboszlai after Wednesday’s win over Wrexham in New York, seemingly over not being handed the captain’s armband when Szoboszlai was substituted during the second half of the friendly.

The new Liverpool head coach, Andoni Iraola, has spoken of the importance of keeping Jones and a local identity at the start of his first season in charge but Inter’s determination to sign the England international, along with the prospect of losing him for free next summer, may well test that resolve.

Sports.title: Chelsea fined £10m and given suspended transfer ban by FA over agent breaches
Sports.content:
Chelsea have been fined £10m by the FA and served with a suspended transfer ban for multiple violations of transfer rules during the Roman Abramovich era.

The sanction reflects a similar punishment handed to the Blues by the Premier League earlier this year after the club were found to have used unlicensed agents and sought to obscure the nature of their transfer dealings between 2009 and 2022. Deals involving Chelsea legends Samuel Eto’o, Eden Hazard and Willian were among those found to have breached the rules. The commission originally handed down a stronger sanction that would have given Chelsea a suspended six-point deduction, but it was overturned after an appeal by the club.

The offences were self-reported by Chelsea when new ownership entered Stamford Bridge in 2022 and the disciplinary panel praised the club for their actions and cooperation through the hearing. Chelsea, who are also operating under a settlement agreement with Uefa, said they had “worked openly and transparently with all regulators” and were “pleased to confirm that this brings all regulatory proceedings against the club to a close”.

Written reasons published by the FA show the independent commission took a very dim view of the Abramovich-era administration, saying their rule-breaking showed “a shameful and arrogant disregard for the rules of the game … which has done so much to bring the game of football in general, and the name of CFC into disrepute”. They also said, however, that there were aspects of the case brought by the FA that caused them “particular concern”.

While praising the FA’s cooperation on the case, the commission criticised the governing body for both failing to charge individuals related to the misdemeanours and for requesting that a sporting sanction should not be applied as punishment. After a submission by the Premier League, which also argued against a sporting sanction, Chelsea appealed against the commission’s original sanction and the six-point deduction was replaced with a suspended two-window ban on registering new players. While the commission had originally argued Chelsea had sought and gained a sporting advantage from their actions, the appeal board found that there was insufficient evidence to show that any advantage had actually been achieved.

“Chelsea’s lawyers performed a masterclass in non-adversarial diplomacy with both the FA and the Premier League,” said Stefan Borson, a football finance expert who is head of sport at the law firm McCarthy Denning.

“Even where the FA’s independent panel disagreed with the position presented by the FA and Chelsea, it still found a way to discount a 15-point deduction starting point down to a six-point suspended penalty. Ultimately, even that was appealed away, leaving Chelsea to pay a final meagre fine out of its retained escrow from Abramovich’s proceeds.”

Quick Guide Mudryk cleared to resume playing Show Chelsea winger Mykhailo Mudryk can return to playing immediately after the Football Association and the World Anti-Doping Agency “resolved his appeal” against a ban for failing a doping test. The Ukrainian was suspended for four years after failing a drug test which revealed the presence of a low concentration of meldonium, a prohibited substance, in 2024. Mudryk filed an appeal with the Court of Arbitration for Sport while changes to Wada procedures in the interim mean that had his failed test produced the same result now, charges would not have been brought. The FA said: “Changes have been made … which, while not retroactive, mean that if Mr Mudryk’s sample was collected today, the concentration of meldonium in the sample would not have been reported and no anti-doping rule violations [ADRVs] would have resulted. Further to that development and to other circumstances of the case, the FA and Mr Mudryk have now – with the agreement of Wada – resolved the appeal proceedings. “As a part of the agreement, Mr Mudryk accepted that he had committed the ADRVs charged and acceded to a period of ineligibility equal to the time served at the date of the agreement. Mr Mudryk is no longer ineligible and may return to competition with immediate effect.” PA Media Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

The Premier League and the FA had been examining tens of millions of pounds in secret payments made by offshore companies that were owned by Abramovich. Details of the transactions were uncovered as part of Cyprus Confidential, an investigation by the Guardian and international media partners, based on a leak of data from Cypriot financial services firms that the Russian oligarch used to manage his vast fortunes.

Deals revealed by the leak included apparent off-book payments to Hazard’s agent and an associate of the title-winning manager Antonio Conte.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Documents published as part of the finding offer a rare insight into the inner workings of Chelsea’s transfer policy during the tenure of Abramovich. They refer to internal conversations at Chelsea about the purchase of Willian in 2013, a deal agreed at the last minute, after the Brazilian had apparently been set to join London rivals Tottenham. According to the documents, an unnamed senior figure at Chelsea felt that to lose Willian was “not good” and that to lose him to Tottenham was “adding insult to injury”.

In its argument, the FA said the unnamed individual may have “loved the power associated with having a bottomless pocket when it came to acquiring players of great quality and/or with great potential, but to seek to suggest that there was no intention to obtain a sporting advantage is stretching our credulity beyond reasonable limits”.

The rulings published by the FA also reveal for the first time that BlueCo, the consortium that bought Chelsea from Abramovich, reached a multi-million pound settlement with HM Revenue & Customs relating to transactions dating back to 2011. The size of the settlement is redacted in the FA’s case against Chelsea but the appeal board’s decision indicated that the club repaid at least £1.35m.

The FA said that the entirety of Chelsea’s £10m fine will be invested into grassroots football.

Sports.title: Arsenal target Bruno Guimarães not on Newcastle’s flight to pre-season camp
Sports.content:
Bruno Guimarães was not on Newcastle’s flight to Murcia on Friday lunchtime as Eddie Howe’s former players prepared to meet their new head coach in southern Spain.

As Guimarães, who is believed to be in Brazil, appeared to inch closer towards a transfer to Arsenal, Matthias Jaissle was completing his managerial move from Saudi Arabia’s Al-Ahli. Howe’s successor is expected to arrive at the club’s pre-season training camp at La Manga at some point this weekend.

By the time, shortly after midday, when the team’s charter plane took off for the Mediterranean, Newcastle had still to provide formal confirmation of Howe’s departure. That did not arrive until late afternoon but it is understood they had been negotiating a financial settlement with their former manager in addition to payoffs for four key members of his backroom staff, including the outgoing No 2, Jason Tindall.

In an emotional message released as part of Newcastle’s statement, Howe said. “It has been the privilege of my lifetime to have been the manager of Newcastle United. After nearly five years of giving my life, heart and soul into this club with unrelenting energy I feel that it is in the best interests of both myself and the club to step away, recharge and take a break. Although it’s been incredibly difficult to make this decision, I know in my heart it’s the right one.”

The amicable nature of the parting was reflected in generous tributes paid by Newcastle’s chief executive David Hopkinson, sporting director Ross Wilson and minority owner, Jamie Reuben. The latter said: “I am proud to have worked alongside Eddie Howe and privileged to call him a friend.” Hopkinson said: “Eddie and his staff leave with the deep gratitude and respect of everyone at Newcastle United and a lasting place in the club’s history.”

Although Howe had told Newcastle of his intention to leave earlier this month, leaks surrounding Jaissle’s imminent installation appeared to catch all parties by surprise. The players had learned of their manager’s departure during a day off on Thursday but had the situation fully explained when Wilson addressed them at the training ground before heading to Spain alongside the squad.

At the same time, Newcastle’s incoming German head coach was understood to be finalising a four-year contract at St James’ Park after an £8m compensation package was agreed with Al-Ahli. Jaissle is already in Europe after remaining in Portugal rather than returning to Jeddah with his squad following the conclusion of a pre-season training camp on the Algarve on Wednesday.

View image in fullscreen Joelinton could be on his way to the Saudi Arabia league this summer. Photograph: Siu Wu/EPA

The 38-year-old former RB Salzburg manager is assembling his own backroom staff and now has only three weeks before his first Premier League season begins with a home game against Liverpool.

One of his first tasks will be to hold talks with Guimarães regarding the Brazil midfielder’s future. Guimarães – who was very close to Howe – is booked on a flight to Spain on Sunday but there are suggestions he could opt to board a London-bound plane instead, should Arsenal offer Newcastle a sum in the region of £75m.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Although Manchester United are exploring the possibility of signing Lewis Hall, Jaissle has reason to be more confident of keeping the influential left back. Newcastle are said to be determined to retain one of their best young players but could be more receptive to any bid from Saudi Arabia for Joelinton. Guimarães’s fellow Brazilian is believed to be keen on a move to the Middle East.

While Besiktas also covet another Newcastle midfielder, Joe Willock, Wilson appears close to securing a new goalkeeper. A £26m deal for the Braga and Czechia goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek is expected to be completed over the weekend.

Should that move for the 24-year-old progress as planned, Nick Pope, Newcastle’s current first-choice keeper, will almost certainly prove yet another departure during a turbulent summer featuring a major changing of the guard on Tyneside.

Sports.title: Humiliated FIFA president Gianni Infantino accepts defeat in controversial plot to sell the World Cup in embarrassing U-turn - now he is in a fight to save his job
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino has been humiliated after his plan to sell stakes in the World Cup died thanks to the heroics of UEFA, CONCACAF, the AFC and two members of the FIFA hierarchy.

While it appears the FIFA president will fight on to save his job, the Swiss football administrator has abandoned his proposal to sell £3.1billion ($4.1bn) in shares in FIFA tournaments to private investors.

Infantino said: 'The FIFA Forward Enterprise project was intended to provide a basis for further strengthening our FIFA Member Associations and our sport worldwide, especially in those countries where support is most needed.

'And more so, as we said from the outset, to do this only if a majority of the FIFA Member Associations were in support and always subject to a consultation process with them, the FIFA Council, the Confederations and wider stakeholders.

Join the discussion Should football's biggest tournaments ever be open to private investment and ownership?

Gianni Infantino waves goodbye to his unilateral plans for private investment in FIFA

Infantino had hoped to create a new enterprise with significant investment from Joshua Kushner (pictured) - brother of Jared, Donald Trump's son-in-law

Carlos Cordeiro, senior adviser to Infantino and member of the White House World Cup task force 'As a Senior Advisor to the FIFA President, a former banker, and a lifelong football fan, I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup. 'Let me be clear: I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally. It is a bad deal for FIFA's Member Associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game. 'Selling a permanent stake in football's most valuable asset to raise $4.2 billion makes little sense. It is mortgaging football's future without any compelling justification. 'Most troubling of all is the absence of answers to fundamental questions. Why this deal? Why now? What oversight exists? Who benefits? Was there a competitive process? What governance will be in place? What will investors ultimately gain, and at what cost to football? 'It has been the privilege of a lifetime to serve FIFA for more than five years and to work alongside dedicated, principled people who care deeply about the game. I hope they, too, will speak up, because decisions of this magnitude should be made in the interests of football, not those who stand to profit from it.'

'Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place.

'Our purpose has always been - and will always be - to unite and improve. As a result, this proposal will not proceed.

'Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, and particularly in those countries that mostly need our support.'

The statement marks an embarrassing u-turn for Infantino, less than 24 hours after he attempted to clarify his plans - blaming the media for misconstruing them.

On Friday, the AFC became the third confederation to reject Gianni Infantino's proposal to raise private capital for the commercial and operational management of FIFA tournaments.

The decision followed CONCACAF's rejection on Thursday and came after UEFA announced a boycott of FIFA competitions. New Zealand Football also objected to the plans, despite the OFC delaying a continent-wide response.

One international football insider told Daily Mail Sport: 'UEFA's response is at the nuclear button end of the spectrum, which is impressive. We thought Infantino would survive the Trump refereeing intervention - but he has overreached this time.'

According to Sky News, UEFA are also thought to have asked for binding assurances that 'FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership' to end their boycott.

It became clear on Friday afternoon that Infantino did not have the support to proceed with his plans, with the opposing nations rising to a staggering 135 - 64 per cent of the FIFA membership.

The proposal appeared to reach a terminal stage when Carlos Cordeiro, senior advisor to Gianni Infantino, announced his resignation from FIFA - becoming the first internal dissident.

Six hours later, FIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour turned against the president - risking his job by criticising the plans and calling on nations to dethrone Infantino. Lamour admitted FIFA Forward Enterprise was the brainchild of 'one person' as he landed a critical blow to the FIFA president.

Carlos Cordeiro (left) quit as an advisor to Gianni Infantino (centre) on Friday

Kevin Lamour, FIFA's Chief Operating Officer 'What has been announced in recent days and what has been happening behind the scenes in recent months defies belief and imagination. 'To put it very clearly and directly: the project that has sparked so much controversy and debate is not a FIFA project. It is even less a project of FIFA's administration. It is the project of one person. FIFA's own administration was deceived. 'Not only must this project not go ahead but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions. Everyone must take responsibility. Because it is becoming increasingly difficult for FIFA's administration to work under these conditions. 'Our mission is to serve football. Not to serve the personal interests of a person who, unfortunately, believes he embodies FIFA when he is supposed to be at its service. A president must bring people together, unite them, and inspire them. Today, we are experiencing the opposite. 'I have no authority to speak on behalf of my colleagues, and perhaps I am mistaken. But my feeling is that we all want to be proud to work for FIFA, and today, unfortunately, it seems that is no longer the case for many of us. That saddens me. The ball is now in the court of those who have the power to change things. 'I know I have a duty of loyalty to my employer. But I also, and above all, have a duty of loyalty to certain values and to the upbringing I have received, and a duty to support my colleagues. And if that means I lose my job, then so be it. I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight.'

Infantino had hoped to create a new enterprise with significant investment from Joshua Kushner - brother of Jared, Donald Trump's son-in-law. Meanwhile, investment bank J.P. Morgan were advising on potential investors.

Democratic senator Ron Wyden, who leads an investigation into Jared Kushner, said on Friday: 'Soccer fans around the world are rightfully outraged by this scheme from Infantino and Joshua Kushner to turn the World Cup into just another commodity for private equity to buy up.

'It seems clear from the global backlash that this corrupt plan is unlikely to succeed, but it is just one of dozens of shady deals by Trump's family and close associates to get rich from the presidency.'

A significant number of FIFA members raised concerns from the initial leak of the plan, questioning how such thorough ideas could be developed unilaterally without prior consultation.

Despite FIFA maintaining throughout that there would be a proper consultation period, there were major questions about how that could be achieved when potential investors were already lined up.

UEFA accused FIFA of trying to bribe members with a £30million ($40m) incentive to approve Infantino's plan, with a September 19 deadline to respond to the offer.

Those plans, though, are now dead in the water after Infantino scrapped them at half past midnight (UK) on Saturday.

There is growing opposition to Infantino's presidency, with sources telling Daily Mail Sport that CONCACAF nations believe he is losing or has already lost their confidence.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham believes Infantino's position is untenable and he is not alone.

Speaking to reporters in Sheffield on Friday, Burnham said: 'This was an outrageous suggestion. The idea that it could even be brought forward shows that, in my view, [he] is the wrong man to lead the organisation.'

With the controversy surrounding Infantino, member nations could still trigger a vote of no confidence. The threshold to initiate the process is 46 FIFA member associations.

UEFA and their member associations are yet to be drawn on that matter. Infantino is seeking a fourth term in next year's elections.

Sepp Blatter, Infantino's predecessor, took to social media to renew his attacks on his successor by writing on Friday evening: 'FIFA is not a private equity fund. It is an association with statutes, regulations, and a fiduciary responsibility to protect the global game.

'If you sell football's crown jewels to private investors, you also sell part of the game – especially its soul. Money matters, but it must never become everything.'

Sports.title: Higher intensity, a more hands-on approach and chats with his stars: How Andoni Iraola's training sessions have injected a new lease of life into Liverpool - as Dominik Szoboszlai and Curtis Jones show they are best of friends again after bust-up
Sports.content:
Higher intensity, a more hands-on approach and chats with his stars: How Andoni Iraola's training sessions have injected a new lease of life into Liverpool - as Dominik Szoboszlai and Curtis Jones show they are best of friends again after bust-up

Unlock more from Lewis Steele inside the Liverpool camp with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight, analysis and more

Like a celebrity couple wanting to dismiss rumours of a rift or break-up, Curtis Jones and Dominik Szoboszlai were eager to show the cameras there was no trouble in paradise.

Not quite holding hands down the streets for the paparazzi but, after a public spat on the Yankee Stadium pitch on Wednesday night that saw the pair and Kostas Tsimikas animated and clearly having a row, the Liverpool pair were keen to quieten talk of an issue.

For those who missed the event, the duo were seen arguing at full-time of the Reds’ 1-0 win over Wrexham in New York City on Wednesday night.

Internet sleuths and online conspiracists instantly clicked into gear and, hours later, there were several theories. One working hypothesis was that Jones was irked at how Szoboszlai passed the captain’s armband to Tsimikas and not him.

Another is that Jones is off to Inter (which may well end up being true) and he was agitated about that. The truth is more that tensions were running high after a zapping pre-season full of tough training sessions and travel, so the pair showed a bit of passion and emotion. Not a bad thing.

But here at Chicago Fire HQ on the suburbs of the so-called Windy City by the banks of Lake Michigan, Jones and Szoboszlai were the first out to training and made a point of walking out together with Tsimikas, the trio doing keepy-ups as they took to the field.

Curtis Jones and Dominik Szoboszlai were spotted in a heated discussion after Liverpool's win over Wrexham

Andoni Iraola was directing drills like an orchestra conductor during Liverpool's training session

Apparently, earlier in the day, they were also spotted at the team’s downtown hotel, also inseparable. Best of pals. A little friendship row, we’ve all had them.

There are two conclusions here, then: either it was a calculated stunt to silence the fans going into overdrive about two players arguing or they are mighty fine actors. For now, at least, the verdict is that all is fine and the issue is resolved.

Jones’s future is less clear-cut. Inter are pushing hard to sign him and, via intermediaries, have informed Liverpool they will be willing to pay around £30m - £5m short of their price-tag.

Head coach Andoni Iraola publicly insisted he wants the locally-born midfielder to stay but it appears the Italian champions, who have already signed one Englishman this summer in John Stones, are going to push hard having had a couple of bids already turned down.

Jones’s potential exit throws into focus the need for new signings, plus the fact defenders Joe Gomez, Jeremy Jacquet and Giovanni Leoni missed training on Friday afternoon to instead focus on recovering from fitness issues in the gym.

Sporting director Richard Hughes has been in the United States, working from afar on signing Bradley Barcola of Paris Saint-Germain and other players, while Fenway Sports Group president Mike Gordon is also understood to be here. Both may need to get the chequebook out to back Iraola before the new season starts.

The new Basque boss has shown a willingness to work with the younger players in the squad and that was obvious at this session at Chicago Fire HQ, which is an apt way to sum up the training camp: some of the players looked on fire with intensity not seen for a long time.

Szoboszlai put it well a day earlier when he said that Liverpool now have ‘the intensity that had been missing’ last season. Without mentioning former boss Arne Slot by name, it was a significant comment as some players felt aggrieved at training sessions last year.

Iraola very animated pic.twitter.com/KJc9fh2dK8 — Lewis Steele (@LewisSteele_) July 31, 2026

Iraola has come in and injected a new lease of life around the place and that was evident here. Players seemed to all be having fun and everything felt quicker, vibrant and intense.

The former Bournemouth boss was hands-on, directing drills like an orchestra conductor. Players would be pulled over for a chat, though the boss seems more of a complimentary coach than one to berate his troops. Always smiling.

Maybe that is needed after a season of doom and gloom where, at times, these top-level professionals looked like they wanted the earth to swallow them up. A miserable year, but positive vibes are everywhere you look (apart from the gym, full of stricken defenders also including long-term absentee Conor Bradley).

Iraola’s assistant Tommy Elphick was vocal and even pulled on a yellow bib to take part in a set-piece drill. Maybe because of the lack of defensive numbers, the former Aston Villa and Brighton centre half was tasked with heading away Florian Wirtz corners.

Iraola’s fellow right-hand man Shaun Cooper was also heavily involved in those drills, where Alexander Isak looked particularly sharp and young forward Josh Sonni-Lambie also caught the eye at the back post.

One would not like to draw too many conclusions from observing training sessions, especially given some of Slot’s drills were also impressive, but the first signs of the intense Iraola are all positive.

There was also time to observe new Chicago Fire striker Robert Lewandowski, who was finishing a shooting drill on a nearby pitch for the MLS outfit, who he has just signed for.

A player who has been there, done that and bought the T-shirt many times over with 662 career goals for clubs like Dortmund, Bayern Munich and Barcelona, it was a joy to see him up close and personal.

Given Liverpool striker Hugo Ekitike is out for several months and Isak has had fitness issues of his own, the mind was wondering to whether Lewandowski could be a canny loan for Iraola. Then he went and spooned a penalty into the Chicago skyline…

Sports.title: 'I want to attack as quickly as possible': Why Matthias Jaissle's 'RB Style' can save Newcastle United - from 'elite' pressing to developing young stars, and the players who will thrive under new boss
Sports.content:
There’s going to be a new man in Toon – Matthias Jaissle is expected to soon replace Eddie Howe as Newcastle United’s head coach.

A close confidant of England boss Thomas Tuchel, under whom he played in Stuttgart's academy, the 38-year-old will take the reins after leading Saudi Pro League side – and Newcastle's sister club – Al Ahli to back-to-back Asian Champions League crowns. Before that he led Red Bull Salzburg to successive titles after taking over at just 33.

So, what can Newcastle fans expect?

Well, first of all, they can strap themselves in for some all-action football.

Jaissle is a fully fledged member of the ‘RB Style’ adopted by clubs in the Red Bull network, a philosophy implemented by German coach Ralf Rangnick of whom Jaissle is a steadfast disciple. Fast, flat-out, intense pressing, win it back high up the pitch and get to the goal as quickly as possible.

‘We want to be courageous, bold, and attack-minded,’ said Jaissle of his style back in 2022, after winning the Austrian double in his first season at RB Salzburg, having joined from their feeder club, second-division side FC Liefering. ‘Naturally, this should be combined with high pressing to put the opposition under a lot of pressure.’

Matthias Jaissle is on the brink of being named as the new Newcastle head coach, after Eddie Howe's abrupt departure this week

The 38-year-old German won the Austrian Bundesliga in both of his seasons at Red Bull Salzburg, and then won back-to-back Asian Champions Leagues at Al Ahli

JAISSLE'S JOURNEY Club Games Win % FC Liefering (2021) 17 64.71 Red Bull Salzburg (2021-23) 93 68.82 Al Ahli (2023-present) 138 65.22

He wants his teams to be relentless off the ball.

‘I want stress on the opponent as soon as possible,’ he told The Athletic in January. ‘And when we win the ball, I want to go as quickly as possible towards the opponent’s goal. I’m very vertical (forwards, rather than sideways) in that approach.’

As a coach, Jaissle likes to keep things simple. He talks of not wanting to ‘overwhelm’ his players with too much information and likes to use one-to-one meetings to convey his messages. While his principles have remained the same, he has tweaked his shape and approach over the years. During his time at Salzburg, he used a narrow diamond formation with his full-backs providing the width.

Since his switch to the Al Ahli, he’s been much more flexible. He’s opted for a 4-2-3-1 with Riyad Mahrez on one flank behind striker Ivan Toney, who notched 32 goals in the league last season. He’s played 4-4-2, 4-3-3 and even gone three at the back on occasion. His structure was more controlled but the demands to win the ball back high remained.

‘It is not about formations that much,’ said Jaissle. ‘It is more how you want to play, how you want to attack, how you want to defend.’ He even managed to get the mercurial Mahrez pressing. Only five other forwards won the ball back in the final third more often than the former Manchester City and Leicester winger.

What it will mean is a style shift for Newcastle. The Magpies were renowned for their intensity under Howe early in his tenure but drifted into a more pedestrian approach, especially as they tried – and struggled – to juggle Champions League commitments, which they do not have to worry about this year.

Jaissle’s Al Ahli moved the ball up the pitch faster than any Premier League side last season while only Sunderland and West Ham played a higher percentage of their passes forward than Al Ahli.

But they were by no means sitting back and counter-attacking. They were in your face at all times. Al Ahli allowed opponents fewer passes before trying to win it back than any Premier League side managed and, on average, started their attacks closer to the opposition goal than all but Man City. There are, of course, caveats to be made between the respective qualities of the two leagues, but Jaissle’s demands are clear.

HOW HE COMPARES TO HOWE Per match, 2025-26 Newcastle Al Ahli Passes 450 346 10+ pass sequences 10.2 6.3 Foward pass % 33.9 36.2 Crosses 16.7 11.6 Through balls 1.6 1.9 Shots 13.0 12.9 Shots faced 12.4 8.6 High turnovers 6.6 7.8

Newcastle were far from being the Premier League's possession kings last season, firmly in midtable with their 450 passes per game but that is Guardiola-esque compared to Al Ahli’s 346, which put them fourth-fewest across the entire Saudi Pro League.

The Magpies averaged far more attacks made up of ten or more passes, and almost twice the number of them that ended up in a shot on goal.

Toon fans can prepare themselves for some high-octane football. No tippy-tappy. Press hard, get it forward. It is, in many ways, exactly the style of football that is starting to dominate the Premier League.

So who will thrive under Newcastle's new man?

For a start, it’s a shame that Anthony Gordon, a willing runner and a real threat in a direct system has now joined Barcelona.

It’s a system that seems purpose-built for Anthony Elanga. The winger failed to score a single league goal last season after a £55million move from Nottingham Forest but a second chance in a side that wants to play in, for want of a less nerdy phrase, a ‘vertical transition team’ could be just what he needs. No player averaged more sprints per 90 minutes than Elanga last season.

Likewise, Newcastle’s £42.3million summer signing Bazoumana Touré, a rapid Ivorian who is highly touted as a star of the future. Get on yer bike, young man. Will Jacob Murphy, now 31, have the legs for the press?

Tino Livramento and Lewis Hall could also thrive under Jaissle. Even when he sets up in a 4-3-3, when his side has the ball, he wants his full backs to push up alongside the winger to help overload in wide areas.

You can see from the average position map of their victory over Al Kholood at the end of last season how the team moves into a 3-2-5 shape – also very common in the Premier League these days – with centre back Merih Demiral shifting wide and right back Ali Majrashi joining Mahrez high up the pitch.

New £42.3million signing Bazoumana Toure could thrive in Jaissle's high-intensity system

What that pitch map also shows is how Jaissle has room for someone to come crashing out of the midfield line. For Al Ahli in that game it was former AC Milan and Barcelona midfielder Franck Kessie, who assisted two of the goals in a 3-0 win.

For Salzburg, that was Brenden Aaronson, now at Leeds, who praised Jaissle for helping him adapt to a new position. ‘He’s taught me a different way of playing the No10 role,’ he said. ‘More runs in behind and late runs into the box. My playmaking skills and final pass have gotten better.’

For Newcastle, that could be Joelinton, although there are doubts over his future at the club after he asked to leave earlier this summer for Saudi Arabia. A few seasons ago, that could well have been Joe Willock, who made a reputation for himself for arriving late in the box to score.

Replacing £100million Sandro Tonali will be far from straightforward and Newcastle have bagged a couple of newbies in 18-year-old Sean Steur and 20-year-old Aladji Bamba. ‘The way he works and develops young players is exceptional,’ said Christoph Freund, the then-Salzburg sporting director. Newcastle fans will hope he’s right.

After a frustrating debut season for Newcastle curtailed by a knee injury, Jaissle’s arrival could well get the best out of Yoane Wissa. Like Elanga, the striker had a good World Cup. And he showed during his time at Brentford that he is superb at leading a team’s press from the front. During his final campaign with the Bees, he was among the leading strikers in the division for winning possession back in the final third.

How Nick Woltemade can adapt is the more interesting dilemma. Howe could never quite figure out where his best position was and you wonder whether Jaissle will have the same problem.

Jaissle has little need for a 6ft 6in target man, off whom he wants knockdowns and flicks with his back to goal, but Woltemade offers more than just that. He can drop between the lines and play as much as a creator as a goalscorer. Jaissle worked with 6ft 5in Manchester United striker Benjamin Sesko at Salzburg, so can get the best out of big men. But Woltemade’s struggles with running the channels or leading the press will likely hold him back if he’s to remain up top.

Toney is hardly renowned as an elite presser, but proved that he’s still a ruthless goalscorer and even he showed he can get stuck in and win the ball back high.

Jaissle's Salzburg reached the knockout stages of the Champions League for the first time in the club's history in 2021, finishing above Sevilla and Wolfsburg in their group

Nick Pope’s future at Newcastle is already uncertain. The club have already signed 20-year-old keeper Ewen Jaouen and are believed to be closing in on Braga stopper Lukas Hornicek.

Jaissle’s arrival will do little to brighten Pope’s chances. ‘Goalkeeper is not a position by itself any more,’ said Jaissle. ‘It is completely included with the other guys. A goalkeeper has to have an understanding of all phases of the game.’ That, sadly, is not Pope's game.

Above all, Newcastle fans will hope Rasmus Kristensen, who played under Jaissle at Salzburg, has the right view of their new man.

‘He is a born winner,’ said Kristensen. ‘He possesses that special winning mentality.’

Sports.title: Jude Bellingham gets a hero's reception on his return to Birmingham City... as England superstar's boyhood club beat Barcelona on penalties!
Sports.content:
Jude Bellingham gets a hero's reception on his return to Birmingham City... as England superstar's boyhood club beat Barcelona on penalties!

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Jude Bellingham was welcomed back to Birmingham City like a hero on Friday night as he watched his boyhood club triumph on penalties against Barcelona.

Barcelona travelled over to St Andrew's for a pre-season friendly against the Championship club, giving Blues fans plenty to cheer about as they were given a rare opportunity to see the LaLiga champions in action.

The occasion was made even more special for those inside St Andrew's when England superstar Bellingham, who began his glittering career at Birmingham before leaving to join Borussia Dortmund in 2020 and later Real Madrid in 2023, was unveiled at the start of the game.

Before kick-off, Birmingham City's official social media account showed Bellingham taking his seat and waving to fans in a touching video captioned: 'Jude. He's home.'

As he raised his arms aloft to greet the adoring fans, Blues supporters loudly bellowed 'Jude' to honour their former starlet and fervently chanted 'he's one of our own' in a special moment for the England midfielder at St Andrew's.

Bellingham is still enjoying some richly-deserved time off after playing an integral role for England at the World Cup this summer and thus has not yet returned to Real Madrid to begin the new season under Jose Mourinho.

Jude Bellingham was given a warm reception as he watched Birmingham defeat Barcelona

Bellingham posed for selfies with Birmingham fans who once cheered him on as a teenager

The £113million midfielder cheered jubilantly as he watched his boyhood club triumph over Real Madrid's bitter rivals, winning on penalties after drawing 2-2 in normal time.

August Priske Flyger and John Solis were both on the scoresheet for the Blues, while Hamza Abdelkarim netted a brace for the Catalans.

Goalkeeper James Beadle was the hero in the shootout as he saved spot-kicks from Roony Bardghji and Brian Farinas, while Jordi Pesquer crashed his effort into the crossbar to hand Birmingham a 3-2 win on penalties.

Few clubs have a fonder view of an academy player than Birmingham City have of Bellingham, who at 23 has already become one of the best midfielders in world football.

Bellingham burst through the ranks at Birmingham as a youngster, starring for the U18s as a 14 year old and later making his debut for the U23s at the age of just 15.

The midfielder was then promoted to the Blues' senior squad for the 2019-20 season, becoming the youngest first-team player in the club's history at 16 years and 36 days old.

Bellingham could hardly believe what he was watching as Birmingham triumphed on penalties

The England international was seen wearing his No22 Birmingham jersey - which was officially retired by the club when he left them to join Borussia Dortmund back in 2020

After making 41 appearances that campaign, Bellingham joined Borussia Dortmund for a £25m fee and became the youngest player ever to have his shirt retired by a professional club, with Birmingham officially retiring his No22 jersey.

Despite arriving at St Andrew's in a white t-shirt, Bellingham finished the match wearing his retired No22 Birmingham jersey, which appeared to give the hosts luck as they pulled off a comeback to force the decisive penalty shootout.

Sports.title: Newcastle agree deal for goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek, Como back in for Trevoh Chalobah, David Moyes makes call over Celtic star... and Inter Milan will go to £30m for Liverpool's Curtis Jones: WINDOW WATCH
Sports.content:
Newcastle agree deal for goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek, Como back in for Trevoh Chalobah, David Moyes makes call over Celtic star... and Inter Milan will go to £30m for Liverpool's Curtis Jones: WINDOW WATCH

It's that time of the year again – the transfer window is now open until September 1 and it's sure to be a busy period with clubs looking to make big signings ahead of next season.

Here are today's latest developments from Simon Jones and the Daily Mail Sport team...

Inter will go to £30m for Jones pursuit

Inter Milan have intimated they are willing to pay £30million for Liverpool midfielder Curtis Jones.

Notice was given via intermediaries but Liverpool maintain the 25-year-old, who has one year left on contract, is valued at a minimum £35m. They dismissed Inter's last offer of £21.75m.

The 25-year-old has cut a frustrated figure in recent months and has wanted more regular game time. He has one year left on his contract and Liverpool say they are relaxed about his situation.

The Italian club were interested in January and proposed a loan with a view to a permanent move but that was also turned down by Liverpool.

Inter Milan are continuing to chase Curtis Jones but are yet to meet Liverpool's valuation

Piero Ausilio, Inter's sporting director, confirmed he was still on their radar earlier this summer, saying: 'Curtis Jones - we are paying attention to him. We didn't hide. We understand what the developments will be.'

Teammate Federico Chiesa, another who could depart, also told Italian media that Jones asked him what it is like to live in Italy.

The midfielder has been with Liverpool since he was nine and signed his first professional contract with them in 2018.

Inter yesterday confirmed the signing of England defender John Stones on a free transfer.

Liverpool have received enquiries for some of their fringe players who have impressed on tour in USA with Luke Chambers, Lewis Koumas, Calum Scanlon and Ifeanyi Ndukwe all attracting interest.

Leeds miss out on Brandt

Leeds United target Julian Brandt has signed for Ajax on a three-year contract.

Leeds had been chasing the 30-year-old free agent following his contract expiry at Borussia Dortmund and his father and agent, Jurgen, had previously been at Leeds’ Thorp Arch training ground to discuss a move.

Julian Brandt has signed for Ajax when Leeds were interested in signing him

Black Cats have Dayann bid turned down

Sunderland have been rebuffed in their opening offer for 20-year-old Toulouse left-back Dayann Methalie.

Villa hope Allan holds key

Aston Villa have asked about Palmeiras striker Allan. The 22-year-old joined the club in 2019 from his hometown club Figueirense.

Villa have already brought in Alejandro Garnacho on loan from Chelsea this summer.

Valentin set for Brighton

Brighton are finalising a deal to sign Blackburn's 18-year-old powerhouse striker Valentin Joseph.

Blades say no to Seriki deal

Sheffield United have rejected an offer from Sassuolo for defender Femi Seriki. The Serie A club offered an initial loan with an option to buy the 24-year-old full-back for £5m.

Newcastle reach agreement on goalkeeper Hornicek

Newcastle have an agreement in principle with Sporting Braga for goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek.

As Daily Mail Sport exclusively revealed last weekend, Newcastle turned to the 24-year-old Czech international after opting against moves for James Trafford and Carl Rushworth.

They also considered Parma's Zion Suzuki but have agreed to activate Hornicek's £25.7m release clause and are now discussing payment structure with the Portuguese club.

Hornicek has been given permission to travel for a medical as the two clubs tie up details and he will become Newcastle' fifth signing of the summer, though two are goalkeepers.

Trafford has opted to join Leeds from Manchester City and Rushworth is joining Coventry City from Brighton. Suzuki is in talks to join Paris Saint-Germain.

Daily Mail Sport revealed on Sunday that Newcastle had turned to Hornicek - and the deal is now set to be completed

Como back in for Chalobah

Como have returned to the negotiating table for Chelsea defender Trevoh Chalobah.

The Italians are playing a friendly in Portugal on Friday against Famalicao but are continuing to discuss another improved offer for the England centre back.

Their last bid of £25m plus add-ons still fell short of Chelsea's valuation but they are looking to include further achievable add ons to see if that will suffice.

Talks are expected to continue tomorrow for the 27-year-old.

Trevoh Chalobah went to the World Cup with England after Tino Livramento was forced out with injury

Arsenal closing in on Bruno

Arsenal have reached an agreement in principle to sign Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle - and have set aside a day next week for the Brazil midfielder's medical.

It is understood that the fee agreed for the Newcastle captain is £77million plus add-ons.

For the full story click HERE

ISAAN KHAN

Szmodics back in at Derby

Derby County are re-signing forward Sammie Szmodics from Ipswich Town on a season loan with an obligation to buy worth £5.4million. He was on loan at Derby in the second half of last season.

Szmodics signed for Ipswich from Blackburn for £9m in 2024 on a four-year deal.

Stoke City are among the clubs keen on Ipswich striker George Hirst.

Sammie Szmodics scored four goals in the Premier League for Ipswich in 2024-25

Moyes makes call as Everton pursue Celtic's Johnston

Celtic manager Martin O'Neill has confirmed Everton have made contact over their interest in right-back Alistair Johnston.

O'Neill said Everton boss David Moyes had called him to warn him the approach was coming.

'Everton have been in contact. I'm not sure whether there has been a bid in for that one.

'In fairness, David [Moyes] did call me last weekend to tell me that there would be contact.

'But I don't know how far that has progressed, or if it has at all.'

Everton say Canada international Johnston, 27, is one of a number of options they are considering.

United keeping tabs on Hall

Manchester United remain appreciative of Newcastle left back Lewis Hall but acknowledge it would be a difficult transfer to pull off.

The club are still assessing market movements, checking who is available at the right price, before deciding on their next priority position. Another midfielder has been at the forefront of their thinking while another forward still hinges on Marcus Rashford departing. Despite interest from other clubs, as it stands, he remains likely to start the season at United.

Cover at left back is required as United are going into the new season with Luke Shaw, who has one year left on contract, as their only senior option in that position. Harry Amass can cover but has been told he would be better seeking first team opportunities elsewhere.

Manchester United are keen on Newcastle left back Lewis Hall

Hall, 21, has three years left on his current contract, and would require a substantial fee with Newcastle looking to stabilise once Matthias Jaissle is in place.

Though midfielder Bruno Guimaraes may yet join Arsenal, if they make a formal offer over £80m, the club want to add players to ensure they are competitive.

Hamer heading back to Coventry

Coventry are closing on a deal to bring back midfielder Gustavo Hamer from Sheffield United. The 29-year-old Brazilian has one year left on his deal.

He spent three years at Coventry after joining from PEC Zwolle, before moving to Sheffield United in August 2023.

Cherries swoop for Silva

Bournemouth have agreed their £25m deal with Benfica to sign defender Antonio Silva.

The 22-year-old centre back captained and played 90 minutes for Benfica in their emphatic 5-0 Europa League qualifying win against St Gallen last night.

The transfer is worth £21.4million plus £4.3m in add-ons.

The Portugal international is due to travel over this weekend to have a medical and complete his move.

Antonio Silva is set to move to Bournemouth from Benfica

Leicester bring in Championship forward

Leicester City have signed Swansea City forward Liam Cullen for an undisclosed fee.

The Wales international, who has agreed a three year deal, can play as a centre-forward, attacking midfielder or right winger.

He previously worked under manager Russell Martin at Swansea.

Cullen, 27, said: 'When this opportunity came about and with the size of the club and the project they’re getting started with now, I thought it was the perfect fit for me.'

Welsh forward Liam Cullen has signed for Leicester, who will play in League One this season

Hammers trying to nail down Engels

West Ham are moving ahead on talks for Celtic midfielder Arne Engels.

The 22-year-old was the subject of bids up to £25million from Nottingham Forest in January which Celtic rejected.

West Ham have a long-held interest in the Belgium international and, after sounding out figures over a couple of conversations with the Scottish champions, are pressing to see if agreement can be reached on bringing Engels to London and making him the midfield replacement for Mateus Fernandes.

Forest, Sunderland and Fulham had also shown interest.

West Ham are pressing ahead in a move for Celtic midfielder Arne Engels
