03

What to See & Do

SATURDAY IN SÃO PAULO

TODAY’S PICK — STREET ART & OPEN SKY Walk the new Paulista under a bright winter sun Avenida Paulista is a classic winter stroll today; tomorrow (Sunday, August 2) it closes fully to cars from 10am to 6pm for the weekly Paulista Aberta (Open Streets) programme, when the entire stretch from MASP to Praça Oswaldo Cruz goes car-free. Start at the MASP vão-livre around 10am. A free exhibition, “Damián Ortega: matéria e energia”, runs at MASP through 13 September, free every Tuesday, taking everyday objects apart and reassembling them into striking installations. Walk west with a fresh-pressed caldo de cana from a street stall. Musicians and capoeira circles pop up every few hundred metres. At Parque Trianon, slip into the shaded trails. It is the city’s best ten-minute forest bath, right in the middle of the avenue. Finish at the Japan House around 5pm. The current exhibition on contemporary Japanese design closes 9 August. Entry is free. The café downstairs does a quiet matcha latte.

OUTDOORS — TWO WHEELS EAST Cycle the Ciclovia do Rio Pinheiros Rent a bike from the Itaú bike-share at Villa-Lobos Park and join the newly extended riverbank path. The 21.5 km route along the Pinheiros edge is flat, wide and surprisingly green. Stop at the Praça Pôr do Sol viewing deck around 4pm. The late-afternoon light over the river bend is a quiet surprise in the west zone.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — PINHEIROS & JARDINS Weekend tables with strong Wi‑Fi For a serious work session, Coffee Lab on Rua Fradique Coutinho opens at 8am on Saturdays. Their cold brew is top-shelf and the back-garden tables have reliable Wi‑Fi. In Jardins, Sofá Café on Rua Oscar Freire offers a quieter upstairs room with power outlets. It fills by 11am, so an early arrival buys you the best spot.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — QUIET COLLECTIONS A slow afternoon at the Pinacoteca Cross the city to Luz and step into the Pinacoteca. The permanent collection of Brazilian modernists occupies the sunlit ground floor, and the sculpture garden café is an oasis of calm. A special temporary show on Tarsila do Amaral’s later works closes 30 August. Entry is R$30, with a half-price Saturday rate for residents.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM Bar counters and a late jazz set Begin with a gin and tonic at Guilhotina Bar in Pinheiros. Their rooftop opens at 6pm, and the sunset over the neighbourhood roofscape is a local ritual. From there, walk to JazzB on Rua Mourato Coelho. A sextet plays hard-bop from 9pm. The cover is R$40. For a later drink, the speakeasy-style Bar dos Arcos in the basement of Theatro Municipal stays open until 1am. Cocktails run R$60–80. Dinner-wise, Tan Tan Noodle Bar in Pinheiros serves steaming bowls until midnight. The pork-belly ramen with a soft egg is the dish for a cool August night.

ALSO ON TODAY Exhibition: “Arte e Resistência” — Memorial da Resistência, Luz — 10am–6pm, free, a powerful look at São Paulo’s political history through art. Feira do MASP — Below MASP, Av. Paulista — 10am–5pm, free, antique fair with a great selection of vintage records and Brazilian modern furniture. Sesc Avenida Paulista: Rooftop Cinema — Sesc Avenida Paulista — 7pm, R$12, screening a 1970s Cinema Novo classic with English subtitles. Workshop: Portuguese for Expats — Weekend Intensive — Casa do Caminho, Vila Mariana — 9am–1pm, R$180 for the day, a focused workshop on ordering, directions and social talk. Feira de Orgânicos do Parque da Água Branca — Água Branca — 7am–1pm, free entry, the city’s best organic produce and a superb pastel tent.

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

No rodízio applies today or tomorrow; all plates circulate freely across the expanded centre. Metrô and CPTM run their Saturday timetables with reduced headways, so budget an extra five minutes between trains.

Line 4-Amarela connects Luz to Vila Sônia and serves Paulista and Pinheiros efficiently. A single trip costs R$5.20; use a contactless card or the TOP app.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Lunch: Hit the ground-floor market at Mercado de Pinheiros. A classic mortadella sandwich at Bar do Mané runs R$55 and feeds two. For a lighter plate, the ceviche at Comedoria Gonzalo costs around R$45.

Dinner: Book a table at Mocotó in Vila Medeiros, a journey worth the Uber for the torresmo and dadinhos de tapioca (plates R$50–90). Closer in, Casa do Porco offers its roasts in a lively, standing-room ground-floor bar setting at similar prices.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Carry a light jacket for the evening chill and a refillable water bottle. Most cafés and Sesc outlets have free filtered water stations.

Pix is now the default payment for everything from street stalls to high-end bars. Keep a small amount of cash (R$50) for the antique fair, where some vendors are card-averse.

Avenida Paulista is safe during the day with a heavy police and CET presence during Open Streets. Stick to the main avenue and well-lit side streets after dark.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

The São Paulo Expats & Digital Nomads WhatsApp group meets this afternoon at 3pm at PikurruchA’s in Vila Madalena for an informal English-Portuguese language exchange. New arrivals are genuinely welcome.

The NomadX SP Telegram channel reports a Sunday morning running club along the Minhocão elevated park, departing at 8am from Praça Marechal Deodoro.

08

Game Day

THE WEEKEND ROUND

No Brasileirão fixtures land on Saturday. The main action comes Sunday: Corinthians host Grêmio at Neo Química Arena at 4pm BRT, and São Paulo FC are away to Fluminense at the Maracanã at 6:30pm BRT.

Watch the Sunday matches at O Pasquim Bar in Pinheiros, which shows every game with sound on a large projection screen. Arrive 40 minutes before kickoff to claim a table.

For a bigger-party atmosphere, Blue Pub on Rua Mourato Coelho carries multiple screens and does a solid half-price caipirinha for the pre-game crowd.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

Friday’s market session closed with the Ibovespa up and the S&P 500 higher on the day, as shown on the WEEK IN FIGURES board. The Colombian peso was the notable mover, falling sharply against the US dollar in a volatile session.

The broader story for an expat professional is the steady improvement in Brazil’s inflation expectations across recent Central Bank Focus reports. Analysts have trimmed 2026 IPCA projections for four straight weeks, edging closer to the 5.1% region.

Combined with a stable-to-softer USD/BRL and a globally risk-on Friday on Wall Street, the mood among local analysts is cautiously constructive heading into the new month. Watch for any August corporate earnings surprises from the big retailers and banks next week.

10

Plan Ahead

THE WEEK

THE DAYS AHEAD Sun Aug 2 — Clear, 24°C; Corinthians vs Grêmio at 4pm at Neo Química Arena; outdoor feijoada lunch at Bar Balcão. Mon Aug 3 — Warm and dry, 25°C; rodízio for plates 1 and 2 (7–10am & 5–8pm); Tarsila exhibition at Pinacoteca open 10am–6pm. Tue Aug 4 — 26°C, 15% rain chance; rodízio for plates 3 and 4; MASP’s Damián Ortega show runs through 13 September. Wed Aug 5 — Pleasant and dry; rodízio for plates 5 and 6; Sesc Paulista rooftop film night with a French classic. Thu Aug 6 — Similar conditions; Japan House contemporary design show closes Sunday; last chance to plan a visit.

Background: Neymar Museum Opens at Brazil’s Santos FC Stadium.

11

FAQ

QUICK ANSWERS

Does the São Paulo rodízio apply today?

No. The municipal vehicle restriction (rodízio) runs only Monday through Friday. On Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays it is suspended. You can drive any car with any plate ending anywhere in the city centre today. The normal schedule resumes Monday with plates ending 1 and 2 restricted during the morning and late-afternoon peaks.

Can I use my foreign card on the Metrô?

Yes, at most major stations. Contactless international Visa and Mastercard cards are now accepted directly at the turnstiles on new readers, particularly on Line 4-Amarela and the busier Line 1-Azul stops. For older lines, it is safer to buy a single-trip ticket (Bilhete Unitário) at the counter using cash or a card with a PIN. A single journey costs R$5.20.

The day’s centrepiece is the acclaimed ‘Vik Muniz — A Olho Nu’ retrospective at CCBB, recently extended through October, paired with free samba circles in Lapa tonight.

Business professionals can digest a week where Brazilian stocks rallied sharply despite a B3 trading outage, with full closing figures on the board (Business & Markets / WEEK IN FIGURES).

This is a day for unhurried Centro wandering, an afternoon coffee in a Praça Mauá coworking spot, and a night given over to street-corner rhythms.

Sunday stays brilliant, and the first half of next week climbs a degree or two each day with no storm clouds in sight—ideal beach conditions persist.

03

What to See & Do

SATURDAY IN RIO

TODAY’S PICK — CLOSING EXHIBITIONS CCBB’s ‘Vik Muniz — A Olho Nu’ runs through October 12 The Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil (CCBB) in Centro hosts the final weekend of ‘Vik Muniz — A Olho Nu’, the largest retrospective of Rio-born artist Vik Muniz’s career, more than 220 works across 43 series. You walk through rooms built like narrow alleyways with prints by Custódio Coimbra, Marcos Bonisson, and Nana Moraes, each capturing fleeting street geometries. Entry is free, with the doors open from 9 am until 8 pm—a perfect midday escape if the sun grows sharp. Take the VLT to the Praça XV stop or Metrô Line 1 to Uruguaiana; the building is a three-minute walk from either. Before you leave, climb the spiral ramp to the fourth-floor permanent modernity display. One of Muniz’s monumental portraits — assembled from scrap, chocolate or wire and best read from a distance — reorients your whole afternoon. Pairs cleanly with a walk through the adjacent Casa França-Brasil, which is showing ‘Arranjos’—a sculptural group show using found beach debris—also free, open until 7 pm. This is a quiet, cool cavern of a Saturday activity that leaves the evening wide open for the city’s rhythms.

OUTDOORS — ATERRO & THE FLAMENGO BEACH STRIP Skate, cycle, and coconut-water stretches With no rain to dodge, the Parque do Flamengo ciclovia becomes the city’s elongated living room. Rent a yellow Itaú bike at the Praia de Botafogo station, ride the flat tarmac past the Modernist museum MAM, and stop for a green coconut at any shack facing the Sugarloaf. The skate park under the Morro da Viúva overpass is humming by 10 am. Even if you do not ride, the concrete bowl’s rhythm makes a fine coffee-watching perch.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — CENTRO & PRAÇA MAUÁ Quiet tables and strong Wi-Fi for the weekend warrior Curto Café on Rua da Assembleia keeps weekend hours (10 am–5 pm), pulls a precise flat white, and gives you a long communal table upstairs where no one will rush your laptop. Wi-Fi is stable and free. For a livelier Sunday-eve start, walk to Futuro Refeitório inside the MAR museum building on Praça Mauá. Open 10 am–6 pm with a terrace view over the bay, it doubles as a gentle, high-ceilinged coworking spot where you order a coado and spread out.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — BARRA’S OPEN HORIZON A west-zone beach brunch away from the density If Centro’s close streets feel too tight, head west. Praia da Reserva offers a wide, nearly empty sand stretch where the only sound is the small surf and the whine of a distant drone capturing the empty horizon. Stop at Cavist in Barrinha for a late morning acai bowl and a sea-facing table. The beach quiosques here serve grilled fish by noon, and the bike lane is so wide you can coast for a kilometre without passing a soul.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM Samba circles, a Japanese indie gig, and the Lapa strip Tonight belongs to Lapa. The open-air samba circle at Pedra do Sal starts around 8 pm, free, with a crowd that spills down the cobbled incline. Policia Militar foot patrols keep the perimeter easy, but go with nothing more than pocket cash and a phone. For something roofed, Carioca da Gema on Av. Mem de Sá opens at 7:30 pm with a roda de samba entry at R$25. Arrive by 8:30 pm for a table; latecomers stand two-deep at the bar. A contrasting lane: Audio Rebel in Botafogo hosts a Japanese math-rock trio tonight, doors 9 pm, R$30 at the box office—tight, air-conditioned, and weirdly good.

ALSO ON TODAY ‘Arranjos’ sculptural group show — Casa França-Brasil — 4–7 pm, free, closes Aug. 9 Feira da Glória (Sunday) — Rua do Russel — 9 am–3 pm, antiques and vinyl sellers Museu do Amanhã — Praça Mauá — 10 am–6 pm, R$30 (half-price for residents) Sunset paddle session — Urca beach — stand-up paddle rental R$40/hr from 4 pm Botafogo vs. Vitória (Sunday 6 pm) — Nilton Santos — check club site for ticket availability

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

Metrô Lines 1, 2 and 4 are operating a standard Saturday timetable with no planned engineering works, but monitor the COR.Rio app for any sudden hold-ups after Wednesday’s wind-triggered power cut paralysed the network for two hours. A single metro ride remains R$4.30 on the RioCard or Jaé card.

The VLT is running its full Saturday headway from Santos Dumont to Praça Mauá—your best hop between the CCBB cluster and the MAR museum. Uber and the official Taxi.Rio app are both active; surge pricing is unlikely given the thin traffic on a clear winter weekend.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Lunch: Park yourself at Nina Bistrô in Centro (R$40–55 per plate) for their chicken with okra, or grab a window seat at Confeitaria Colombo’s Cristal Room by 1 pm for the R$95 executive lunch.

Dinner: Pre-samba, try the Argentine grill at Corrientes 348 (Lapa) with a chorizo steak at R$60, or keep it cheap at Leviano Bar with bolinho de bacalhau around R$28 before the first set.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Carry a thin jacket after sundown and a reusable water bottle—the dry winter air dehydrates quicker than you expect. Card and Pix are accepted at nearly all venues listed, but keep R$60 in small notes for street vendors at Pedra do Sal and the Glória feira.

Book a table ahead for Carioca da Gema via their Instagram DM; walk-ins often queue. As night fills Lapa, keep your phone in a zipped front pocket and avoid lingering in the narrow alleys behind the Arcos da Lapa after midnight—that specific area sees opportunistic phone snatches in low-lit gaps.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

The ‘Digital Nomads Rio’ WhatsApp group is murmuring about a beach volleyball outing on Sunday at Praia de Ipanema (posto 9) starting at 10 am—find the link on their Instagram Stories. The Rio Expats Meetup group has a ticketed Portuguese conversation brunch this morning at 10:30 am in Catete (R$40).

08

Game Day

THE WEEKEND ROUND

No Rio-based Brasileirão match falls today—Botafogo host Vitória at Estádio Nilton Santos only on Sunday at 6 pm BRT, so expect a build-up of shirts in Zona Sul from late afternoon tomorrow. Flamengo are travelling this weekend; the city’s heavy football noise is on hold until Sunday evening.

To catch the Sunday match on a big screen, grab an outdoor table at Boteco Belmonte in Ipanema by 4:30 pm—it fills solid by the first half—or head to Bar Urca, where you watch the wall-mounted screens with a cold chopp and a view of the bay.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

Brazilian stocks gave foreign professionals a sharp reason to check portfolios yesterday, with the Ibovespa rising in a session disrupted for hours by a technical failure at the B3 exchange. The outage froze screens across the morning before trading resumed, and the rally was later fuelled by Vale’s quarterly earnings and Santander Brasil’s share buyback offer.

The interruption reignited quiet concern among expat analysts about exchange infrastructure, though the swift resolution—confirmed in a B3 statement—kept the pricing day largely intact. The Brazilian real also strengthened against the dollar in a week driven by appetite for carry trades.

Full closing levels for all indices and FX pairs are on the board (Business & Markets / WEEK IN FIGURES). Monday’s local agenda is light, so attention turns to Brazil services PMI data due Tuesday morning.

10

Plan Ahead

THE WEEK

THE DAYS AHEAD Sun Aug 2 — Sunny 25°C—morning vinyl hunt at Feira da Glória, then Botafogo vs. Vitória 6 pm at Nilton Santos Mon Aug 3 — 26°C and clear—a beach-office day at Ipanema posto 9, low tide mid-morning Tue Aug 4 — Warming to 27°C—Brazil Services PMI out, check market board; VLT to MAR museum after work Wed Aug 5 — Slight cloud build-up—Metrô Line 1 to Saens Peña for Feira de São Cristóvão forró night Thu Aug 6 — Another dry day—CCBB’s new theatre programme opens, evening tickets from R$20

11

FAQ

QUICK ANSWERS

Is the Metro running normally after the big blackout on Wednesday?

Yes, MetrôRio Lines 1, 2 and 4 are running a full Saturday timetable with no reported residual delays. The July 29 disruption was caused by a power failure at a substation in Grajaú, not a Metro fault, and it lasted a few hours before full restoration. Still, download the COR.Rio app before you travel—it gives live Metro and VLT status, and the city’s operations centre pushes alerts if anything changes suddenly.

What do I do if I don’t have a RioCard for the Metro?

You can buy a single-trip or prepaid RioCard at any station counter or machine with cash, debit, or credit card. The flat metro fare is R$4.30. Many stations also now accept the Jaé card. Contactless bank cards are also working at an increasing number of turnstiles, but a dedicated transport card is still your surest bet.

Stronger crack spreads supported the move reflecting higher US Gulf Coast refinery margins that bolster integrated producers’ cash generation. reflecting higher US Gulf Coast refinery margins that bolster integrated producers’ cash generation. Petrobras shares rose 1.46% to US$19.40 as firmer crude highlighted the appeal of Brazil’s low-cost, long-lived pre-salt barrels. as firmer crude highlighted the appeal of Brazil’s low-cost, long-lived pre-salt barrels. Argentina’s YPF advanced 0.75% to US$52.54 tracking the oil price and an improved local backdrop, signalling cautious optimism for Vaca Muerta drilling. tracking the oil price and an improved local backdrop, signalling cautious optimism for Vaca Muerta drilling. Colombia’s Ecopetrol dropped 1.58% to US$16.77 bucking the regional trend as investors weighed policy debates on new exploration and taxation. bucking the regional trend as investors weighed policy debates on new exploration and taxation. Guyana’s offshore boom remained a focal point with higher WTI levels enhancing the economics of future floating production units in the Stabroek block. Today’s Focus Crude’s summer advance continued on Friday, with the US Oil Fund, the exchange-traded vehicle tracking WTI, settling at US$129.17 for a 1.33% daily gain. The move reflected a market pricing tighter physical supply, steady global demand, and lingering threats to shipping lanes. Brazil’s state-controlled giant Petrobras rode the wave, its New York shares climbing 1.46% to US$19.40. Investors treated the stock as a liquid way to bet on high oil prices via the company’s prolific and comparatively cheap pre-salt deepwater fields. Argentina’s YPF also participated, closing 0.75% higher at US$52.54, as the rally in crude strengthened the investment case for the Vaca Muerta shale formation despite the country’s chronic capital controls. Bucking the trend, Colombia’s Ecopetrol slid 1.58% to US$16.77, punished by domestic political debates that have clouded its exploration future. What matters today. Strong crude prices are a rising tide, but they cannot lift boats anchored by country-specific political and policy risks, as Ecopetrol’s drop made clear.

Gerdau’s ADRs meanwhile stayed immobile at US$4.96, a flat 0.00% session, signalling that foreign investors are withholding conviction on Brazil’s long-steel demand for construction rebar and beams until fresh infrastructure data arrives. Industry bodies in Brasília and Mexico City have repeatedly warned that Asian mills are offering flat and long steel at prices local producers cannot match. The Ternium Brasil Santa Cruz plant—a capital-heavy complex with its own private port and a 490 MW thermoelectric plant—has faced intensified import competition in plate products destined for shipbuilding and energy. Brazil’s policy response, a periodic review of anti-dumping duties on Chinese rebar and hot-rolled coil, has become a pivotal variable for Gerdau and CSN. Any sign of looser protection would remove a crucial safety net from beneath their domestic pricing power. Auto and construction pipelines are the other side of the equation. Ternium and its Brazilian subsidiary Usiminas feed flat-steel sheet directly into automotive assembly lines from São Paulo to Monterrey, making Mexican vehicle exports to the United States a primary demand signal. Gerdau leans heavily on Brazil’s residential and infrastructure cycle, where any acceleration in public works could revive pricing for long products. For now, with CSN’s mining miss casting a shadow and Gerdau locked in neutral, the Latin American steel story is one of waiting for a clear tariff catalyst to counter the Chinese export wave. What matters today. China remains the price-setter at the margin, and Latin America’s steel trade defence policy is the variable that determines whether domestic mills can restore profitability.

Global electric-vehicle sales growth has slowed from its previous breakneck pace as European subsidy schemes are adjusted and consumers postpone big-ticket purchases amid high interest rates. Today’s Focus Lithium-related equities closed lower on Saturday as the market absorbed an increasingly interventionist policy stance in Chile, the world’s second-largest producer of the battery metal. The sharpest pain was felt by Santiago-based SQM, whose New York-listed shares shed a full 2.00% to settle at US$67.06, reflecting investor anxiety over a new public-private partnership model that will bring state-owned Codelco into the prized Atacama salar operation once the current contract expires. The fund serves as a proxy for foreign investors seeking indirect exposure to the Lithium Triangle—the high-altitude brine reserves straddling Chile, Argentina, and Bolivia—without holding local securities, but that structure means it amplifies every policy tremor from Santiago. Rising short interest in the ETF underscores a growing conviction among hedge funds that a wave of new supply from Australian spodumene mines and Argentine brine projects will prolong a chemicals glut, just as destocking by Chinese battery makers cools spot demand. The demand side is providing little cover. Global EV sales growth has downshifted as high interest rates and adjusted European subsidy schemes prompt consumers to delay purchases. Meanwhile, Chinese, Korean and Japanese battery producers are working down inventories built up during the lithium price spike, which has forced producers from the Lithium Triangle into a buyers’ market where long-term contracts dictate increasingly subdued pricing. For Argentine and Bolivian project hopefuls, the message is mixed: Argentina continues to court foreign capital with provincial tax incentives, while Bolivia’s technically challenging Uyuni flat remains a longer-dated option reliant on unproven direct-extraction technology consortia. What matters today. Chile’s structural shift to state control is recasting the investment case for the world’s most prolific brine district.

World.title: Krismar Espinosa found guilty of executing Wilbert Banks Jr. in jealousy-fuelled execution
World.content:
Krismar Espinosa found guilty of executing Wilbert Banks Jr. in jealousy-fuelled execution

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Thirty-six-year-old Krismar Espinosa was found guilty on Friday afternoon of the April 2024 murder of bicycle technician and cycling enthusiast Wilbert E. Banks Jr., who was shot seven times after being lured to the Lake Garden area of Ladyville by a woman at the center of the feud.

Justice Nigel Pilgrim delivered the verdict shortly after 1 p.m. in a courtroom filled with relatives of both men. The decision brought an emotional moment for Banks’ family, who had waited more than two years for the case to be concluded.

After reviewing the evidence, Justice Pilgrim said the court was satisfied that Espinosa shot and killed Banks without legal justification in what he described as an execution-style killing. The judge rejected Espinosa’s defence as untrue and found the prosecution’s main witness—Espinosa’s former girlfriend and Banks’ former partner—to be truthful, credible and reliable.

The woman testified by video link that Espinosa became jealous after finding a photograph of Banks and accused her of continuing a relationship with him. She said Espinosa threatened to kill her and her son unless she helped lure Banks to Lake Garden Road.

According to her testimony, Espinosa borrowed his employer’s vehicle and dropped her off in Belize City. Banks later encountered her and offered to drive her back to Ladyville. When they reached Lake Garden, she exited Banks’ vehicle and Espinosa emerged and opened fire from the passenger side.

Banks attempted to escape but was struck by additional gunfire, lost control of his vehicle and crashed. The witness said she ran from the scene, but Espinosa chased her, forced her into his vehicle and threatened her against speaking about the killing.

Police recovered her cellphone near the murder scene, leading investigators to the Lords Bank home where she and Espinosa were found. Officers had also recovered nine expended 9mm shells at the scene. Public reporting at the time stated that Banks was found mortally wounded inside his crashed vehicle shortly after 11:30 p.m. on April 5, 2024.

Justice Pilgrim acknowledged that the woman’s evidence had to be treated cautiously because she had participated in luring Banks to the location. However, he concluded that she acted under threats of violence and that her account was strongly supported by the gunshot damage to Banks’ vehicle, the medical evidence and the physical evidence recovered by police.

The court also questioned Espinosa’s credibility, particularly the conflicting explanations he gave for borrowing his employer’s vehicle. Espinosa claimed he had taken the vehicle to run an errand, later said he went to purchase food and also alleged that the vehicle ran out of fuel. The judge found that those explanations did not correspond with his employer’s testimony.

Espinosa had denied the allegations, claiming he was home between approximately 8:50 and 11 p.m. on the night of the murder and that the case against him had been fabricated.

Banks, 38, worked for several years at Ordonez Bike Shop and was well known within Belize’s cycling community. Friends and relatives publicly remembered him as a quiet, humble and helpful man who was passionate about bicycles and cycling.

Crown Counsels Maria Santana-Nembhard and Joseph Perez prosecuted the case, while Espinosa was represented by attorney Michael Peyrefitte.

Sentencing has been scheduled for September 7, 2026. Justice Pilgrim ordered the preparation of a Social Inquiry Report, a prison report and a Victim Impact Statement ahead of the sentencing hearing.

World.title: Belize Rural North Area Representative rejects voter transfer “incentives”, says resources should benefit community
World.content:
Belize Rural North Area Representative rejects voter transfer “incentives”, says resources should benefit community

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Today, Belize Rural North Area Representative Marconi Leal publicly rejected the practice of offering incentives to encourage voters to transfer into a constituency, saying he will not compromise his principles or divert resources away from community development to increase the voters list.

Leal described the voter transfer period as a “stressful season” for area representatives and said he has faced direct requests from individuals seeking payment in exchange for transferring and voting for him.

“As much as I want to increase my voters list, I will not do it at the expense of having to give ‘something’ before you have even had the opportunity to vote for me,” Leal wrote.

He questioned the commitment of individuals who transfer into the constituency for incentives and later move their registration elsewhere, describing them as “jumpers” who, in his view, have little interest in the long-term development of the communities he serves.

Leal said he has been receiving messages from people asking, “What are you willing to give me to transfer and vote for you!?” He criticized what he described as a transactional approach to voter transfers, arguing that some individuals are more concerned about what they can receive than the development of the constituency.

The area representative said he remains focused on serving the 24 villages in Belize Rural North and responding to their development priorities. “If I were to lose the next elections because of not doing so then so be it,” Leal said adding that he would rather use available resources to support residents and communities than pay individuals to transfer their votes.

Leal said he welcomes eligible voters who seek guidance on polling locations, electoral boundaries or limited transportation assistance, saying such requests demonstrate concern for their communities and country.

World.title: International News: Heat wave scorches U.S. as millions face alerts and temperatures near 120°F
World.content:
International News: Heat wave scorches U.S. as millions face alerts and temperatures near 120°F

By Zoila Palma: A dangerous heat wave is gripping large parts of the United States, with more than 39 million people under heat alerts as temperatures soar across the South and Southwest.

Temperatures have climbed above 100°F in several cities, while highs of 119°F were recorded Thursday near Topock, Arizona, and Tecopa, California, according to the National Weather Service.

The heat dome that previously brought extreme temperatures to central and eastern parts of the country has shifted west and is expected to intensify before spreading into the Intermountain West and northern High Plains.

Parts of the Southwest could see temperatures between 110°F and 120°F through early next week, with some areas potentially experiencing one of their 10 hottest days on record, Yahoo reports.

Extreme heat warnings are in effect across parts of Arizona, California, Nevada, Utah, Oklahoma and western Arkansas, including major population centers and popular national parks. Heat index values could reach 120°F in parts of southern Arizona and South Texas, while overnight temperatures are expected to remain dangerously high, offering little relief from the heat.

World.title: International News: Fast- fashion giant Shein reports $99 million quarterly loss as US tariffs weigh on sales
World.content:
International News: Fast- fashion giant Shein reports $99 million quarterly loss as US tariffs weigh on sales

By Zoila Palma: Fast-fashion giant Shein has reported a $99 million loss for the first three months of 2026, a sharp reversal from the $395 million net income recorded during the same period a year earlier.

The company attributed part of the decline to slower US sales following the removal of a tariff exemption on low-value packages, while ongoing uncertainty over US-China trade tensions has also affected its business.

Shein said the elimination of the US “de minimis” exemption, which previously allowed goods valued at $800 or less to enter the country without tariffs, has negatively affected sales and overall revenue growth.

In response to higher duties and taxes, the company said it is considering several measures, including raising prices in the US to offset some of the increased costs, BBC reports.

The company also reported that the conflict involving Iran had weakened demand, raised operating costs and caused delivery delays in some markets. However, the first-quarter loss included a $328 million paper loss linked to an accounting change involving special investor shares, meaning the underlying financial performance was affected by factors beyond direct operating results.

The latest financial disclosure comes as Shein prepares for a potential stock market debut in Hong Kong after receiving approval from China’s securities regulator.

World.title: Consumer confidence dips slightly in June as Belizeans remain cautious about major purchases
World.content:
Consumer confidence dips slightly in June as Belizeans remain cautious about major purchases

By Zoila Palma: Consumer confidence in Belize edged lower in June 2026, with the national Consumer Confidence Index (CCI) falling marginally by 0.4 percent to 41.1, down from 41.3 in May, according to the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB). The decline continues a downward trend seen in recent months, although at a slower pace than the sharper decreases recorded earlier in the year.

The SIB said the decline was mainly driven by weaker sentiment toward major household purchases and current economic conditions. The Durable Goods component fell by 8.5 percent, from 37.6 to 34.4, indicating increased pessimism about purchasing items such as homes, vehicles, furniture and appliances. The Present component also declined by 0.9 percent, from 37.9 to 37.6, as consumers became slightly more pessimistic about current economic conditions and their household finances.

However, consumers were more optimistic about the year ahead. The Expectations component rose by 6.4 percent, moving from a pessimistic 48.3 in May to an optimistic 51.4 in June, reflecting improved views of future economic conditions and household finances. By district, Orange Walk recorded the largest decline in confidence, falling 8.9 percent to 36.0, while Cayo saw the biggest improvement, with confidence rising 6.5 percent from 38.5 to 41.0.

The CCI, which ranges from zero to 100, measures consumer sentiment about the economy, household finances and major purchases, with a score above 50 generally indicating optimism. The index is considered an early indicator of future household spending, saving and investment, and therefore can provide insight into potential economic growth.

World.title: Ministry of Agriculture conclude Value-Added Beekeeping Products Training for Maya Mopan Bee Cooperative
World.content:
Ministry of Agriculture conclude Value-Added Beekeeping Products Training for Maya Mopan Bee Cooperative

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Stann Creek Department of Agriculture, through the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries (MAFSNGI), successfully conducted a Value-Added Beekeeping Products Training for members of the Maya Mopan Bee Cooperative.

The training was funded through the Climate Resilient and Sustainable Agriculture Project (CRESAP).

The training was designed to strengthen the capacity of beekeepers by introducing value-added processing techniques that enable participants to diversify their enterprises and maximize the economic potential of hive products.

CRESAP noted that by expanding beyond honey production, beekeepers can explore new market opportunities, increase the value of their products, and improve the sustainability of their operations.

World.title: UNICEF, Caribbean Climate Change Centre strengthen partnership on child-focused climate action
World.content:
UNICEF, Caribbean Climate Change Centre strengthen partnership on child-focused climate action

By Zoila Palma: UNICEF and the Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre (CCCCC) have signed a five-year Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) aimed at strengthening efforts to protect children’s rights and well-being from the growing impacts of climate change across the Caribbean.

The partnership will promote child-sensitive climate policies, resilient social services, climate adaptation and disaster risk reduction, while giving young people greater opportunities to participate in climate action and decision-making.

Children across the region are increasingly exposed to hurricanes, flooding, droughts, extreme heat and environmental degradation, threatening access to education, healthcare, nutrition, clean water and sanitation.

UNICEF Representative Sajid Ali said climate change is not only an environmental issue but also a child rights challenge, noting that children are among those least responsible for the climate crisis while facing some of its greatest consequences.

CCCCC Executive Director Dr. Colin Young welcomed the agreement, saying children and youth have not traditionally been a central focus of climate resilience programming and that the partnership will help place them at the heart of regional climate action.

A key area of collaboration will focus on climate-resilient sanitation services, alongside efforts to strengthen education, health, nutrition, water and sanitation systems and disaster preparedness.

World.title: Market Bag: Food prices trending up at Spanish Town Market
World.content:
ST CATHERINE, Jamaica — Consumers are facing higher costs at the Spanish Town Market, where prices for several key food items have increased this week.

Among the items fetching higher prices are sweet peppers at $500 per pound; ginger at $600 per pound; Scotch bonnet peppers at $400 per pound; and onions at $300 per pound.

Ripe bananas, which have remained costly at other markets in recent weeks, are being sold in Spanish Town for between $400 and $600 per hand, while green bananas are priced at $400 per hand.

Farmer Samuel King, who features in this week’s episode of Market Bag, said extreme heat conditions, torrential rainfall and rising fertiliser costs are contributing to higher food prices across markets islandwide. He also noted that consumers’ reduced spending power has affected market traffic.

In the latest feature, host Carlysia Ramdeen journeys from farm to market, starting in Hartlands, St Catherine, where King shares the realities of farming, selling produce and the price gap between what farmers earn and what consumers ultimately pay.

World.title: Wheatley granted injunction barring IC charges until judicial review
World.content:
Andrew Wheatley

The Supreme Court has granted an injunction preventing the Integrity Commission (IC) from charging Cabinet Minister Dr Andrew Wheatley until the hearing and determination of an application by his lawyers for judicial review.

Wheatley had applied for leave to pursue judicial review against the IC’s recommendation that he be charged with illicit enrichment.

Observer Online understands that the Supreme Court on Friday granted Wheatley’s application, recommending that the judicial review be heard by a panel of three judges.

Before granting the injunction, presiding Judge Justice David Batts had suggested that the IC consider an undertaking not to charge Dr Wheatley until the hearing and determination of the judicial review.

The commission said it could not give an undertaking at this time. The judge then granted the injunction.

It is understood that the IC’s application for leave to appeal the ruling was denied.

The Integrity Commission had alleged that there is a disproportionality in Wheatley’s assets when compared to his income to the tune of $164 million.

Wheatley rejected the allegation and accused the IC of failing to take into consideration $168 million in rental income accumulated over a decade.

He is being represented by a high powered legal team including King’s Counsel Ransford Braham, Abe Dabdoub and Neco Pagon.

The Integrity Commission is being represented by King’s Counsel Kevin Powell.

World.title: DROUGHT ALERT!
World.content:
Principal Director of the Meteorological Service of Jamaica, Evan Thompson gives the forecast for the island over the next few months during a press briefing Thursday afternoon.(Photo: Karl McLarty)

With projections from the Meteorological Service of Jamaica showing prolonged dry conditions stretching into October this year, Water, Environment and Climate Change Minister Matthew Samuda has put Jamaicans on alert for full prohibition orders for water usage, which he says will take effect on August 10 if the forecast remains unchanged or worsens.

The warning comes following a Thursday morning meeting of the Integrated Water Resources Management Council — a Cabinet subcommittee comprising all stakeholders in the water sector; academia; municipalities; and the ministries of agriculture, health and national security. That report was complemented by forecasts of the Met Service and assessments of the Water Resources Authority, according to Samuda.

Since earlier this year, nightly water restrictions and scheduled supply cuts have been implemented in vulnerable Corporate Area networks, such as Kingston 20, given the drought conditions.

Speaking during a media briefing at the Half-Way-Tree Road offices of his ministry to discuss the rainfall and drought conditions, Samuda said given the indications that there will be “a dry August, a dry September, and a dry October…it is clear and should be clear to all Jamaicans that conservation is indeed imperative at this stage”.

“We are first encouraging conservation, but being very clear that as at August 10th…if the situation has not changed — meaning if the Met Services evaluation of rainfall in July is as we suspect — that we will have continued declines in rainfall, and if the rolling three-month forecast has not changed, or has worsened, prohibition orders will come into effect,” Samuda said.

The water minister said those orders will be targeted at “irrigation and watering of gardens, lawns, grounds, and farms, filling or supplying of pools, and other things for domestic services”.

“Washing of cars, watering and washing of roadways, and any purpose that would require unusual or non-essential use of water would be prohibited,” Samuda added.

He emphasised that the announcement was not to be interpreted to mean “that the systems and the storage are at critical levels today, but the rainfall that would normally come at the end of August is not projected to be experienced”.

Pointing to the learning loss that has already resulted from the COVID-19 pandemic as well as weather events such as Hurricane Beryl, Tropical Storm Raphael, and Hurricane Melissa, the minister said every effort will be made to ensure that schools receive the support needed.

“We simply cannot afford water to contribute to learning loss in September. So we will take the measures that we absolutely need to ensure that we’re able to safeguard the opening of schools in September and not contribute to learning loss. So that needs to be understood. We do hope that the situation will change, but with the information that we have, this is the best decision that we can make at this stage,” Samuda stressed.

“We do hope that the situation will change, but with the information that we have, this is the best decision that we can make at this stage,” he added.

Speaking during the briefing, principal director of the Meteorological Service of Jamaica Evan Thompson said as at the end of June the parishes of St Elizabeth, St James, St Ann, and St Mary “were determined to be experiencing drought conditions”. He said the parishes of Manchester and St Catherine “were both basically on the borderline, in that they were just about moving toward drought conditions”.

“It’s most likely that having not experienced significant rainfall during the month of July, that situation would have been worsened. We should be seeing that drought conditions at least would have extended to these two parishes. That’s what we’re expecting to pick up after the month of July has ended, as we begin to gather and collate and compare our data,” Thompson told members of the media.

He noted that the projections did not mean there would be “no rainfall” at all for the island, but that “the number of incidents of rainfall will be fewer”, influenced by the El Nino phenomenon which has caused “lesser than normal amounts of rainfall and higher than normal temperatures” over the past few months.

“However, we could have a bulk of rainfall that is intense, and so we could have very small areas that experience maybe even flooding events in small areas as these systems develop and as they continue to affect us, but generally we will experience dry conditions,” Thompson explained further.

He cautioned that with the forecast for August showing “higher-than-normal temperatures right through the month” and “lower-than-normal rainfall”, Jamaicans should be on the lookout for “climate-induced bushfires”.
