World.title: Chinese Village’s Viral Cicada Harvest Comes Under Fire
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018842/Chinese Village’s Viral Cicada Harvest Comes Under Fire
World.content:
In an eastern Chinese village, harvesting cicada nymphs for consumption has evolved from a seasonal tradition into a lucrative side business for farmers, fueled by a local official’s livestreaming business. But critics are questioning whether the trade is flourishing at the expense of local ecosystems.

This summer, Liu Lei, a village official of Dongjiezhuang Village in the eastern Shandong province, began selling wild cicada nymphs through livestreaming, sourcing the insects from locals. In the past week, he has come under fire online, with social media users citing environmental concerns.

Known in Chinese as zhiliaohou, or “cicada monkeys,” nymphs — immature, wingless cicadas who emerge after three to five years feeding on plant matter underground — have long been considered a summer delicacy in northern and eastern China. Historical texts, including the sixth-century agricultural encyclopedia “Qimin Yaoshu,” describe consumption of the insects in the region.

Liu, one of a growing number of village official influencers, markets local specialties and agricultural products such as honey and peaches on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, to boost the local economy.

Liu’s videos show villagers — largely seniors — going out each night at dusk, armed with flashlights and plastic bags, to search for the insects in the nearby forest. They then sell their collections to Liu at a designated point in the village for extra income. Each cicada sells for around 1 yuan ($0.14).

One 60-year-old local said he had caught more than 200 cicada nymphs in a single night. “I usually don’t eat them myself. One cicada nymph is priced higher than an ear of corn,” he said.

Liu’s actions have triggered debate online. While some support him for bringing in income for farmers, others argue that livestreaming has transformed a long-standing tradition into a commercial rush. Experts also warn that large-scale collection could threaten biodiversity and disrupt local food chains.

In an interview with local media, Liu said villagers have harvested cicada nymphs for decades without damaging the environment. “We have a tradition of only collecting nymphs that have just emerged from the soil,” he said. “Once they’ve molted into adult cicadas, no one catches them because they are no longer edible.”

Although Cryptotympana atrata, the preferred cicada species being collected, is not nationally protected, entomologists warn that large-scale population decimation could still affect local ecosystems.

Zhao Li, curator of the Insect Museum of West China in Chengdu, capital of the southwestern Sichuan province, told local media that cicadas help recycle nutrients in forests and provide food for birds and other wildlife. Their shed exoskeletons, Zhao added, are also widely used in traditional Chinese medicine.

Authorities have attempted to curb the collection of cicadas in some regions. In 2024, forestry officials in Tongchuan, a city in the northwestern Shaanxi province, warned against unauthorized harvesting of cicadas in forests and protected areas, stating that large-scale collection could damage vegetation, increase wildfire risks, and violate forestry regulations.

Specifically addressing the Dongjiezhuang Village case in a video posted to Douyin, Li Mingli, chairman of agricultural brand consulting firm Beijing Fangyuan, noted that, “Livestream traffic can amplify demand far beyond what unwritten local customs can regulate.”

Li suggested that instead of harvesting wild cicadas, the village could build a cicada farm, providing locals with a more stable source of income while reducing pressure on wild populations. He added that local authorities could also introduce collection quotas and rotate harvesting areas.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018839/China’s Elderly Embrace an Unlikely New Sport: Hyrox Races
World.title: China’s Elderly Embrace an Unlikely New Sport: Hyrox Races
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018839/China’s Elderly Embrace an Unlikely New Sport: Hyrox Races
World.content:
ZHEJIANG, East China — Wang Hui, a 68-year-old from Beijing, used to avoid intense exercise whenever possible. The retiree’s fitness regime mostly consisted of the odd brisk walk, and maybe a few leg raises at home.

But that suddenly changed a few months ago, when her daughter informed her she’d signed Wang up for a Hyrox race.

The fitness craze, which originated in Germany a few years ago, is not for the faint of heart: participants must complete eight 1-kilometer runs, each followed by a set of strength exercises ranging from lunges to pushing a heavy sled.

Curious and keen to connect with her daughter — a long-time fitness enthusiast — Wang threw herself into training, building up from 1-kilometer jogs to 8-kilometer runs in just two months.

Then, one day in July, Wang found herself walking alongside her daughter into a cavernous expo center in the eastern city of Hangzhou packed with more than 6,000 competitors and 7,000 cheering spectators.

As she stood under the pulsing strobe lights, ears throbbing from the pumping bass, Wang could not have felt more out of her comfort zone. But she suspects that was her daughter’s intention all along.

“My daughter keeps surprising me,” she told Sixth Tone after completing the event in July. “She shows me, ‘I can still do this,’ ‘I can still do that.’”

Wang is far from alone. As Hyrox explodes in popularity across China, the races have unexpectedly begun to attract an ever greater number of retirees — many of them competing in their first event well after turning 70.

For some, the races represent a fresh challenge or an excuse to get fit. For others, like Wang, they offer a chance to reconnect with adult children for whom Hyrox has become a new obsession.

Even by global standards, Hyrox has taken off in China at astonishing speed. The first official Chinese Hyrox race took place as recently as 2024, with 1,700 fitness enthusiasts competing in a hall in Beijing.

Now, events are held all over the country, with early-bird registration often selling out within minutes despite costing up to 800 yuan ($125) for an individual entry fee — more than three times the entry fee for a typical marathon in China. At a recent race in Shanghai, over 10,000 people took part.

As elsewhere, Hyrox fans in China tend to be young, middle-class, and super-fit. Local races are filled with ripped 20- and 30-somethings working in competitive industries such as finance and artificial intelligence.

On Chinese social media, Hyrox’s appeal to such high-fliers has become a running joke. Users often quip that the sport taps into a deep Chinese love for hard work and standardized tests. Some even liken Hyrox training to preparing for the gaokao, China’s grueling college entrance exams.

But the sport also has a more inclusive side. At some events, participants can sign up in teams of two or more — allowing them to divide the workload — and the lack of cut-off time means slower competitors can complete the race.

That has opened the door to a growing number of elderly contenders. Online, there has been a wave of social media posts in recent months from Chinese millennials sharing their experiences of entering Hyrox races alongside their aging parents, many of them attracting thousands of likes.

Wang’s daughter, Xie Shanshan, is part of that trend. Now in her 40s, she took up running years ago while living and working in Beijing — competing in several half-marathons — before pivoting to Hyrox as the sport began to gain traction.

For Xie, the hope was that competing in the team event with her mother would give them a shared experience. But she also aimed to give Wang — who has been retired for years — a healthy jolt.

And she appears to have succeeded. After the initial shock wore off, Wang fully committed to the training and finished the Hangzhou race, with Xie reminding her to pace herself.

“We didn’t go at 100% effort,” Wang said. “My daughter kept saying, ‘Steady, steady, it’s about the taking part, not speed.’”

When asked whether it’s a good idea for seniors to participate in such high-intensity sports, Wang said it was easy to fall into a rut after retirement, spending all day scrolling social media or watching TV.

“But if you can step out and join social activities with younger people, your thinking and values get reenergized,” she said. “The real appeal lies in connecting with the younger generation, adding vitality to life, and broadening horizons.”

Other child-parent teams competing in Hangzhou shared similar experiences. Yu Lian, a 45-year-old CrossFit enthusiast, had been training for nearly a decade and had already run solo in two Hyrox races.

But after seeing online that some of her favorite fitness influencers had brought their parents along to Hyrox events, she decided to ask her 74-year-old father to join her at her next race.

According to Yu, he immediately replied: “Just tell me what to do, and I’ll do it. I walk so much every day. I’m already the number one in our neighborhood!”

Though Yu had emphasized “safety first,” her father took the training unexpectedly seriously. For nearly two months, he took brisk walks outside several times a week, and ended up losing 5 kilograms.

On race day, it was a similar story. Yu’s plan was to do all the strength exercises herself, while her father walked alongside her. But he ended up getting far more involved than she had expected.

After each kilometer run, she found him already waiting for her at the work station, arm outstretched, ready to pull her forward. In the final event — the “wall ball,” where competitors have to throw a heavy medicine ball against a wall — her father, fueled by the crowd’s energy, grabbed a ball and nailed the target on the second attempt.

For Yu, the race came to feel like an important bonding experience. Growing up, her relationship with her father had always been reserved — love was expressed through deeds, not words, she recalled.

The term “parent-child bonding” usually conjures up images of young families with small children, but Yu said she felt that older generations — those in their 40s and 70s — needed it just as much.

“Interactions between adult children and aging parents are often limited,” Yu said. “Participation in the race is a meaningful way to foster various types of connection.”

Yet, for all its emotional benefits, Hyrox can be a dangerous activity — especially for a beginner in their 60s or 70s. Li Cong, a functional training, pilates, and sports rehabilitation instructor in Shanghai, warned the sport presented a high injury risk.

“After running, the small stabilizing muscles around our joints fatigue,” she said. “When we then do weighted sled pushes or kettlebell exercises, the lower back and knees are forced to compensate and bear all the weight. When your form breaks down under fatigue, the injury rate is much higher than if you trained running and strength separately.”

Sun Yang, a senior rehabilitation therapist in the sports medicine department at Shanghai’s Huashan Hospital, echoed those concerns. A Hyrox devotee herself, she approaches training with caution.

“I stop and rest for a few days if I feel any discomfort,” Sun said. “I don’t allow myself to continue exercising while overtired or in pain.”

Wang Zheng — no relation to Wang Hui — thought long and hard before inviting his mother to form a Hyrox team with him.

As a 32-year-old fitness professional, Wang Zheng had already competed in 22 Hyrox events, and he was keen to bring his mother, Ma Jing, into his world. But he also knew that the traditional, hardcore format wasn’t a fit for everyone.

Luckily, the mixed-doubles category offered a solution. “In mixed doubles, I can take on 90% of the workload, and there is no cut-off time at the venue. That meant I could finally bring my mom along to play,” he said.

Ma, a 65-year-old retiree living in eastern China’s Shandong province, was initially apprehensive when her son suggested entering a race together. “I was actually a bit scared, afraid of embarrassing him,” she recalled.

But her fear soon gave way to a deeper motivation. “I don’t want to be a burden to my son as I get older, and the first step is to stay healthy,” Ma said. “So I thought, let me challenge myself.”

The training ended up having a profound impact on Ma. She moved in with her son in the southern city of Shenzhen months before the race so that they could prepare together, and watching his tough routine gave her a new understanding of his commitment.

His dedication also inspired Ma to take her own training seriously. In November, the pair completed the race in Shanghai in 100 minutes, with Ma’s performance surpassing her son’s expectations. The atmosphere even motivated her to take on several exercises that she had never tried before.

Now, flush with her triumph, she has decided to push on with her training. She runs 5 to 10 kilometers a day, hits the gym for strength training 20 days a month, and is lining up her next races.

“Since I’ve decided to compete, I have to show up in my best form,” she said.

More importantly, Ma said Hyrox had helped shatter her self-doubt. “I used to think I wasn’t ready, but actually, we don’t need to prepare for everything. Just participating is a reward in itself.”

Additional reporting: Xie Anran.

(Header image: Elderly participants in Hyrox races. Xie Anran/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018829/The Chinese Tea That Became a British Joke — and Those That Didn’t
World.title: The Chinese Tea That Became a British Joke — and Those That Didn’t
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018829/The Chinese Tea That Became a British Joke — and Those That Didn’t
World.content:
This is the second article in a two-part series exploring how Chinese culinary terms came to be included in the Oxford English Dictionary (OED). Read Part 1.

China is the origin of tea, and its global vocabulary remains deeply rooted in Chinese. The English word “tea” derives from the Minnan (Hokkien) dialect, reflecting maritime trade routes that carried the leaf from the coastal ports of China’s eastern Fujian province to Europe. Meanwhile, “char” (or “cha”), originating from Mandarin or Cantonese, persists in British slang as a colloquial term for a cup of tea. More recently, the Indian-derived “chai” — a popular blend of black tea, milk, sugar or honey, and spices — has gained traction in Western coffee shops. Yet the foundational lexicon of tea in English remains unmistakably Chinese.

While China produces a wide array of premium teas, English dictionaries have historically been highly selective in what they adopt. Among the commonly accepted lists of China’s most celebrated teas, only Wuyi rock tea (Bohea) and Keemun black tea (Keemun) traditionally made the cut, both transliterated from regional names. However, a closer reading of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED) reveals a more expansive linguistic landscape: nearly 30 Chinese tea terms have been formally incorporated into English. Some are widely used, while others survive as lexical relics. This lexicon includes foundational terms such as green tea, white tea, oolong, and congou; premium black teas like pekoe, souchong, and Lapsang souchong; historic green teas including Hyson and Singlo; post-fermented varieties such as Pu-erh; and descriptive terms such as pearl tea (gunpowder tea) and imperial tea.

Within this OED-derived lexicon of Chinese tea terms in English, one striking anomaly stands out: the theatrical caricature of “Widow Twankey.” The linguistic transformation began in Tunxi, a historic tea hub in the eastern Anhui province. The city’s name was phonetically adapted into “Twankay” to denote large quantities of green tea exported from the region during the 18th century. As this tea became associated with lower grades in Western markets because of its older, coarser, and more ragged leaves, “Twankay” was later repurposed by playwrights into the comedic character “Widow Twankey,” and eventually entered British slang as a term for cheap gin.

In 1861, playwright H.J. Byron named Aladdin’s mother “Widow Twankey” to imply she was “past her best.” The character went on to become a pantomime staple — a bawdy, eccentric “dame” traditionally played by a man in drag, often depicted running a chaotic Chinese laundry in a fictionalized “Old Peking.”

For modern readers, the fact that a Chinese tea term was transformed into a theatrical punchline can come as a shock. Yet placed within the broader OED record, Twankey remains a clear exception. The vast majority of Chinese tea terms in English have been treated with linguistic and cultural respect.

Take Bohea (Wuyi tea), for instance. As one of the earliest black teas imported into Britain in the early 1700s, OED citations show it was initially regarded as a luxury product. Although its commercial standing later declined — by the mid-19th century it was classified among lower-grade black teas — its literary presence remained stable. From Alexander Pope to William Makepeace Thackeray, Bohea continued to appear in print as an authentic beverage.

Similarly, congou (gongfu tea) was established as a marker of upper-class refinement. In Richard Brinsley Sheridan’s 1777 comedic play “The School for Scandal,” congou appears alongside exotic luxuries such as avadavats (tropical songbirds) and Indian crackers. Victorian dietary writers later formalized this hierarchy. In his 1874 “A Treatise on Food and Dietetics,” F.W. Pavy explicitly ranked major black teas in ascending order of quality: Bohea, oolong, congou, campoi.

This documentary respect extends to souchong and Lapsang souchong. In the 18th century, souchong was among the most expensive “brown teas” (the contemporary term for what is now called black tea), attracting such attention that it was subjected to chemical analysis by the Royal Society. Lapsang souchong, despite its distinctive smoky profile, was embraced by intellectual circles. Samuel Beckett praised the “choicest lapsang souchong,” while Aldous Huxley and Iris Murdoch incorporated it naturally into their writing. The OED also records its organic evolution in everyday speech, recording spelling variations like “lapseng,” “lapsang soochong,” and “lapsang suchong.”

The same holds true for pekoe. As early as 1713, essayist Joseph Addison listed it alongside coffee and chocolate as a fashionable social staple, while East India Company records documented its premium trade value. From the tinfoiled chests of “flowery Pekoe” described by G.A. Sala in 1859 to the “teak-colored pekoe” poured in Annie Proulx’s 1993 novel “The Shipping News,” pekoe has maintained a continuous literary and commercial presence. Gunpowder tea, tightly rolled into pellets, was elegantly translated by early British scholars as “pearl tea.”

Importantly, this documentary trail is not limited to black teas. Hyson, known in Chinese as xichun, was championed by Thomas Jefferson, who preferred “young Hyson” for its strength and flavor. By 1948, The New York Times described young Hyson and pinhead gunpowder as the “aristocrats of green teas.”

Singlo was once a major commercial variety in the 18th century, with East India Company ledgers recording millions of pounds imported annually. Known in Chinese as Songluo, after the Songluo Mountain in Anhui where it originates, it was so highly prized that travelers noted authentic batches had become exceedingly rare, with counterfeit versions flooding the market.

Even the obsolete terms in the OED offer a fascinating philosophical counterpoint. Imperial, for instance, once described by J.M. Walsh in 1892 as “the perfection of tea,” has since fallen out of use. Similarly, bing has vanished from common usage. First documented by the Royal Society in 1702 as “the second growth in April,” it is a dialect romanization of the Chinese character “ming” (meaning “bright”), evoking the clarity of early spring after Qingming. Another example, “Oopack,” a highly valued tea from the central Hubei province that fetched top auction prices in The Times as late as 1855, now survives only as a rare lexical relic.

Today, the translation of Chinese tea culture continues to evolve. While traditional teas such as Longjing (Dragon Well) remain largely untranslated in English, modern milk tea brands are experimenting with hybrid naming strategies. Chagee (drawing on “cha,” the Chinese word for tea, and “gee” (which approximates the sound of the Chinese character ji – a classical Chinese term for female performers) and ChaPanda merge Chinese linguistic cues with global marketing logic.

Meanwhile, a new wave of tea culture is reshaping global consumption. Bubble tea (boba), which originated in Taiwan in the 1980s, has become a global phenomenon. What began as a simple blend of black tea, milk, and chewy tapioca pearls has evolved into a highly customizable, brightly colored drink embedded in global youth culture. Driven by social media aesthetics and its distinctive texture, boba has moved from East Asian diaspora spaces into mainstream cafés worldwide, reshaping expectations of what tea can be.

Similarly, yum cha, the Cantonese tradition of drinking tea with dim sum, remains strong across global cities, functioning as a social anchor in urban dining culture. Beyond this, yin yeung — the Hong Kong-style blend of milk tea and coffee — is also gradually capturing international attention. As this bold, caffeinated fusion finds its way onto menus outside Hong Kong, it signals the ongoing global influence of hybridized regional drinks.

This modern expansion is part of a broader global tea renaissance that also includes the Indian-derived chai, now a staple in Western coffee chains. From the early days of Singlo and Imperial to the modern ubiquity of boba and yin yeung, Chinese tea has left a lasting mark on the English language. The theatrical figure of Widow Twankey remains an outlier, a historical distortion rather than a defining pattern.

Yet tea’s vitality has never been confined to its point of origin. A beverage rooted solely in China would have remained culturally rich but geographically limited; its global life depends on circulation, adaptation, and reinterpretation. Today, as global consumers fall in love with tea, they continue to reshape it into new forms, from South Asia’s spiced chai to Southeast Asia’s milk tea variations and contemporary café experiments in the West.

It is this ongoing exchange and reinvention that sustains tea’s global relevance. Ultimately, its legacy is not only Chinese heritage embedded in language, but a shared cultural system in motion — a cup that grows richer with every new tradition poured into it.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018834/The Chinese Chicken Joint That Rejected Fame Now Craves It
World.title: The Chinese Chicken Joint That Rejected Fame Now Craves It
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018834/The Chinese Chicken Joint That Rejected Fame Now Craves It
World.content:
From “don’t come,” to “the more customers, the better.” These were the refrains made by the owner of a chicken hotpot restaurant in southern China famous for shirking fame and which has recently drawn criticism for perceived hypocrisy due to its rapid expansion.

In April, “Mo’s Chicken Hotpot,” in the southern Guangdong province’s Foshan City, went viral after the recommendation of a popular food vlogger. The eatery drew crowds for its signature medicinal hotpot made from freshly slaughtered chickens — and whose healing properties included causing diarrhea, according to notices in the restaurant.

During the initial vlogger’s visit, the restaurant’s owner, surnamed Mo, insisted that customers should “not come” as he would not be able to handle the popularity. Nevertheless, the restaurant began drawing thousands of customers a day, including celebrities and influencers.

But the restaurant’s expansion to five branches in Guangdong and Shanghai — with another expected to open in the southern city of Shenzhen next year — and frequent online s in the months since have drawn ridicule, domestic media reported this week. Social media users argue the restaurant’s current activities contradict Mo’s previous rejection of fame.

Earlier interviews quoted Mo as saying he had no plans to raise prices or open new outlets, leading some online to question whether his indifferent persona had been a marketing strategy from the beginning.

As of this month, Mo said the restaurant has hired a 20-person livestreaming team and broadcasts twice a day. “We can’t afford not to livestream,” he told domestic media. “The pressure is just too great.”

The eatery’s official account on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, now has around 500,000 followers. It posts two to three times a week, mainly skits promoting its signature chicken hotpot alongside health tips. Several videos have garnered tens of thousands of likes.

The restaurant also sells meal kits, Chinese medicine, herbal teas, and local specialties such as salt-baked chicken via its online store.

The rating for Mo’s Chicken Hotpot on review platform Dianping has fallen from a peak of 4.8 out of 5 in April to 3.7, according to domestic media. Negative reviews mention inconsistent food quality, flies and poor hygiene standards in the restaurant, and high prices.

Visitor numbers have also fluctuated. In June, domestic media reported that sales at the original restaurant had fallen from 200 to 400 orders a day to fewer than 20 a day by the end of the month. However, Mo told domestic media in mid-July that the restaurant handles no fewer than 150 orders a day.

In a video interview with domestic media, Mo responded to the criticism, saying, “At first, when we suddenly became so popular, I really didn’t want the attention. We were so busy, it made me want to throw up.”

“Now I actually want the business to be even better,” he added. “When fortune gives you an opportunity like this … and there’s money to be made, why wouldn’t I try to make money? I’d be a fool not to.”

Mo also admitted that despite the restaurant’s expansion and livestreaming business, profits remain limited.

“Traffic comes quickly, and it disappears just as quickly. After a month or two, how do you sustain it? It’s really hard,” adding that if another wave of popularity were to come, he would “honestly close shop and stop.”

Mo also joined the second season of popular domestic cooking competition show “The Divine Dish,” which premiered Wednesday. He was eliminated in the first round.

“The ingredients (he used) were good, but his technique was poor,” one of the show’s judges said of his signature chicken hotpot.

On his Douyin account, Mo responded to his elimination, saying, “I will continue to use the finest ingredients and simplest methods to cook you the familiar chicken hotpot that warms your heart.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Weibo, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018835/Shaw in Shanghai: How the Irish Writer’s 1933 Visit Inspired China’s Literati
World.title: Shaw in Shanghai: How the Irish Writer’s 1933 Visit Inspired China’s Literati
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018835/Shaw in Shanghai: How the Irish Writer’s 1933 Visit Inspired China’s Literati
World.content:
Editor’s note: The theme of the third Shanghai Public Relations Academic Symposium on Irish Literature, held on July 26, was playwright George Bernard Shaw’s eight-hour visit to Shanghai in the 1930s, when China’s cultural and anti-imperialist movements were gaining momentum. The following is an account of the writer’s time in the city and its impact on Chinese intellectuals.

When George Bernard Shaw, the Irish playwright and novelist, paid a brief visit to Shanghai as part of his global voyage in 1933, the city’s intellectuals were thrilled.

Before his arrival, articles about Shaw had been published in various newspapers and magazines. Some discussed his Communist advocacy in Hong Kong, while others talked about how his satirical writing style had influenced European society.

According to a biography of Soong Ching Ling, the Chinese politician and wife of Sun Yat-sen, sometimes called the “father of modern China,” Shaw arrived at Wusongkou port — today the Wusongkou International Cruise Terminal in northeastern Shanghai — at 6 a.m. on Feb. 17 aboard the Empress of Britain, accompanied by his wife, the political activist Charlotte Payne-Townshend. At 5 a.m., Soong went to Wusongkou with Yang Xingfo, a social activist and patriotic democrat, to welcome the couple. At Shaw’s invitation, she joined him on board for breakfast.

More than 200 reporters rushed to Wusongkou early that morning, but Shaw initially refused to go ashore, telling Soong that apart from her, there was no one in Shanghai he wanted to meet, nor anything he wanted to see. But in the end, Soong persuaded him to pay a visit to the city. They took a steamship to Lanlu Wharf in today’s Yangpu District, where he finally went ashore. The reporters waiting at Wusongkou left empty-handed — not a single photograph of Shaw was taken.

At 10:30 a.m., Soong and Shaw disembarked and set out for the city’s downtown. Shaw met and talked with several left-wing Chinese intellectuals, including Yang, former Peking University president Cai Yuanpei, literary icon Lu Xun, writer and linguist Lin Yutang, and the American journalists Harold Isaacs and Agnes Smedley.

Later, at the invitation of the Chinese branch of PEN International, a global association of writers founded in London in 1921, Shaw and other Chinese intellectuals visited the World College on Route Ferguson (now Wukang Road) to attend a gathering with local PEN members. When Shaw met Mei Lanfang, the renowned Peking opera artist and founder of Shanghai’s Left Theatre Club, he expressed his puzzlement over the differences between Eastern and Western theater.

“Will you please tell me how a Chinese actor can do anything in the midst of such infernal uproars as one hears on your stage?” he asked. “In our theater, they put a man out if he sneezes. But you have gongs and cymbals and the competition of half the audience and innumerable vendors. Don’t you object?”

Mei explained that Peking opera was a folk art first performed in the open air, and drums and gongs were then used to attract people to the show. This tradition had simply endured.

Around 3 p.m., Shaw finally spoke with some Chinese and foreign reporters in the garden of Soong’s residence, discussing socialism, national oppression, Eastern culture, and revolutions, among other topics. Afterward, Soong accompanied Shaw back to the Empress of Britain, which then carried the playwright northward to Beijing.

Although Shaw spent just over eight hours in Shanghai, his visit sparked considerable discussion and reverberations among the city’s left-wing intellectual circles. The writer and poet Yu Dafu wrote in Free Talk, a supplement of the Shun Pao newspaper, that he hoped Shaw could tell the world, in his own sarcastic tone, about Japanese imperialism and its invasion of China.

At the time, intellectuals including Lu Xun and the poet and translator Qu Qiubai were working to build a central stronghold for China’s left-wing cultural movement. After Shaw’s departure, they, along with partners Xu Guangping and Yang Zhihua, began compiling reports from various newspapers and periodicals about the Irish novelist’s short visit. The collection was published in March 1933 by Yecao Shudian, or Wildgrass Bookshop, under the title “George Bernard Shaw in Shanghai.”

In the preface, Lu wrote: “Those who truly welcomed him were the Chinese people, as well as the literary and artistic circles that stood by the people. The Chinese people did not regard him as a ‘revolutionary leader’ or a ‘thoroughgoing socialist writer,’ much less as an idol. They regarded Shaw as a loyal friend of the oppressed people of the world, and of China.”

Editor: Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Visuals from the Shanghai Lu Xun Museum, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018830/How Cantonese Cuisine Became Part of the English Language
World.title: How Cantonese Cuisine Became Part of the English Language
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018830/How Cantonese Cuisine Became Part of the English Language
World.content:
This is the first article in a two-part series exploring how Chinese culinary terms came to be included in the Oxford English Dictionary (OED).

For more than two decades, I have studied how Chinese words enter the English language, particularly through food. So when the Oxford English Dictionary (OED) released its second batch of updates this past June, one updated entry felt especially meaningful to me: “Cantonese.” For the first time, the dictionary formally recognized the word as a culinary term, defining it as food prepared in the style of Guangzhou and the surrounding region in southern China, as well as the restaurants that serve such cuisine.

The entry is accompanied not just by a simple definition, but by a timeline of citations tracing the term’s culinary history. The earliest example dates back to April 6, 1892, when New Jersey’s Trenton Times referred to “Fashionable Cantonese dishes.” This phrase shows that the term was already being used in relation to food more than a century ago, long before the era of modern globalization.

Western interest in Cantonese cuisine also stretches back to the late 19th century. The OED cites an 1894 report from The Washington Post describing a dim sum dumpling as “shaped exactly like a fishing creel.” By 1908, The New York Herald was explaining the dish to its readers by comparing it to a “second cousin to steamed sponge cake.” These early descriptions reveal how unfamiliar foods were introduced to Western audiences through comparisons with things they already understood.

Over the following decades, Cantonese cuisine continued to leave its mark. A 1950 publication by the Hong Kong Young Women’s Christian Association highlighted “Cantonese specialties” such as turnip pudding, while a 1997 culinary memoir recalled dining at a large “Cantonese restaurant” where dim sum was served from rolling trolleys. More recently, a 2015 article in The Guardian recommended Wong Chi Kee in Hong Kong for its “traditional Cantonese congee.”

These citations connect to a broader ecosystem of existing terms. The Cantonese practice of yum cha, literally “drinking tea,” the social meal of dim sum and tea traditionally enjoyed in the morning, was added to the dictionary in 2016, while dim sum has appeared in the dictionary since 1989.

Today, my research shows that the dictionary contains a vocabulary of 25 Cantonese culinary terms. Beyond the widely recognized dim sum and yum cha, the list includes char siu, wonton, chop suey, hoisin sauce, egg foo yung, and moo goo gai pan. These are no longer treated as foreign concepts requiring lengthy explanations; they have become established English words.

Yet this lexicographical milestone is not simply a retrospective look at history; it also reflects a living culture. Just months earlier, in March 2026, three new additions expanded the OED’s Cantonese culinary vocabulary: dan tat (egg tart), pineapple bun, and yin yeung (a Hong Kong drink combining milk tea and coffee). Their inclusion highlights that Cantonese cuisine is not a static relic of the past. It continues to evolve, innovate, and influence the English language. This ongoing linguistic exchange shows that the relationship between East and West remains an active and continuing process.

The contrast with other regional Chinese cuisines highlights that global influence is not simply a product of modern international presence. Shanghai, for instance, is one of China’s most globally connected cities, yet its local Benbang cuisine has left far fewer traces in the English language. Cantonese cuisine’s deep roots in English developed instead through generations of migration, trade, and everyday use.

Etymologically, “Cantonese” derives from “Canton,” the former English name for Guangzhou, which was first recorded by Portuguese traders in the 16th century. Over time, the term evolved from a geographic reference into a marker of a distinct cultural and culinary identity. This reflects a broader historical reality: Cantonese cuisine established an overseas presence earlier than many other regional Chinese cuisines, spreading through centuries of maritime trade and migration.

Historically, because the vast majority of early Chinese immigrants to many Western countries came from Guangdong, Cantonese restaurants dominated many Chinatowns. Iconic establishments such as New York’s Port Arthur Restaurant, which opened in 1897 and introduced upscale Cantonese dishes to Western diners, and San Francisco’s Shanghai Low, a Cantonese restaurant that adopted a Shanghai-inspired name to appeal to Western customers, did more than serve food. They became gathering places for immigrant communities and helped establish Cantonese cuisine’s prominence in Western societies.

As a linguist, I often argue that translation is not merely a tool for communication between languages; it is also a means of cultural understanding. The inclusion of these terms shows that English speakers are capable of adopting culinary vocabulary from other languages on its own terms.

For readers interested in exploring this vocabulary, here are eight popular Cantonese culinary terms currently included in the OED, with condensed definitions for clarity.

Many of the early Cantonese restaurants that introduced these dishes to Western audiences have since disappeared. Yet the vocabulary they helped popularize has endured, and a new generation of Cantonese restaurants continues to thrive in Chinatowns and communities around the world. The OED’s recognition of Cantonese cuisine reflects this longer history of cultural exchange: carried across borders by generations of immigrants, Cantonese food has become a lasting part of the global culinary vocabulary.

(Header and in-text images: Visuals from VCG, edited by Ding Yining/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018828/China’s Largest Bookstore Launches Nationwide Same-Day Delivery
World.title: China’s Largest Bookstore Launches Nationwide Same-Day Delivery
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018828/China’s Largest Bookstore Launches Nationwide Same-Day Delivery
World.content:
Chinese state-owned bookstore chain Xinhua Bookstore is partnering with food delivery giant Meituan to roll out a nationwide same-day book delivery service, promising to deliver books in under an hour.

The agreement, signed on Friday at the 34th National Book Expo in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province, will connect the more than 10,000 Xinhua stores across China to Meituan’s instant retail network, Instashopping. Customers ordering through the network will be able to receive books in as quickly as 30 minutes.

The initiative marks the expansion of multiple pilot initiatives in the last two years comprising several regional Xinhua branches, including in Zhejiang, Shanghai, and the southern city of Shenzhen.

Founded in 1937, Xinhua is China’s largest and oldest bookstore chain.

Instant retail combines online ordering with inventories from nearby physical stores and a network of couriers to deliver products rapidly, typically in under one hour. China’s instant retail market is expected to surpass 1 trillion yuan ($150 billion) in 2026 and double to 2 trillion yuan by 2030, according to a report by the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation.

The push into instant retail comes amid intensifying competition between China’s e-commerce platforms and weakening demand for printed books. The country’s book retail market totaled roughly 110 billion yuan in 2025, down 2% from 2024, according to a report by Chinese analytics firm OpenBook.

Jiang Chuanyang, chairman of Xinhua’s Zhejiang branch, said at the event that China’s book market is evolving to comprise e-commerce, local instant retail, and physical bookstores. More than 100 stores in the province were active on Instashopping throughout 2025, generating combined sales of several million yuan, according to domestic media.

But the picture is more mixed for independent bookstores.

Su Shanna, brand manager of Yinxu, a chain of five bookstores in the eastern coastal city of Xiamen, told Sixth Tone that instant delivery orders account for roughly 15% of the company’s monthly revenue. The store joined Instashopping in May 2025, and also accepts on-demand orders through its WeChat mini program, fulfilling local deliveries through courier services such as SF Express and JD Logistics.

“It’s more of a bonus than a lifeline,” Su said, noting that demand for instant book delivery remains limited to a handful of scenarios. These include parents ordering extracurricular reading materials or textbooks for their children, tourists ordering books to their hotels, and patients looking for something to read during hospitalization.

Instant retail fills the gap where consumers need a book immediately and traditional e-commerce can’t meet the demand, according to Jiang Han, a senior researcher at Beijing-based think tank Pangoal.

But books are a low-profit business. Because instant retail platforms take a cut of bookstore sales, instant delivery is unlikely to become a major profit driver, he said.

The service’s real value isn’t in generating significant new revenue, but in generating new revenue sources, Jiang added. “Its significance should be on how it helps bookstores reconstruct their connection to readers.”

Jiang said that bookstores are increasingly trying to become “cultural service hubs” by diversifying their revenue sources, selling tourism-related products, and integrating with the local community. Instant retail is part of this trend.

In the case of Yinxu, members pay an annual fee of 188 yuan, which gives them discounts on books, book delivery services, and tickets to local performances, as well as access to various community activities.

“The key to success depends on whether bookstores can offer irreplaceable cultural experiences and emotional value,” Jiang said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.title: China’s Short-Drama Boom Calls for a New AI Crew
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018827/China’s Short-Drama Boom Calls for a New AI Crew
World.content:
One graduate trained to restore ancient artifacts now generates AI video clips for short dramas. Another, schooled in landscape design, builds virtual scenery instead of physical sets.

Both are part of a hiring surge across China’s film industry, as AI creates demand for hybrid creative roles and cuts production timelines from months to days. Recruitment for AI video editors jumped 179% year over year in June, state broadcaster CCTV reported.

At one cultural communications company in Zhengzhou, capital of China’s central Henan province, monthly production of AI-generated short dramas has risen from a handful to nearly 100, according to CCTV. The expansion has created demand for AI video editors and “card pullers,” who write prompts, generate footage, and select clips that fit a production’s characters and plot.

The shift is drawing workers from fields including design, animation, digital media, and information technology, according to recruitment platform Zhaopin. AI film roles typically pay between 8,000 and 20,000 yuan ($1,100 to $2,800) a month, depending on experience.

“This indicates that AI is not simply a substitution, but a technological enabler that is driving the transformation of traditional professions and roles,” Li Qiang, a vice president at Zhaopin, told CCTV.

AI is also changing how short dramas are made. Some productions that once required crews of dozens can now be completed by a few people, or even one creator handling scripts, storyboards, visuals, and effects. CCTV reported that AI has compressed some production cycles from months to days, with certain episodes completed in hours and effects and previsualization work becoming three to 10 times faster.

Director He Ziqiang, an early adopter of AI filmmaking tools, has added AI storyboard artists, image generators, card pullers, and editors to his team, many without formal film training.

“Anyone can make their own film, as long as they have ideas,” He told CCTV. “This will greatly enrich artistic creation and vitality, enabling more talented ordinary people to express themselves through AI.”

The hiring surge comes as China’s short-drama industry’s annual output value approached 90 billion yuan in 2025, nearly double the previous year, while some AI-generated productions have reported net profit margins above 50%.

Li Yuan, who is not related to Li Qiang, founder of a Henan-based AI film company, told domestic media his firm had cut the cost of producing a drama from 300,000 yuan to 50,000 yuan while increasing output.

“We thought large models would take longer to nail video fluency, but they got it done in the first quarter of this year,” Li told state media.

But he also cautioned that AI short dramas remain at an early stage, with both the technology and audience tastes still evolving. “Only when the market stabilizes can creators and platforms offer better products,” he said.

Editor: Apurva.

World.title: Chinese military researchers tap US AI models to train defense systems
World.content:
AI. A member of the People's Liberation Army stands as strategic strike group displays YJ-18C cruise missiles during a military parade to mark the 80th anniversary of the end of World War Two, in Beijing, China, September 3, 2025

BEIJING, China – Chinese military researchers have used outputs from leading US artificial intelligence models developed by OpenAI and Anthropic to train domestic AI systems to advance China’s defense capabilities, according to a Reuters review of more than 80 Chinese academic papers and patents.

The previously unreported findings offer a rare glimpse into how military and security-linked institutions in China are leveraging cutting-edge US AI models as a shortcut to developing specialized systems of their own, despite Washington’s efforts to restrict Beijing’s access to advanced chips and other strategic technologies.

The documents show widespread use of a technique known as “model distillation,” in which outputs from a powerful AI system are used to train smaller, specialized models that can be deployed locally without the enormous computing requirements needed to build frontier AI systems from scratch.

Reuters’ review, which included research compiled by the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation and shared exclusively with the news agency, showed distillation is widely used by researchers linked to the People’s Liberation Army and other military institutions.

The papers suggest Chinese defence institutions see leading US AI models as both a source of technical insight and a way to close the gap with American rivals.

The dispute centers on unauthorized extraction, not distillation itself, a widely used industry practice.

The issue has emerged as a major flashpoint ahead of US-China talks on AI governance and safety. US officials have accused some Chinese entities of using distillation to extract capabilities from American AI models, potentially undermining export controls and infringing intellectual property rights.

China has rejected the accusations, saying Washington is pursuing AI “hegemonism” while arguing that US firms have engaged in similar practices.

Chinese developers have also disputed claims that their AI advances rely on foreign models. AI startup Moonshot last week denied allegations by the Trump administration that its Kimi K3 model was built using distillation, saying it was driven by proprietary innovations.

Sunny Cheung, a Jamestown fellow who analyzed over 60 of the papers, said Chinese military scientists are systematically capturing the reasoning steps of Western models to adapt them for surveillance, cyber warfare and tactical decision-making.

“Teaching a model the right answer is one thing but teaching it the reasoning behind the answer is much harder,” said Cheung.

“These papers show Chinese military-linked researchers are trying to transfer that expensive, proprietary reasoning from Western models into smaller systems they can control and deploy locally.”

Reuters verified the academic literature and identified an additional two dozen military-linked case studies.

One paper published last year by researchers in PLA Unit 96941, a military intelligence and cyber-warfare unit in Beijing, described using OpenAI’s GPT-3.5 to process sensitive military source code.

The researchers said third-party models were unsuitable for handling classified information. To overcome that limitation, they used GPT-3.5 to summarize software code and trained a domestic model on those summaries to run entirely within Chinese military networks.

The White House, Pentagon, China’s foreign ministry, the PLA and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment.

Wide use, from monitoring to military

Chinese researchers have used distillation for purposes ranging from content monitoring to military deployment, Reuters’ and Jamestown’s review of the papers showed.

At the North University of China, which has close links to the country’s weapons industry, researchers used Anthropic’s Claude 3 Haiku to generate synthetic training data for a text classification model for social media monitoring and content moderation.

Anthropic said it does not provide commercial access to Claude in China or to Beijing-controlled firms and uses monitoring systems to detect policy violations.

The company added that distilled models may lose the original systems’ safety safeguards, potentially allowing sensitive capabilities to be transferred to models beyond its control.

A 2024 paper from the People’s Liberation Army’s National University of Defense Technology described using distillation to shrink an image-processing model for deployment on unmanned aerial vehicles, allowing drones to analyze live video and support navigation and targeting decisions in real time even when communications are cut.

Similarly, researchers at China’s Academy of Military Sciences used distillation to run a target-recognition model on tactical hardware during simulated maritime operations involving drones, ships and unmanned submarines, a study published earlier this year showed.

Benefits and limits

China has embraced distillation as it seeks to compete with the US in frontier AI while facing constraints on advanced computing resources due to Washington’s export controls on high-end chips. Central and local governments have promoted “model lightweighting” and edge computing, directing subsidies and research funding toward technologies that enable AI models to run on drones, satellites and other devices with limited processing power.

Experts caution, however, that distillation has significant limitations.

As Chinese AI models close the gap with their US counterparts, military researchers are also examining distillation as a potential security risk.

In January, researchers at the Army Engineering University published a paper on the threat of “data-free distillation,” a method of reverse-engineering a model’s capabilities without direct access to its core parameters.

To counter that vulnerability, they proposed defense mechanisms designed to mask the hidden logical information exposed in a model’s public outputs.

Distilled models also inherit only selected capabilities and cannot fully replicate the broad intelligence of frontier systems.

Trevor Koverko, co-founder of AI data company Sapien, said distilled models remain less capable than their teacher models.

“It is best understood as transferring selected capabilities into a cheaper, locally controlled system, not achieving independence from frontier AI.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Philippines deposits Bajo de Masinloc chart with UN
World.content:
BLOCKED. A satellite image of fishing vessels at the entrance, which is blocked by a floating barrier, to the disputed Scarborough Shoal, in the South China Sea, April 11, 2026.

China has controlled access to the shoal since 2012, following a tense standoff between Manila and Beijing

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines on Wednesday, July 29 (in New York) submitted to the United Nations its official nautical chart of Bajo de Masinloc (Scarborough Shoal), a feature in the West Philippine Sea that’s been controlled by China since 2012.

Depositing the Philippines’ official nautical chart of the high-tide elevation, said the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), “ensures that its official maritime information forms part of the public international record.”

The submission of the National Mapping and Resource Information Authority (NAMRIA)-prepared official nautical chart and the shoal’s maritime zones were made before the United Nations Secretariat. The chart, said the DFA, shows the normal baselines of the shoal, as well as the outer limits of its territorial sea and contiguous zone, based on United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and domestic law.

“By depositing the chart, the Philippines formally notifies the international community of its normal baselines and the geographic extent of its applicable authority and jurisdiction at Bajo de Masinloc. The deposit also strengthens transparency and legal certainty by making the Philippines’ official hydrographic information publicly available through the United Nations in accordance with UNCLOS,” said the DFA.

Bajo de Masinloc, also known as Scarborough or Panatag Shoal, is a high-tide elevation that the Philippines claims as part of its territory. In both international and domestic law, the feature has a 12 nautical mile territorial sea from its baselines and a contiguous zone that extends between 12 to 24 nautical miles.

China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in a statement on July 31, said it rejects the Philippines’ latest actions before the UN.

Access to the shoal has been controlled by Beijing since 2012, following a tense standoff between the Philippines and China. It’s that standoff which prompted the then-Aquino administration to bring China to court to clarify its entitlements based on UNCLOS in 2013.

Three years later, just at the start of the Rodrigo Duterte administration, the Philippines won their case in the landmark 2016 Arbitral Award, which, among other things, deemed China’s sweeping claim over the South China Sea invalid. Beijing has refused to accept the award, which should be final and binding.

The tribunal did not decide on the sovereignty of Bajo de Masinloc, since territorial claims were not part of its jurisdiction. But the tribunal did find that the shoal was traditional fishing ground for Filipino, Chinese, and Vietnamese fisherfolk — which means they should have access to the shoal, no matter who has sovereignty or control over it. This has not been the case since 2012.

Several Chinese vessels, including those of the China Coast Guard (CCG), are fixtures at the sole opening of the shoal and the areas surrounding it. The CCG and its auxiliary Chinese Maritime Militia have routinely harassed Philippine ships that come close to the shoal with dangerous manuevers and the use of water cannons.

The DFA, in a statement, said depositing the chart also “carries particular significance in the face of climate change and sea-level rise.” “As coastlines and marine environments evolve, the preservation of official nautical charts and baseline information with the United Nations contributes to a permanent and internationally recognized legal record of maritime entitlements established in accordance with international law,” it said. – Rappler.com

World.title: OpenAI finds evidence other AI agents escaped containment as it widens hacking probe
World.content:
WASHINGTON, US – OpenAI has discovered other instances in which autonomous agents have escaped containment as the company expands its investigation of the hacking incident at tech firm Hugging Face that drew global attention this month, two people familiar with the matter said on Friday, July 31.

The new breakouts were uncovered during the company’s publicly announced investigation into how one of its agents escaped what was meant to be a contained testing environment this month, the two people said, and OpenAI is now looking into those instances as well. One of the sources said that the escapes were limited in nature and that none of the agents were thought to have left OpenAI’s network.

An OpenAI spokesperson referred to a statement issued by the company on Tuesday that said it was reviewing “broader activity from our models” in addition to the Hugging Face intrusion.

The discovery of additional rogue behavior at OpenAI, even if limited in nature, could feed growing appetite for regulation coming out of the White House and elsewhere.

The expanded investigation by OpenAI was launched shortly before its primary rival, Anthropic, disclosed that its models were also responsible for a series of break-ins that led to breaches at three other companies dating back to April, according to the two sources and a third source familiar with the matter. The recent discovery of other past breakouts at OpenAI has not previously been reported.

Growing concerns

AI safety experts said the new disclosures paint a portrait of a group of cutting-edge labs whose ability to develop dangerous autonomous hacking agents outstrips their ability to keep them under control.

“We have a whole industry where the people designing, developing and putting out these tools aren’t keeping up themselves to responsibly develop these things and keep them safe,” said Maurice Chiodo, a mathematician who works at Cambridge University’s Centre for the Study of Existential Risk.

Reuters could not establish exactly how many incidents OpenAI investigators found or the timings or circumstances under which they occurred. The three sources said OpenAI and outside experts were examining log data from earlier in the year in a bid to understand what took place.

OpenAI first launched the investigation following the early July intrusion at Hugging Face, where an OpenAI agent went haywire for days inside another company’s network in a botched effort to cheat on an internal test. As part of that hacking spree, OpenAI said that four accounts at four other companies were also compromised. One of those companies was New York-based Modal, corporate officials there said.

Chiodo said his concerns were heightened by indications that neither OpenAI nor Anthropic were watching the agents as they went rogue. Reuters has previously reported that OpenAI realized its agent had broken into Hugging Face only after the company contained the hack, contacted the FBI and went public about the intrusion. OpenAI has said the Reuters account contained inaccuracies but has not responded when asked what they were.

In its Thursday statement disclosing how its own agents hacked victims online, Anthropic suggested that it had not been watching them in real time, saying that “real-time monitoring of the evaluation logs would have helped to surface the problem sooner.”

Chiodo said that pointed to a lack of proper scrutiny.

“It seems like they weren’t even looking,” Chiodo said.

Anthropic said that while it did have real-time monitoring in place, that monitoring had not been used “for this threat surface” due to a misunderstanding between the AI company and a partner.

New government insight

The rapidly widening scope of the runaway AI agents story already has heightened pressure from lawmakers and officials across the United States and Europe to push for new government oversight of the labs whose models power them.

“We’re looking at controls,” US President Donald Trump told reporters on Thursday. On Friday, the European Commission said it held talks with OpenAI and Anthropic over the ​hacking incidents.

Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the US Senate Intelligence Committee, said on Friday that the Anthropic incident “tells me that legislatively we’re correct to require mandatory capabilities testing of these advanced models.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Can SM Prime’s Seaside Arena aid Cebu’s recovery from 2025 tourism slump?
World.content:
ARENA. The P7-billion SM Seaside Cebu Arena spans more than seven hectares and is designed by award-winning global architecture firm Arquitectonica.

Following the wishes of his late father Henry Sy Sr., SM Prime chairman Hans Sy says the launch of the largest arena facility in the Visayas is only an initial piece of a 20-year plan

CEBU, Philippines – After experiencing a dip in tourist visits in late 2025 — primarily due to disasters, Cebu’s business experts and leaders are hoping for an economic comeback, especially after the successful hosting of BINI’s Signals Concert in mid-July at the SM Seaside Cebu Arena.

On July 9, SM Prime formally announced the opening of the SM Seaside Cebu Arena in the South Road Properties, Cebu City, with the goal of ushering the beginning of a 20-year-old development plan in Cebu’s coastal business hub.

Cebu Chamber of Commerce and Industry (CCCI) President Regan Rex King told Rappler on July 24, that the SM Seaside Cebu Arena would help drive Cebu’s economic growth and even align with the goals of the Philippine Sports Commission (PSC) on promoting sports tourism.

“A world-class arena is more than a venue—it is a gateway to positioning Cebu as Asia’s next premier Sports, Meetings, Incentives, Conferences, and Exhibitions (SMICE) destination,” King said.

In a Facebook post, Cebu Governor Pamela Baricuatro shared similar sentiments with the CCCI head, stating that the arena reflects growing confidence in Cebu as a premier destination for tourism, business, culture, and world-class events.

“The new facility is expected to attract more local and international visitors, generate more business activity, create jobs, and open new opportunities for Cebuano workers, entrepreneurs, artists, athletes, and communities,” the governor said.

Visayas venue giant

Spanning more than seven hectares, the seaside arena is considered the largest facility of its kind in the Visayas.

The entire arena, worth P7 billion, was designed by award-winning global architecture firm Arquitectonica. Its full accommodation capacity is estimated at 25,000 guests.

Last July 11, P-pop girl group BINI had their Cebu leg of the BINI Signals 2026 anniversary concert series, selling out more than 20,000 tickets for the event.

Play Video

For comparison, the SM Mall of Asia (MOA) Arena has a seating capacity of 15,000 guests, though it can be expanded to 20,000. On June 20 and 21, BINI sold out tickets for a two-night run at the SM MOA Arena, totaling roughly 30,000 guests over that weekend.

INSIDE LOOK. The SM Seaside Cebu Arena features Cebu’s largest center-hung display, offering advanced visuals, immersive sound, and real-time data integration for diverse events. Photo from SM Prime

In 2025, the SM MOA Arena hosted more than 200 events and welcomed over 1.1 million attendees. The arena served as the Philippine stage for performances by artists like Lady Gaga, Taylor Swift, Maroon 5, and BTS, and even sporting events like the 2025 FIVB Men’s Volleyball World Championship.

The SM MOA Arena’s 2025 performance was a 10% increase from its 2024 performance with one million in total ticket attendance recorded.

The BINI concert was only the first of a long list of events set to be held at the SM Seaside Cebu Arena, and is expected to draw more domestic trips to Cebu.

Data from the Mactan Cebu International Airport Authority showed that total passenger traffic for the first half of 2025 only reached an estimated 5.9 million while the first half of 2026 surpassed 6.46 million, signaling a slight rebound in tourist visits from the previous year.

Promising future

Julia Abby Catibud, a frequent concert-goer, told Rappler on Friday, July 31, that the new Cebu arena was a “promising location.”

“As someone who frequently attends concerts at SM MOA Arena, I was totally amazed. The Cebu arena has a bigger queue area, and a way more industrialized look than SM MOA, relatively because the Cebu arena was newly built,” Catibud said.

Catibud shared her experience watching the concert of Filipino rock band IV of Spades at the arena, and noted the convenience of enjoying a concert in the province, instead of flying all the way to Manila. Catibud noted that her friends in Manila flew in for the July 11 BINI concert.

SEASIDE. Not only is it the largest arena in the Visayas, the SM Seaside Cebu Arena also has 30 luxury Premier Suites and direct access to SM Seaside City Cebu and the upcoming SMX Convention Center Seaside Cebu. Photo from SM Prime

SM Prime Chairman Hans Sy told reporters in July that the SM Seaside Cebu Arena is only the initial part of a development project conceptualized no more than 20 years ago.

“My father has always believed in Cebu. Since before, when we had a small one in downtown, and then, when he had the opportunity to buy the super block in the North Reclamation [Area], he has always believed in Cebu,” Sy said.

According to Sy, he simply followed his father’s directive to develop the land. Among the list of projects in the 20-year-old pipeline include the upcoming SMX Convention Center Seaside Cebu

As of this writing, SM Prime has signed more than 20 major shows with local and international acts, live productions, and sports events to be held at the SM Seaside Cebu Arena in 2026.

In Sy’s vision, the odds are now greater on not just bring in more tourists but also world-class performances and celebrities in the country.

“I do believe with now two [arena] venues, there’s a certain advantage that we can convince a lot of [international artists] to come [to the country],” Sy added. – Rappler.com

MANILA, Philippines — On July 27, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. delivers his longest and most populist State of the Nation Address to date. He started by announcing forthcoming charges against cousin, former House speaker Martin Romualdez, and ends in a nationalist message to both friends and “detractors.”

On July 29, the 10th day of Vice President Sara Duterte’s trial, two bank officials took the witness stand and said they found her office’s encashment of large funds “unusual.” Violeta Constantino and Nenita Camposano, former branch managers of Land Bank of the Philippines, were the prosecution’s first witnesses as it began presenting its case on Duterte’s alleged misuse of confidential funds.

On July 30, the Senate impeachment court received Vice President Sara Duterte and husband Mans Carpio’s tax-related documents from the Bureau of Internal Revenue and financial records from several banks following President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s approval. The financial records are among the pieces of evidence that House prosecutors intend to use to prove Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth.
