"Lauren didn't just wake up one day and think, 'I'm going to go and have drastic alternative medical treatment.' She'd been making her way on this path for a long time.

"I actually found that for everything she did, there was a truth at the beginning of it, and there was a reason that she did it.

"While a lot of it was based on misinformation, her logical steps were ones that I think so many people would take, especially if you're experiencing chronic pain or mysterious illnesses."

Lauren 'let down' by healthcare system

Hannah says Lauren's mother was the only person in their family who knew the full extent of alternative treatments she had been trying.

Hannah says her aunt would take Lauren to doctors, seeking help to explain the risks of the treatments she was undergoing, but was often left disappointed.

Hannah says we should be careful not to isolate family members who are looking into alternative therapies. (triple j hack: Arianna Lucente)

"She desperately wanted someone from the medical field to intervene and engage, but so often, and understandably, they feared getting entangled in alternative medicine.

"In particular, one doctor sort of rolled their eyes at my aunty over Lauren's head while she was talking about some of the treatments that she was looking at.

" While I understand why, it's the removal of a point that could have kept that person connected to evidence-based treatment. "

Hannah says the healthcare system is letting down Lauren and other people living with mysterious chronic conditions.

"This is a systemic issue, certainly not one with individual practitioners," Hannah says

"From a systemic point of view, I think there is a lack of information, a lack of understanding about these conditions."

The peak medical body for GPs in Australia has long recommended practitioners validate patient concerns when they present with medically unexplained symptoms.

In sharing Lauren's story in her book, Wormhole, Hannah hopes to change how we talk about people who fall into "wormholes" while looking for answers.

"I think we can focus our efforts as family members on the invalidation that people with these illnesses often feel," Hannah says.

"If we can just make sure that we believe their symptoms, we validate their symptoms, and that they know that we are committed to supporting them as they find something that will help them, I think that goes a long way."

World.title: Canberra food and garden waste collection scheme delayed a third time
World.content:
The rollout of a program to recycle food and garden waste into compost across the ACT has been delayed again.

Food Organics and Garden Organics (FOGO) collection was originally scheduled to come into effect in 2023, but in 2024 the need to replace Canberra’s recycling centre after a fire saw the scheme's expansion deferred until 2026.

In 2025, the scheme's Canberra-wide expansion was further delayed until 2028.

But in a budget estimates hearing last week, ACT City and Government Services Minister Tara Cheyne confirmed the territory government was now aiming to introduce FOGO collection throughout the territory by 2030.

Tara Cheyne told senate estimates the FOGO scheme will be delivered through a two-stage procurement process. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

"This is a complex city-shaping project," Ms Cheyne said.

" There is also only so much capacity in the market when it comes to capital projects, and capital projects of this size. "

ACT Greens Leader Jo Clay said she was horrified to hear of the hold-up.

"This is not climate action; this shows that climate is just not a priority for this government," she said.

"It's also a real shame for Canberrans. A lot of people really want to be able to recycle their food waste."

Ms Clay said she had not seen "any good reasons" for the delay.

Jo Clay says her constituents regularly ask when the FOGO collection scheme will be expanded to their homes. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

"This is not difficult technology. This is very well established," Ms Clay said.

"And actually, the ACT now is a decade, and two decades, behind a lot of other regions."

She said her constituents regularly ask when the FOGO scheme will be available to them.

"I actually don't mind how we deliver FOGO services, but we cannot simply put it off for seven years, 10 years, 20 years if we are going to say that we take climate change seriously," Ms Clay said.

Scheme delayed by need for new facility

Before the FOGO collection scheme can be rolled out across the territory, a dedicated facility needs to be built to process at least 50,000 tonnes of waste.

The FOGO pilot program provides households with a kitchen caddy and liners to store their scraps. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

Ms Cheyne told senate estimates that the scheme is being delivered through a two-stage procurement process.

The request for proposals is expected to be released in the coming weeks, shortlisting three contractors for the new facility.

But Ms Cheyne highlighted FOGO does exist for some Canberrans, with the ACT having been one of the first jurisdictions in the country to implement it.

A pilot program has been in place for more than 6,000 households in Belconnen, Cook, Macquarie and some Tuggeranong apartments since 2021.

Ms Cheyne said it had received positive feedback.

Tara Cheyne says the ACT's FOGO collection scheme pilot has received largely positive feedback. (ABC News: Jostina Basta)

"Attitudes have always been pretty positive about FOGO, but they have also improved over time," Ms Cheyne said.

"We have been able to shape our response for some households where the fortnightly red bin collection has been challenging for whatever reason.

" I largely believe those concerns, where they have been raised, have been addressed — and that will inform our overall rollout. "

As of September 2025, 38 per cent of Australians had access to a FOGO collection service.

The National Waste Policy Action Plan aims for the service to be available to all metropolitan houses and businesses by 2030.

A problem Canberrans 'can solve in their kitchens'

More than 5,000 homes in Belconnen, Cook and Macquarie have had access to the FOGO collection pilot since 2021. (ABC News: Jostina Basta)

From 2024-25, waste accounted for six per cent of Canberra's emissions.

Ms Clay questioned whether delaying the FOGO implantation would impact Canberra's ability to meet its target of net zero by 2045.

"This is a real problem, because food waste generates climate emissions for 20 years after going into landfill," she said.

" That food that we send to landfill in 2030 will still be wrecking our climate in 2050. "

She said the ACT Greens would continue to push the territory government on the scheme's rollout.

"Our waste emissions are going up; climate change is a problem," Ms Clay said.

"We have a climate crisis and people know that they want to solve this, and this is a problem that they can solve in their kitchens.

"People really want this solution."

World.title: Dozens of greyhounds to land in Australia as NZ racing ban begins
World.content:
Chartered flights will ferry up to 150 greyhounds to Australia as trainers pivot from a racing ban coming into effect in New Zealand.

The ban, which was first announced in December 2024 and legislated in April this year, took effect on Saturday after years of animal welfare concerns.

Ten greyhounds were euthanised during New Zealand's final racing season, including one days before the ban began.

Heather Simpson, the Greyhound Transition Agency (GTA) head, said she was aware that Greyhound Racing New Zealand had organised charter flights for about 150 dogs to go to Australia to continue racing.

"There is nothing in the legislation that stops trainers choosing to export their dogs to Australia; some of these dogs actually will be partly owned by Australians," she told Radio New Zealand.

Greyhound ban legislation delayed until government gets support A bill to ban greyhound racing in Tasmania has been delayed until the government can secure enough support.

Greyhound racing remains legal in most Australian jurisdictions, banned only in the Australian Capital Territory.

Plans for an industry phase-out in Tasmania have stalled after the government pulled a bill from the upper house in April when it appeared not to have enough support to pass.

Word of the chartered flights first emerged through a leaked message from a private greyhound racing group, Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi told a Senate Rural and Regional Affairs and Transport Legislation Committee hearing in April.

She said the move appeared "to be kind of a deliberate attempt to avoid" New Zealand's transition agency.

"If they survive, they will become the responsibility of Australians to rehome," she said.

"And you would know we're already in a rehoming crisis."

The greyhounds brought to Australia will be classed as "companion animals". (Reuters: Action Images/Scott Heavey)

Brant Smith, a senior biosecurity executive at the Department of Agriculture and Fisheries, told the senate hearing the government had been working with New Zealand's Ministry for Primary Industries on the dogs' import.

He said they would be classed as "companion animals", but may be used for racing once in the country.

"As to how they are then used, that's not something that we have control over thereafter because they're being imported as companion animals like other animals … and this is not unusual," he said.

Mr Smith said a similar contingent of greyhounds was imported to Australia in April 2025.

"In the previous consignment, I think approximately 80 came similarly, and they were just imported under our normal conditions," he said.

It is estimated a further 1,400 dogs will remain in New Zealand and require rehoming by the GTA.

Ms Simpson said the rehomed dogs would be regularly checked under a welfare program.

World.title: Live: Panthers and Raiders return to scene of 'Mudgee Miracle', Wahs beat Titans
World.content:
— reporting by AAP

The Warriors are savouring redemption after answering the Sydney Roosters' challenge to stay in the NRL's top-two finals race with a crushing 42-6 victory over the Gold Coast.

After wobbling with a poor loss to Canterbury last week, the Warriors rebounded with a vital eight-try rout of the Titans at Robina Super Stadium on Saturday.

They were never going to match the Roosters' record 82-12 mauling of North Queensland on Thursday night, but a 13th win of the season nevertheless kept the Warriors within two competition points of the second-placed Tricolours.

Critically, the New Zealand outfit enjoys a considerable 61-point superior points differential over the Roosters to be well placed to snatch second spot on the table if Trent Robinson's side slip up in the run to the finals.

A top-two finish guarantees a home qualifying final and then a home prelim with victory in the first week of the September play-offs.

"I just liked the way we bounced back from last week. We hold really high standards here at the club and we didn't meet the standards last week," said Warriors lock Erin Clark.

"We've got a little bit to work on defensively today but, overall, really proud about the performance and just a better 80 minutes too.

"We owe it to ourselves and our fans and just to bounce back from last week, so that's amazing."

The Titans had been chasing three straight wins for the first time since 2017 to keep their own very slim mathematical finals hopes flickering.

But the home team were all but done by the break after the Warriors piled on five tries through Dallin Watene-Zelezniak, Alofiana Khan-Pereira, Chanel Harris-Tavita, Leka Halasima and Jacob Laban to lead 26-6 at halftime.

The Warriors completed the drubbing with second-half tries to Eddie Ieremia-Toeava and a double to playmaker Te Maire Martin.

In a timely turnaround a month out from the finals, the Warriors racked up 40 points or more for the third time this season.

Next up is a real gauge of their title credentials against ladder-leading Penrith back home in Auckland on Friday night.

First, though, the Warriors will celebrate Saturday's statement win.

"That was awesome," fullback Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad said.

"We wanted to play a brand of footy that we would be proud of and, man, there was a lot of good patches there where that was us.

"That's been us for the majority of the year this year."

World.title: Hawthorn's last Launceston game of the year brings nostalgia and hope
World.content:
As Hawthorn's penultimate season in Launceston draws to a close, there's a mix of sadness, nostalgia and hope within the club and the northern Tasmanian community.

Sitting third on the AFL ladder going into the match against 13th-placed North Melbourne at York Park — and with just three rounds remaining of the home and away season after this weekend — the Hawks are well placed for finals action.

"There's a bit of sadness and nostalgia around," Hawthorn's head of operations in Tasmania, David Cox, said of today's game.

Hawthorn has been playing home games in Launceston for 25 years.

"That's a really significant part of Hawthorn's story, we've won four flags while we've been part of … that partnership," Mr Cox said.

One of Hawthorn's biggest names in recent years, Lance Franklin, played some exciting football at York Park. (Getty Images Quinn Rooney)

Hawthorn has been paid about a million dollars per game by the Tasmanian government to play four games a year in Launceston since 2001.

In 2022, Hawthorn games in Launceston generated $20.8 million in direct expenditure and $23.6 million in total economic impact to the Tasmanian economy, according to accountants PriceWaterhouseCoopers.

About 12,500 people went to each game that year, with 16 per cent of those jetting in from interstate or overseas.

Victorian Alan Pell is one of those people. In Launceston for today's game, he is combining cheering on the Hawks with a chance to play golf in Tasmania.

Terri Isaac, Alan Pell and Dee Wilson travelled from Victoria to cheer on the Hawks in Launceston. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

"It's just sensational," he said of the atmosphere in the city on game day.

"Because it's the second-last year that we're going to be over here, people are really experiencing their last efforts," Mr Pell said.

"Twenty-five years Hawthorn's been here, we've probably been here six or seven times, so we feel like it's part of us, too."

The Hawks have an impressive record at York Park, which has been nicknamed "the fortress". (AAP: James Ross)

Another hit for northern Tasmania

For a community grappling with the impending closure of Boag's brewery and the Liberty Bell Bay manganese smelter, there is concern about what the Hawks' departure will mean.

Devils must deliver after booting Hawks out of Tasmania Having just played a key role in evicting what has been a model tenant for 25 years, the Devils must now deliver on the economic and social boon they've promised.

Alex Britton is a restaurant co-owner and a Launceston City Councillor.

"Losing the Hawks, coupled with losing Boag's, coupled now with loosing Liberty Bell Bay up in George Town, is horrible for the town, really," Cr Britton said.

"There's lots of good things going on, you don't want to be too depressed about it all, but it's a major hit."

The AFL announced in May that Hawthorn would leave Tasmania to make the Tasmania Devils, who make their AFL debut in 2028, the focus of football in the state.

The brown and gold was on display in Launceston as some fans enjoyed the city before heading to the game. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

At the time, the Hawthorn Football Club said it was "extremely disappointed in the AFL's decision to force an end to our relationship with Launceston and Northern Tasmania post 2027".

It also said the club had put forward a "strong argument that it should continue to play games in Launceston into the future".

The Hawks will play their final home game at York Park next season. (City of Launceston)

Cr Britton said he was hopeful the Devils' games, some of which will be played at York Park initially, would bring in much-needed custom for hospitality businesses.

"I think it will work, but I think at the moment in Launceston, it does just feel like we've had hit after hit," he said.

York Park has been Hawthorn's home away from home since 2001. (Wikimedia Commons: Kspilling)

Hawks fans are also filled with hope at the prospect of their team going all the way this year, and for the club to start its final Tasmanian year as premiers.

"There's definitely a bit of sadness around us leaving, but they really want to see out next year with joy and celebration," Mr Cox said.

And the Hawks are hoping to return to Tasmanian turf when the Devils enter the competition in 2028.

"I would expect that there will be a Devils' home game that will play against Hawthorn here that will clearly be blockbuster sellout, and what an amazing way to kick off the Devils' journey in Tasmania," Mr Cox said.

Mr Pell said he hoped to be among the crowd for a Devils versus Hawks game.

"Loud and clearly for the Hawks, but I'll be very interested to see how the Devils go," he said.

World.title: Dry July for Western Australia as stunning pictures tell story
World.content:
Despite a wet start to winter, July has been one of the driest on record for large parts of Western Australia.

A lack of consecutive cold fronts and strong storm systems left rainfall totals across Perth and the southern half well below what would normally be expected for one of the state's wettest months.

The city gauge only managed to record 56.8 millimetres of rain this month, less than half of its long-term July average of 147 mm.

Across the broader South West region, average rainfall was about 39.7 mm for the month — the lowest since records began.

A crisp morning in Ferguson Valley near Bunbury. (Supplied: Kerry Fleming )

So if you hear someone mention a dry July in WA, chances are they're not talking about the alcohol-free fundraiser.

Let's take a look back at some of the amazing photographs sent in by ABC readers from across the state.

The sun rises in Denmark on WA's southern coast. (Supplied: Ros Thies)

Double rainbows

July began with the same conditions that dominated the rest of the month, with mostly clear and settled skies under a stubborn ridge of high pressure.

The South West region got its first decent drenching nearly a week in as the first cold front of the month arrived.

While Busselton airport and Walpole North recorded their highest daily rainfall for the month, areas further inland missed out completely.

We saw double rainbows in between showers, something that happens when sunlight is reflected through water droplets twice.

A double rainbow over Gelfro Organic Farm in Williams. (Supplied: Anne Battley)

Stubborn highs block rain

The state receives almost all of its winter rainfall from cold fronts originating in the Southern Ocean, but there's been an absence of those rain-bearing systems this month due to a stubborn pattern in the atmosphere.

A golden sunset in Dongora in the Midwest. (Supplied: David Jackson)

Rather than allowing a procession of cold fronts to sweep across the state's south-west, strong high-pressure systems have repeatedly settled over southern Australia, steering much of the winter rainfall further south.

Just as a storm would arrive to deliver much-needed rain, another high would be chasing its tail, ready to slip the state back into fairly calm and settled conditions.

If you have a great weather photo you'd like to see featured in ABC Perth's 7PM News or online, send them through to Tabarak at waweather@abc.net.au.

Cool, foggy mornings

The clear skies saw temperatures plummet overnight for much of the southern half, while inland areas across the Wheatbelt, Great Southern and Goldfields experienced frosty and misty mornings throughout the month.

A horse braves the chilly temperatures in Darling Downs in Perth's south-east. (Supplied: David J )

Wandering in the Great Southern dropped below zero six times over the past month, while Salmon Gums was just shy of recording its coldest July minimum on record after dipping to a fresh -4.4 degrees.

The cloudless skies also made for some great astrophotography conditions for keen stargazers like Judy.

Astrophotography from Geraldton. (Supplied: Judy Leitch)

Residents in Perth woke up to eerie conditions on the 10th day of the month as thick fog blanketed the city.

Morning fog over the Canning River in Wilson. (Supplied: Mark Ham)

Fog occurs when there are clear skies and light winds overnight, allowing the temperature to cool down and reach saturation point.

A heavy fog settled over Perth CBD. (Supplied: Adrian Firth)

(Almost) beach weather in July

The dry spell continued over Perth and much of the southern regions into mid-July, under a broad ridge of high pressure.

It led to an unseasonably warm day on July 15, when temperatures soared about 5 to 10 degrees above average for areas around the west coast.

Jurien Bay reached a top of 26.9C, its highest July maximum on record, while Cape Leeuwin also posted a record of 23C.

The sun rises over Perth's CBD. (Supplied: Greg Brown)

Perth experienced its hottest July day in 32 years, with the city reaching a high of 25.7C, about 7 degrees warmer than average.

Beach weather in July at North Cottesloe. (Supplied: Clive Addison)

Despite the distance, a huge high-pressure system near Tasmania influenced the weather in WA, preventing cold fronts from dropping much rain near the south coast.

Rain returns

The calmer weather was brought to an abrupt end on July 17, as the month reminded us what winter was supposed to feel like, delivering a series of cold fronts.

Clouds roll in over Mandurah estuary right before a cold front. (Supplied: Lyn Taylor)

The storms swept through the South West land division, bringing heavy rain, thunderstorms and strong winds to the region.

The Harris Road gauge near Bunbury picked up 65 mm in 24 hours, Dardanup East and Ferguson Valley got over 50 mm and Mandurah notched up 44mm.

The Perth metro gauge didn't miss out, recording just under 15mm, while nearby Kings Park managed a decent 27 mm.

The following front packed an even bigger punch, prompting warnings for heavy rainfall and potential flood watches near the central west.

Peter managed to snap a photo of a drenched road in Coorow after his gauge recorded 58 mm of rain overnight.

A road in Coorow in the Midwest was left impassable after 58mm of rain overnight. (Supplied: Peter Randell)

Rainfall well below average

Despite the boost to rainfall totals, it was far from enough to make up for the dry month.

With one week left of July, much of the South West had only received a fraction of the month's usual rainfall, with some areas on track to record one of their driest Julys since records began.

On the south coast, Albany only managed to pick up just under 51 mm of rainfall compared to its monthly July average of 146.6 mm.

Manjimup fell 120mm short of its July average, while the Perth metro gauge fell 90mm short.

A rainbow at Lake Claremont in Perth's western suburbs. (Supplied: Trish McGarry)

Across much of the agricultural region, paddocks have remained dry through what is normally the peak growing season.

The Wheatbelt town of Northam has recorded just 12.2 mm, about 15 per cent of what it would usually get, making it the driest July it's had in nearly 150 years of records.

A cold and foggy morning in Northam. (Supplied: Vicki Vincent)

North feels the chill

Strong high-pressure systems dominated the state's weather across the month, but they didn't just impact the southern half.

The effects were felt as far as the Pilbara and Kimberley regions, where warnings were issued for strong south-easterly winds.

Elephant rock overlooking Ord River in Kununurra in the far north. (Supplied: Sam Cinanni)

Because those winds were coming from the centre of the country, they were predominantly dry and cool, leading to chilly minimum temperatures.

Some parts of the Kimberley were colder than Melbourne, Hobart and Canberra.

A number of locations, including Broome and Fitzroy Crossing, observed their coldest morning of the year so far on July 29.

Any hopes of a last-minute drenching to lift July's rainfall totals faded as the month drew to a close on a warm, dry note.

And with the Bureau of Meteorology forecasting a drier than usual August, the final month of winter could follow the same script.

World.title: AFL Live: Australia make a statement against Ireland in history-making clash; injury carnage overshadows Swans’ win over Saints
World.content:
Sydney have overrun the brave Saints to win by 19 points at Marvel Stadium during an afternoon of injury mayhem that saw a 42-minute final quarter.

Play was suspended during the last term after Sydney defender Will Edwards suffered a badly broken ankle in a marking contest. He required a green whistle for pain relief and was taken from the ground on a motorised cart.

William Edwards is taken from the ground with a broken leg. via Getty Images

Not long after, Jack Silvagni had to be helped from the field in pain with a dislocated shoulder.

Sydney also lost James Rowbottom with a broken hand in the first term, while St Kilda superstar Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera spent time off the ground with a hip ailment and teammate Tom De Koning needed treatment for a hamstring concern.

Jack Silvagni leaves the ground with a dislocated shoulder. via Getty Images

The Swans kicked the first two goals of the game, but then trailed by nine points at quarter time, 13 points at half-time and 12 points at the final break as St Kilda dominated possession and Wanganeen-Milera booted three goals.

But with the St Kilda midfielder clearly hampered in the final term, finishing the game out as a forward, Sydney’s midfielders went on a rampage and the Swans kicked seven last-quarter goals to St Kilda’s two. They won 16.11 (107) to St Kilda’s 13.10 (88).

“These guys are really physical,” Swans star Isaac Heeney told Fox Footy after the game. “I found out the hard way in the guts there, and a few of the boys came off not that great, unfortunately.

“So hopefully, Rowy’s OK. I think he has broken the middle bone, so hopefully it is a pretty quick turn around. And then, Will, poor fella, that was one of the grosser ones I have seen, so hopefully he can bounce back pretty quick. But he’s been outstanding for us.”

Play was stopped for 10 minutes while medical staff attended 23-year-old Edwards for what appeared to be a compound fracture.

He did not make his AFL debut until this year after a serious leg infection and then a broken leg threatened his career.

World.title: Teen on bail charged with dealing drugs, weapons
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Teen on bail charged with dealing drugs, weapons Carla Jaeger August 1, 2026 — 5:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A teenager allegedly linked to Melbourne gangland boss Kaz Hamad’s crew known as The Commission is accused of dealing meth and firearms while already on bail for other offences. Rivin Muthucumarana, 19, from Fraser Rise, was charged on Saturday with a series of drug and firearm trafficking offences the day after his arrest after a series of police raids. Operation Eclipse detectives executed the raids as part of an ongoing investigation into one of the suspected orchestrators of Melbourne’s so-called bar wars. “The investigation commenced in April of this year when police received intelligence in relation to drug and firearms trafficking linked to an offshore syndicate leader,” police said. Officers seized quantities of suspected cocaine, methamphetamine and ecstasy during the co-ordinated searches of a Keilor Downs business and homes in Port Melbourne and Fraser Rise.





His lawyer, Seda Kilic, said it was her client’s first time in custody. She noted that Muthucumarana has a knee injury and has recently injured his neck. A bail application might be made at a later date, Kilic said. The Commission is the dominant force controlling Australia’s multibillion-dollar illicit tobacco market and large-scale drug importations. Hamad’s gang, also known as the 313, has been linked to dozens of other violent attacks, including shootings and murders. Operation Eclipse, originally formed in April to investigate the violent rampage targeting Melbourne’s nightlife, is now dedicated to dismantling The Commission’s extensive crime network.



Related Article Exclusive

Crime Nightclub promoter believed to be intended target of botched kidnapping The tobacco kingpin – described by two police sources as “one of the world’s most dangerous men” – was sentenced to life in prison by Iraqi authorities this week. In his place, 23-year-old Ali al-Huseini took control of the command structure of the 313s. According to five police and underworld sources, Huseini is one of two gunmen who ambushed Suleiman “Sam” Abdulrahim outside Fawkner cemetery and shot him eight times in 2022. The then-18 year old fled to Iraq less than a day after the shooting, which Abdulrahim survived. Since Hamad’s arrest, Huseini is alleged by police to have been the prime mover in the resumption of violence in the tobacco market and more than 40 attacks waged against bar and nightclub owners and promoters since March. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: NRL live updates: Penrith Panthers face Canberra Raiders in Mudgee
World.content:
Thank you for joining us this evening.

It’s not all that often that the 5:30 Saturday clash is the match of the round, but that will indeed be the case when top-of-the-table Penrith and 10th-placed Canberra meet again at Mudgee’s Glen Willow Oval today. Riding a four-game winning streak, the Raiders need the win to stay in the finals race; while the Panthers will remain two points in front at the top of the table if they prevail.

You may recall that in the corresponding game last year – dubbed “the Miracle of Mudgee” – the Raiders pulled off a win so exciting that Cooper Cronk on Fox Sports declared it “the most remarkable finish to a golden-point game I have ever witnessed.”

Penrith halfback Nathan Cleary tried to win the game in extra time, but his field-goal attempt struck an upright. Raiders winger Jed Stuart grabbed the bouncing ball and passed it to Ethan Strange, who bolted 70 metres upfield and fed Kaeo Weekes in support to score the sensational match-winning try (see video below).

A man is in a stable but serious condition after an alleged stabbing attack in the Perth CBD on Friday night left the victim requiring surgery. Police are investigating. Peter de Kruijff According to WA Police, a group of males, understood to be known to each other, were involved in an altercation outside a café near Brookfield Place on St Georges Terrace at around 11.15pm on Friday night. A police spokesperson said that during the incident, it is alleged that a man in his 30s was stabbed in the back. “About 11.50pm, the victim arrived at the Royal Perth Hospital emergency department in a white Toyota Corolla hatchback,” the spokesperson said.



“Two males assisted the injured man into the emergency department before immediately leaving the area. “The victim sustained life-threatening injuries and underwent emergency surgery at Royal Perth Hospital.” The victim is understood to be recovering in the hospital’s state trauma unit. Perth Detectives are seeking the public’s assistance with information as they investigate. In a separate incident on Friday, Joondalup Detectives have charged a 15-year-old male after a ride-share driver was the alleged victim of a spray attack.



A WA police spokesperson said that about 12:00pm, the teenager and a second male were collected from an address in Balga by a ride-share vehicle. “It will be alleged once inside the ride-share vehicle, the two males made threats towards the ride-share driver, before the 15-year-old male brandished OC spray,” they said. “The ride-share driver drove to service station on Canham Way in Greenwood and exited the vehicle. “It will be further alleged the 15-year-old male followed the driver out of the vehicle and sprayed him with OC spray.” The two males are understood to have then left the area on foot.



WA Police said the 15-year-old male was located at an address in Balga a short time later and taken into custody. He has since been charged with one count of made a threat to unlawfully do an act and one count of cause poison to be administered. The teenager was also charged with one count of aggravated armed robbery, in addition to a charge of attempted to steal motor vehicle. The second male remains outstanding and WA Police are seeking assistance to locate his whereabouts.

World.title: Answer in 10 seconds or lose your fleet: The e-bike row dividing Yarra
World.content:
An inner-Melbourne community group is defending the world’s largest e-bike operator, claiming the company was “set up to fail” before a local council tore up its years-long deal. City of Yarra councillors earlier this month voted against endorsing a permanent e-bike hire contract with American-headquartered hiring company Lime, rubbishing their pitch and terminating an almost six-year trial. Streets Alive Yarra president Jeremy Lawrence has been highly critical of the council’s approach to e-bike operators. Luis Enrique Councillors criticised the operator’s unwillingness to clean up dumped vehicles or punish unruly riders at a July 14 council meeting, saying Lime made millions of dollars from local trips during the trial, while the council didn’t see a cent. Lime’s Asia-Pacific head Will Peters has since derided accusations about lacklustre penalties as “absolutely untrue” – and questioned why local governments have the power to ban e-bikes in the first place.



“This is not for a council to make a decision on willy-nilly,” Peters told this masthead. Jeremy Lawrence, president of local active transport advocacy group Streets Alive Yarra, said excessive financial and operational requirements sought by Yarra Council in its tender specifications meant that even a major e-bike provider was “set up to fail”. Lawrence spoke at the July 14 council meeting in favour of awarding Lime the tender. “In my view, it was so onerous [that] no share bike operator, even if it was Lime … could make it work in a financially viable manner,” Lawrence said.



The tender asked e-bike companies to cover all council’s costs for a permanent shared e-bike scheme without specifying or estimating what those costs would be, Lawrence said, adding that it was “absurd”. Related Article City life ‘Taking the mickey’: Inner-city council tears up e-bike deal Operators were also required to relocate “dangerously placed” e-bikes within 30 minutes of a complaint, according to the tender. Faulty or otherwise inappropriately parked bikes were required to be moved within an hour. “Even if you have a really rich, wealthy, profitable share bike operator … it’s just not realistic to scale across the municipality with those type of restrictions,” Lawrence said. Lime took particular issue with the tender’s requirement to answer all phone calls from members of the public within 10 seconds, 24/7 – similar to NSW Ambulance performance target to answer Triple Zero calls, Peters said.



The tender threatened e-bike operators would be fined $5000 the first time they failed to answer a call in this timeframe, and then $10,000 penalties for every further breach in the same month. Their local e-bike fleet, capped at 250, would also be cut by 20 per cent with every consecutive breach in a month. Head of Lime Asia-Pacific, William Peters, in 2025. Nick Moir Lime asked the council to amend the tender contract before the company was knocked back. “You could actually get a person who did not support active transport, or did not like this at all, with no reasons, calling up three times”, Peters said.



“If we did not pick up that phone call in 10 seconds, [and] you do that three times, 20 per cent of the fleet’s gone. “No other applicant applied to this tender. I think that, in itself, says enough.” A City of Yarra spokesperson said that the tender requirements addressed issues that were frequently brought forward by residents. They emphasised that a permeant contract would be awarded only if it did not place a burden on the community, either financial or in terms of accessibility. Yarra sought to ensure that the program would be “cost neutral to council as a minimum”. “Given the small overall size of Yarra … 30 minutes is appropriate for an operator that is sufficiently resourced to move a bike,” the spokesperson said.



“E-bikes obstructing footpaths and causing other hazards are not an acceptable to our community.” Lime maintained that it punished riders effectively, using a staged process and ultimately banned those who repeatedly parked poorly. The company was always going to agree to zero cost to council for an e-bike scheme, but instead faced the “sad” reality riders around Melbourne would be geo-fenced, Peters said. “They’re instantly going to go through a red line that no one knew existed, which is a council LGA, because people decided they had a vendetta against e-bikes,” he said. “We never dreamt of councils doing this for e-bikes … There has to be a statewide approach here.”



Lime was yet to receive feedback on the tender – only confirmation its e-bike trial was terminated – but wanted to keep working with council to find a solution for Yarra, Peters said. The council, too, hasn’t ruled out a future shared e-bike scheme with another operator. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: AFL Live: Australia make a statement against Ireland in history-making clash; injury carnage overshadows Swans’ win over Saints
World.content:
Sydney have overrun the brave Saints to win by 19 points at Marvel Stadium during an afternoon of injury mayhem that saw a 42-minute final quarter.

Play was suspended during the last term after Sydney defender Will Edwards suffered a badly broken ankle in a marking contest. He required a green whistle for pain relief and was taken from the ground on a motorised cart.

William Edwards is taken from the ground with a broken leg. via Getty Images

Not long after, Jack Silvagni had to be helped from the field in pain with a dislocated shoulder.

Sydney also lost James Rowbottom with a broken hand in the first term, while St Kilda superstar Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera spent time off the ground with a hip ailment and teammate Tom De Koning needed treatment for a hamstring concern.

Jack Silvagni leaves the ground with a dislocated shoulder. via Getty Images

The Swans kicked the first two goals of the game, but then trailed by nine points at quarter time, 13 points at half-time and 12 points at the final break as St Kilda dominated possession and Wanganeen-Milera booted three goals.

But with the St Kilda midfielder clearly hampered in the final term, finishing the game out as a forward, Sydney’s midfielders went on a rampage and the Swans kicked seven last-quarter goals to St Kilda’s two. They won 16.11 (107) to St Kilda’s 13.10 (88).

“These guys are really physical,” Swans star Isaac Heeney told Fox Footy after the game. “I found out the hard way in the guts there, and a few of the boys came off not that great, unfortunately.

“So hopefully, Rowy’s OK. I think he has broken the middle bone, so hopefully it is a pretty quick turn around. And then, Will, poor fella, that was one of the grosser ones I have seen, so hopefully he can bounce back pretty quick. But he’s been outstanding for us.”

Play was stopped for 10 minutes while medical staff attended 23-year-old Edwards for what appeared to be a compound fracture.

He did not make his AFL debut until this year after a serious leg infection and then a broken leg threatened his career.

World.title: Teen on bail charged with dealing drugs, weapons
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Teen on bail charged with dealing drugs, weapons Carla Jaeger August 1, 2026 — 5:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A teenager allegedly linked to Melbourne gangland boss Kaz Hamad’s crew known as The Commission is accused of dealing meth and firearms while already on bail for other offences. Rivin Muthucumarana, 19, from Fraser Rise, was charged on Saturday with a series of drug and firearm trafficking offences the day after his arrest after a series of police raids. Operation Eclipse detectives executed the raids as part of an ongoing investigation into one of the suspected orchestrators of Melbourne’s so-called bar wars. “The investigation commenced in April of this year when police received intelligence in relation to drug and firearms trafficking linked to an offshore syndicate leader,” police said. Officers seized quantities of suspected cocaine, methamphetamine and ecstasy during the co-ordinated searches of a Keilor Downs business and homes in Port Melbourne and Fraser Rise.





His lawyer, Seda Kilic, said it was her client’s first time in custody. She noted that Muthucumarana has a knee injury and has recently injured his neck. A bail application might be made at a later date, Kilic said. The Commission is the dominant force controlling Australia’s multibillion-dollar illicit tobacco market and large-scale drug importations. Hamad’s gang, also known as the 313, has been linked to dozens of other violent attacks, including shootings and murders. Operation Eclipse, originally formed in April to investigate the violent rampage targeting Melbourne’s nightlife, is now dedicated to dismantling The Commission’s extensive crime network.



Related Article Exclusive

Crime Nightclub promoter believed to be intended target of botched kidnapping The tobacco kingpin – described by two police sources as “one of the world’s most dangerous men” – was sentenced to life in prison by Iraqi authorities this week. In his place, 23-year-old Ali al-Huseini took control of the command structure of the 313s. According to five police and underworld sources, Huseini is one of two gunmen who ambushed Suleiman “Sam” Abdulrahim outside Fawkner cemetery and shot him eight times in 2022. The then-18 year old fled to Iraq less than a day after the shooting, which Abdulrahim survived. Since Hamad’s arrest, Huseini is alleged by police to have been the prime mover in the resumption of violence in the tobacco market and more than 40 attacks waged against bar and nightclub owners and promoters since March. Luis Enrique Councillors criticised the operator’s unwillingness to clean up dumped vehicles or punish unruly riders at a July 14 council meeting, saying Lime made millions of dollars from local trips during the trial, while the council didn’t see a cent. Lime’s Asia-Pacific head Will Peters has since derided accusations about lacklustre penalties as “absolutely untrue” – and questioned why local governments have the power to ban e-bikes in the first place.



“This is not for a council to make a decision on willy-nilly,” Peters told this masthead. Jeremy Lawrence, president of local active transport advocacy group Streets Alive Yarra, said excessive financial and operational requirements sought by Yarra Council in its tender specifications meant that even a major e-bike provider was “set up to fail”. Lawrence spoke at the July 14 council meeting in favour of awarding Lime the tender. “In my view, it was so onerous [that] no share bike operator, even if it was Lime … could make it work in a financially viable manner,” Lawrence said.



The tender asked e-bike companies to cover all council’s costs for a permanent shared e-bike scheme without specifying or estimating what those costs would be, Lawrence said, adding that it was “absurd”. Related Article City life ‘Taking the mickey’: Inner-city council tears up e-bike deal Operators were also required to relocate “dangerously placed” e-bikes within 30 minutes of a complaint, according to the tender. Faulty or otherwise inappropriately parked bikes were required to be moved within an hour. “Even if you have a really rich, wealthy, profitable share bike operator … it’s just not realistic to scale across the municipality with those type of restrictions,” Lawrence said. Lime took particular issue with the tender’s requirement to answer all phone calls from members of the public within 10 seconds, 24/7 – similar to NSW Ambulance performance target to answer Triple Zero calls, Peters said.



The tender threatened e-bike operators would be fined $5000 the first time they failed to answer a call in this timeframe, and then $10,000 penalties for every further breach in the same month. Their local e-bike fleet, capped at 250, would also be cut by 20 per cent with every consecutive breach in a month. Head of Lime Asia-Pacific, William Peters, in 2025. Nick Moir Lime asked the council to amend the tender contract before the company was knocked back. “You could actually get a person who did not support active transport, or did not like this at all, with no reasons, calling up three times”, Peters said.



“If we did not pick up that phone call in 10 seconds, [and] you do that three times, 20 per cent of the fleet’s gone. “No other applicant applied to this tender. I think that, in itself, says enough.” A City of Yarra spokesperson said that the tender requirements addressed issues that were frequently brought forward by residents. They emphasised that a permeant contract would be awarded only if it did not place a burden on the community, either financial or in terms of accessibility. Yarra sought to ensure that the program would be “cost neutral to council as a minimum”. “Given the small overall size of Yarra … 30 minutes is appropriate for an operator that is sufficiently resourced to move a bike,” the spokesperson said.



“E-bikes obstructing footpaths and causing other hazards are not an acceptable to our community.” Lime maintained that it punished riders effectively, using a staged process and ultimately banned those who repeatedly parked poorly. The company was always going to agree to zero cost to council for an e-bike scheme, but instead faced the “sad” reality riders around Melbourne would be geo-fenced, Peters said. “They’re instantly going to go through a red line that no one knew existed, which is a council LGA, because people decided they had a vendetta against e-bikes,” he said. “We never dreamt of councils doing this for e-bikes … There has to be a statewide approach here.”



Lime was yet to receive feedback on the tender – only confirmation its e-bike trial was terminated – but wanted to keep working with council to find a solution for Yarra, Peters said. The council, too, hasn’t ruled out a future shared e-bike scheme with another operator. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Silver Ferns face England in netball semis
World.content:

Previously, netball gold had been split between Australia and New Zealand, before the Ferns were shockingly ousted from the podium at Gold Coast 2018 and had to settle for bronze at Birmingham.

Unbeaten through pool play, they face England in the semifinals, as they try to return to the gold-medal game at Glasgow.

World.title: Four in custody after staff assaulted, haul of perfume taken, at Hamilton store, police say
World.content:
Police responding to a report of a perfume heist say they quickly were able to quickly "sniff out" the leads and detain four young people.

Just before 2pm on Saturday, Hamilton police were called to a report that staff at a store at The Base shopping centre "had been assaulted and thousands of dollars' worth of perfume had been taken," a Police bulletin said.

"No weapons were used, nor were there any injuries."

Senior Sergeant Pete Simpson said officers who responded were given details about the possible identity of the suspects, and video captured by a person at the scene.

By 2:25pm on Saturday, officers had found "a bag full of the stolen items" at a nearby address, Simpson said.

Four young people were taken into custody, and are expected to appear in court on robbery charges next week.

World.title: Two new Auckland stations part of $2.4b rail spend
World.content:
Two new railway stations in South Auckland are among the final elements of a $2.4 billion government investment in Auckland's network, Minister for Auckland Simon Watts says.

He was speaking at the formal opening on Saturday of the Drury and Paerātā stops.

The stations will serve Drury, Paerātā, Franklin and South Auckland, with each station providing two platforms, 350 car parks and bus connections.

Services begin stopping at the new stations on Sunday. During the week, peak trains will run every 10 minutes.

Rail Minister Winston Peters at the opening of the new Drury station. RNZ / Pretoria Gordon

Other speakers at the opening were Rail Minister Winston Peters, KiwiRail chief metro officer Bevan Assink and Franklin ward councillor Andy Baker.

Watts said that while much of the recent investment in the rail network had been about preparing for the opening of the CRL, "the extension of the overhead electrification from Papakura to Pukekohe and these new train stations represent something more".

"Trains stopping at Drury and Paerātā stations from tomorrow and Ngākōroa station when it opens next year will help open up this part of Auckland.

"Around 130,000 more people are expected to be in the southern part of Auckland over the next three decades. More than 40,000 new homes are expected to be built, a new hospital in Drury, a number of new schools, new roads, including in time the Mill Road extension.

"For locals, it means ... being part of an Auckland that is properly connected to the rest of the city... It will give people greater confidence to move to this part of Auckland, knowing that they will not be reliant on their cars, and overall it's a great choice about where people live and how they get around," Watts said.

Auckland's new Paerātā railway station. RNZ / Pretoria Gordon

KiwiRail's Bevan Assink gave the gathering some project numbers - 6500 cubic metres of concrete; 600 tonnes of locally sourced steel; 25,000 cubic metres of material moved to make way for the facilities.

"We've also planted around 40,000 trees and everything to beautify the area. Also there were 22 apprenticeships that were able to be enacted as part of this project and also 32 local companies were also involved in the project as well.

"So it just shows how broad and vast-reaching these projects can be in supporting the communities and everything around them," Assink said.

Franklin ward's Andy Baker told a story of two girls, aged 11 and 12, writing to him in 2011 to ask if Drury could get a railway station.

"They had done a petition here in Drury. They had hundreds and hundreds of signatures about wanting a park and ride and a station at Drury.

"One of those girls is here today - my daughter ... she may have had some egging on ... the other, the 11-year-old at the time ... is now an emergency doctor at Christchurch Hospital, so time has moved on.

"I did promise Emma it would be built before she left high school, which was 2015, but we haven't quite made that.

"But it shows that there's been a demand for this type of infrastructure in this area for a very, very long time. It is fantastic to see it today," Baker said.

RNZ / Pretoria Gordon

Rail Minister Peters echoed Watts' figure of 130,000 more people expected in the area over coming decades "and infrastructure must come before growth - not years afterwards, as too often happens in this country".

"These stations are here because we funded them when last responsible for rail, as part of our wider commitments to unlock capacity, lift train frequencies, invest more than $500 million to get the network up to standard, and enable electric trains from Britomart right down to Pukekohe.

"While others say nice words about rail, we fund it, deliver it, and on this happy occasion are still here to open it.

"We will keep advocating for rail because taxpayers have built an asset with real potential to move people and goods efficiently - and we intend to make full use of it."

In an earlier statement, Transport Minister Chris Bishop said the stations were among the final elements of a $2.4 billion government investment in Auckland's rail network.

"The Auckland Rail Network Rebuild has been completed in time for the City Rail Link to open soon. We're also replacing level crossings across the network to support more frequent train services.

"The Third Main Line is now open, separating freight and passenger rail services, while the rail line to Pukekohe has been electrified. Looking ahead, new rail stations at Ngākōroa are also set to open in 2027.

The work was about investing in infrastructure "that would help our largest city to grow".

World.title: 5.2 magnitude quake strikes near Te Anau
World.content:
Te Anau has been hit by a magnitude 5.2 earthquake, just a week after being jolted by a 5.9.

The latest quake, at 3:23pm on Saturday, was centred 35 kilometres north-west of the town at a depth of 102 kilometres, GeoNet said.

Felt reports showed more than 1400 people felt the shaking, mostly in the lower South Island.

There were no immediate reports of damage.

On 25 July a magnitude 5.9 earthquake struck 40 kilometres north of Te Anau, sparking a brief tsunami warning and an evacuation notice for some areas of the West Coast, which was later cancelled.

On Friday night, a magnitude 4.6 quake jolted the lower North Island and upper South at 11:09pm. It was centred 30 kilometres offshore, north-west of Porirua at a depth of 38 kilometres, and more than 8900 people logged Felt Reports.

GeoNet scientist Jonathan Hanson said New Zealand has been living up to its Shaky Isles reputation. While it had been a busy few weeks in terms of earthquakes, overall it was not unusual.

There are typically 15 to 20 magnitude five events in the country every year, but having a couple approaching magnitude six in a month is less common.

"These deep earthquakes are typically widely felt," GeoNet wrote on Facebook on Saturday afternoon.

World.title: Rising shop violence demands stronger penalties: Retail NZ
World.content:
Retailers need stronger powers to protect staff and customers from violent repeat offenders, Retail NZ says, amid reports of rapidly escalating aggression.

The Justice Select Committee is recommending by majority that The Trespass Amendment Bill be passed into law.

The bill would give retailers the power to trespass people from multiple sites, double fines to $2000 and increase the maximum trespass period to three years.

Retail NZ chief executive Carolyn Young said violence in stores was on the rise, with people becoming more agitated and entering businesses with concealed weapons.

"They will come in with knives, with hammers, with screwdrivers, with machetes ... Some stores within their stores sell things that can be turned into a weapon ... People will come in to a hardware store and use things on their shelves to threaten staff to be able to steal goods or do harm to people," she said.

"We have also seen guns that have been presented in certain circumstances, and all of those things mean that it's not a safe environment for staff members or customers."

Young said clear guidance would be needed to ensure new powers were used appropriately.

'Not convinced' - Labour and Greens

Opposition parties have raised concerns about the proposed changes, while questioning if harsher penalties would work as an effective deterrent to retail crime.

Labour said that despite some improvements to the bill, it remained concerned about the proposed scope of multi-location trespass notices.

"We remain concerned that there will be situations when vulnerable individuals may be unable to access essential goods and services due to the scope of these notices.

"We are also not convinced that the increase in penalties will act as an effective deterrent and consider there are other policies that may more effectively address the drivers of crime," it said.

The Green Party said it did not support the bill and remained concerned that the increase in fines from $1000 to $2000 would be "unrealistic" for offenders, who often resorted to retail crime as a result of the cost-of-living crisis.

"It is important that we have the right balance between clarity for retail stores and safety of retail employees and owners. However, we do not believe this will result in the expected effect of deterrence for retail crime," it said.

World.title: Queenstown mayor wants ideas on relieving traffic snarls
World.content:
An influx of tourists is causing massive traffic problems across the Wakatipu Basin, the mayor of the Queenstown-Lakes District says.

The council was setting up a mayoral taskforce on reducing congestion, Mayor John Glover said.

"Our state highway networks are really struggling to cope at peak times ... we are seeing some significant gridlock.

"A drive that probably would have taken 10 minutes at times is taking 90 minutes," he said.

The gridlock was prompting complaints on social media. Those living in new housing developments were struggling to get on to the state highway as well.

"We actually need some traffic control to wave people through in the right places so that traffic can keep flowing," Glover said.

"Maybe a bit of human intervention to keep things going at some of these junctions might do the job."

World.title: Police seek witnesses to fatal Hawke's Bay crash
World.content:
Police are turning to the public to find out what happened in a car crash that killed a 24-year-old woman in the Central Hawke's Bay last week.

On Saturday 25 July about 3pm, a silver Holden VX Commodore left the southbound lane of State Highway 2 near Ōtāne and crashed, killing Sonique Glodean Campbell, from Waipawa.

Two other occupants of the car are in a serious condition in hospital.

Police Senior Sergeant Craig Vining said police wanted to speak to anyone who may have seen the car on the day of the crash.

"We would like to hear from anyone who saw the vehicle or has dashcam footage of it travelling towards Ōtāne. This information will help us piece together how this happened," he said.

World.title: Funding for more local GPs to remove suspected skin cancer
World.content:
The government has announced funding for more local GP clinics to be able to remove suspected skin cancer.

Health Minister Simeon Brown said it's the first stage of a $23 million investment in community healthcare.

He said in some parts of the country, the only option to check and remove suspicious skin spots and moles is a long hospital wait or paying to go private.

"This first stage will build on the skin cancer services that already work well across the country, creating a nationally consistent approach to how this care is delivered."

The funding was set to go towards upskilling more GPs to offer skin cancer services, including training in dermoscopy, which uses a specialised magnifier to examine spots closely, and skin excision.

Brown said over time it would also include cataract follow-up with optometrists, symptomatic bowel cancer detection, and respiratory care.

"New Zealand has among the highest rates of melanoma in the world. Skin cancer is our most common cancer, and it is one of the most treatable, but only if it is caught early."

Brown highlighted this as a build on the $5 million the government invested last year to enhance general primary care services.

"This initiative means more New Zealanders will be able to have suspicious spots checked and removed sooner, without waiting for a hospital appointment or paying to go private.

World.title: Live: Irish star hurt as Aussies turn up heat, Swan suffers horror injury
World.content:
Nick Watson was at his menacing best with a career-best five goals in Hawthorn's win over North Melbourne. (Getty Images)

Nick Watson has kicked an equal career best five goals to keep Hawthorn firmly in the hunt for a top two spot with a 16-point win over a plucky North Melbourne.

The Hawks trailed by one point heading into the final quarter in Launceston on Saturday against an opposition needing a victory to boost their AFL finals hopes.

But they did enough to hold on for the 14.15 (99) to 12.11 (83) result, with Mabior Chol getting a crucial breathing-space goal at the back end of the game.

With his side ahead by 11 and less than six minutes on the clock, Chol earned a free kick with a tackle and then nailed a goal from about 50m out near the boundary line.

North cut the margin to 10 points with less than three minutes left thanks to Harry Sheezel but were left to rue several key misses in the fourth quarter.

Watson's haul gives him 52 goals for the season, putting him right in the hunt for the Coleman Medal.

Jai Newcombe was heavily involved and picked up a game-high 34 disposals, plus 12 clearances and one goal assist.

Hawthorn, which is two points behind Sydney in third, have won four in a row ahead of a blockbuster against reigning premiers Brisbane next Friday.

The Kangaroos have slumped to five losses on the trot and sit 13th on the ladder.

Hawthorn nabbed the opening goal of the game through Will Day before the Kangaroos got four straight for a 26-9 lead at the first break.

North Melbourne's Nick Larkey, who has struggled for accuracy in recent times, produced a shocking first shot but nailed his second from off centre.

Team mate Zac Banch squeezed one through from the goal square in the last minute of the first quarter to give his side a boost.

Hawthorn came to life early in the second with Watson, who only picked up one touch in the first term, getting three goals in a row including two in 60 seconds.

The lead then changed hands multiple times before a behind after the halftime buzzer to Chol levelled the scores at 46-46.

Watson fired again with two goals early in the third before a major to Chol broke the run of tit-for-tat scores as Hawthorn threatened to pull away.

But the Kangaroos rallied and Larkey's second gave his side a 69-68 lead heading into the final quarter.

AAP

World.title: Boxer earns Tuvalu's first ever Comm Games medal without winning fight
World.content:
A boxer from Tuvalu earned her tiny South Pacific nation's first ever Commonwealth Games medal without winning a fight overnight.

Tarona Taafaki lost her only bout in the women's 75-kilogram class to India's Lovlina Borgohain, losing every round on all three of the judges' cards.

Because there were only five entrants, Taafaki received a bye to the last four, meaning she was automatically guaranteed at least a bronze medal.

Tarona Taafaki arrives at the Commonwealth Games during the opening ceremony. (AP: Kin Cheung)

But her coach and father said the population of Tuvalu, an island south-east of Tonga, will celebrate the medal and use it to highlight a climate change emergency.

Badi Taafaki, whose son Pasoni competed earlier in the Games and lost his only bout at 70kg, told the British Press Association: "For the people of Tuvalu, this medal means everything.

"We're one of the smallest nations in the world, so a medal like this is hugely significant. We have worked so hard to get here. For me as a coach, it's a stepping stone."

Tarona and Pasoni are the two eldest of eight children, all of whom are boxers. They are based in New Zealand in order to take advantage of better facilities.

"My children are very fortunate," Badi said.

"They have opportunities and facilities that I never had. Boxing is our whole life. Strength is in our bloodline."

Athletes on the island famously train on its airport runway, the most stable land mass on an island increasingly threatened by rising sea levels. Climate experts predict half of the nation's capital, Funafuti, could be submerged by 2050.

A group of locals play volleyball on the airport runway in Funafuti, Tuvalu. (Getty Images: Fiona Goodall)

"Yes, we train on the airport runway," Badi said. "When a plane comes in, everyone moves aside. As soon as it leaves, we go back on the tarmac, because there is nowhere else to train.

"If we can win medals, more people around the world will recognise Tuvalu and begin to understand the challenges we face because of climate change.

"It is very real for us. The coastal erosion is unbelievable, and the countdown is now measured in years, not decades. Some islands have lost half their land. At high tide the sea comes right through. People living on the coast can't sleep if there's a storm, because the waves can come straight through their homes."

Tarona is not the first boxer to win a Commonwealth Games medal without winning a fight. Australia's Taylah Robertson picked up a bronze in the women's flyweight category on the Gold Coast in 2018 despite losing her bout to England's Lisa Whiteside.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.
